PROLOGUE
BORROWED TIME
Another explosion rocked the metro.
Marzanna stumbled to her knees. “Seventy -seven, still
running. I’ll never get used to it.”
“Countin’ years or bodies, Marz? Move, or you won’t make
seventy-eight.” Klara hooked both hands under her arms and
dragged her upright. Marzanna’s knees cracked as her weight
came down on them.
“Easy. These legs are new.”
New enough to belong to a woman thirty years younger. The
morning dose hadn’t finished taking hold. Each stride still
CHAPTER ONE
DUNYA
Pale morning light pressed through Dunya’s lashes. She
blinked, dragging herself out of sleep. The dream fell away in
fragments, except for a dark bird flashing violet as it circled a
tree whose branches had closed over the sky. The bird passed
the same br anch again and again, fading as the room
sharpened around her. Muscles heavy, she stretched until her
knuckles bumped the VR headgear half -buried in the sheets
beside her. She nudged it away and worked her fingers
through a snarl of ginger hair turned wild by the night.
Her arms sank back into the rumpled sheets while she
CHAPTER TWO
MARIA
The only sound in the room was the low hum of the exposed
electrical box, a dull counterpoint to the pounding in Maria’s
temples. She sat up slowly, disoriented, muscles aching,
fragments of the failed simulation still spinning in her mind.
The cold, metallic taste of regret lingered on her tongue. She
longed for a simplicity she could no longer recall,  a time that
might never have existed. Back when her world had been
defined by clean execution, commands completed, objectives
met. The upgrades had taken that from her. Each new
iteration pulled her further from that clarity, burying her in
CHAPTER THREE
VESNA
The faint creak of the foyer door jolted Vesna awake. She
could barely tell if the sound was real or if it lingered from a
dream. Then it came again : footsteps. She’s never this quiet,
even when she’s late.
Vesna slid her hand under her pillow, fingers flinching at
the cool metal of her gun. She rose from her bed with the grace
of a snow leopard , careful to lift the blankets without a
whisper of sound. Then down the hallway she crept, gun held
in a two -handed grip and peered around the corner into the
living room.
CHAPTER FOUR
ZAKHAROVNA
In the hushed bowels of her laboratory, the rhythmic hum
of broken machinery played a somber symphony for an
audience of one.
Doctor Anastasia Zakharovna moved between the benches.
She caught herself in the mirrored walls as she passed, thin
and severe, her frost -white hair set like a crown. Coolant
spread in silver sheets beneath her boots, threaded with pale
fungal lace from the ruptured seals.
Incubators sat dark. Glass tubes gaped open. Nutrient vats
stood empty, their inner walls filmed with dead mycelium and
CHAPTER FIVE
YANA
“CAN MONEY BUY HAPPINESS?”
“Friggin yeah.”
The exchange boomed from the open-mic stage beyond the
laserfall, followed by a burst of laughter. Bass and chatter
spilled into the damp entrance corridor. It felt like half the
peninsula had squeezed into The Flock on a Monday evening
to drown their troubles in neon and cheap burn.
Yana stood in the vestibule, shifting light washing over her
skin in quick flashes of blue and pink. She didn’t usually come
here on open -mic nights. The crowd always struck her as
CHAPTER SIX
VESNA
“Vesna.”
The voice seeped into her dreams like a dagger ’s edge,
slicing through her attempts to ignore it. Relentless, the voice
would not be silenced.
“Wake up.”
The sensation of a hand shaking her shoulder stirred her
from sleep. She opened her eyes to find Zakharovna looming
over her.
“What happened?” Vesna asked, voice still thick with sleep.
“You hit your head when you fell, ” Zakharovna replied.
CHAPTER SEVEN
YELENA
The Grand Mariner’s Cathedral rose from the heart of Gred,
its stone and glass cutting into the winter sky. From the
boardroom chamber high in the tower, Pra Matron Yelena
Petrova watched the city beneath her. Birch trees sagged
under snow, their branches rattling as hail clouds pressed low
above the spires. The streets lay muted, smoke rising thin
from the Derge, life clinging on where it could.
The irony was not lost on her. In a world that had banished
old faiths, the cathedral still ruled the skyline, its shadows
falling over a city built on contradictions. Dreamt by men who
CHAPTER EIGHT
DUNYA
Dunya crossed the quad, her wheelchair’s tires whispering
over the concrete. Students loitered beneath the Temple of
Gamayun, whose stone wings enclosed a laurel wreath with
all the subtlety of a state seal.
Vesna had been gone for days. Dunya’s messages showed
delivered and nothing else. Yana had stopped replying too.
Two dead channels made a pattern, and patterns were
supposed to be Dunya’s thing.
Had she pushed too hard? Probably. She had once sat
through an Arkyv therapy module about personal boundaries
CHAPTER NINE
KLARA
The Derge had once tried to rival Gred, prosperous and
loud, its markets packed with traders, repair stalls, and
engine smoke. Now it sat on the horizon as a ruin, a nest of
outlaws and scavengers tearing each other apart over scraps
of metal and warmth. T he approach was worse, a corridor of
dead haulers, cracked pylons, and ice -swallowed road
markers. She pushed through the elfin cedar and waist -deep
snow, each drift collapsing under her weight with a muffled
groan. The cold gnawed through her coat, sharp and familiar.
It was the same kind of cold that had nearly killed her once.
CHAPTER TEN
VESNA
Something was building, low and steady, and Vesna wasn’t
sure she’d come back from it. The machines surrounded her
with a slow, resonant hum that worked its way into her chest.
Light shifted across the walls in fluid motion, the colors
folding into one another like waves. She kept her hands on the
armrests, resisting the urge to move, to break the rhythm that
held the room together.
Nadya drifted through the glow, her fingers shaping quick
commands that scattered the colors into new patterns. She
glanced back with a measured calm. “Nervous?”
CHAPTER ELEVEN
YANA
Yana tossed back another shot of spudka, the authentic
burn igniting her throat like wildfire. She was surprised they
even served it here—real spudka meant someone, somewhere,
was growing potatoes off the record —but she embraced it. It
was her third in as many minutes, and the barroom’s edges
started to smudge and blend. But that didn’t matter. She only
craved the numbing embrace of oblivion. Cheap alc ohol was
better than cheap synth, she mused. After all, what’s a fat
liver to a fried brain? As she chased the burn with memories
that haunted her, she couldn’t help but wonder if she’d ever
CHAPTER TWELVE
ZAKHAROVNA
In the greasy light of a Vilnius night, they lingered beneath
flickering neon, faces rippling in the reflected glow. Rain fell
steady, never enough to wash the city clean. The scent of
seared fat and cigarette haze hung heavy, settling deep into
coats and hair. Zakharovna moved through it as if she
belonged there. These streets had shaped her, every alley and
doorway etched into memory. The mingled reek of meat and
exhaust was the perfume of a city that never stopped feeding
on itself.
Between lab sessions, she drifted to the brothels. They had
CHAPTER THIRTEEN
VESNA
It had been Nadya who first introduced her to Marfa and
Gala. “They’re the best we have from the University’s training
program,” Nadya had said flatly. Vesna had been skeptical at
first, fresh from the rigorous combat sims. She was still
adjusting to the fact that she would soon be leading flesh-and-
blood soldiers again.
Nadya had assured her of their physical and mental
readiness, listing their records as if they were gospel. Marfa,
the detonations expert, could supposedly dismantle any
explosive device. Gala, meanwhile, was a prodigy with the
CHAPTER FOURTEEN
MARIA
Maria breathed into the frigid air as she surveyed the
warehouse. The outskirts of Gred had always whispered of a
forlorn past, but here in the shadows of this dilapidated
structure, the whispers roared. This was a place forgotten by
time, remembered only by those who danced with danger.
Tatyana’s instructions had been clear, a stark command
that cut through the haze of Maria ’s thoughts. “Trust in the
skills that have kept you alive. Serafim is a tool; use her.”
Maria replayed Tatyana ’s warning in her mind as she
stepped carefully over the scattered debris on the warehouse
The higher they climbed, the less time behaved. Minutes
stretched, folded, and snapped forward without warning.
Maria stopped trying to measure the ascent and counted
doors instead.
As they ascended further, the walls became lined with
mirrors, each reflecting a different chapter of Maria’s life. Are
these mirrors throwing back Serafim ’s demons  too, or is she
getting a rerun of my mess ? Maria couldn’t tell; Serafim had
been silent for what felt like days, her thoughts shielded
behind an impenetrable front.
Maria saw herself in various interactions with Zakharovna,
glimpses of a life repeatedly segmented by uploads and
CHAPTER FIFTEEN
DUNYA
The doors to the Grand Mariner’s Cathedral loomed over
her. Dunya paused beneath them, tracing the joints where the
panels met, too precise for human work. Of course, they
weren’t. In the Arkyv, she had studied the Aquilonian
Pantheon, raised on the ruins of older temples by hands that
never worshiped there. A society that thought its monuments
eternal, blind to the labor buried beneath them. The thought
lingered as she rested her palm against the door, the chill
seeping into her skin and settling somewhere deeper, where
memory and doubt met. The wood was coarse and cold, the
CHAPTER SIXTEEN
KLARA
As the memory of the blizzard faded, Klara pressed on
through the Derge’s endless white. The wind clawed at her
hood and the snow hissed beneath her boots. She knew the
price of survival, had paid it more than once, and would pay
it again if she had to. Not dying isn’t the same as living,  she
thought, lifting her flask and taking a long pull of spiced
brandy. She had learned that lesson in field tents long before
she ever learned how to kill.  The burn steadied her, a small,
defiant flame against the cold.
The western snow lay heavier than in the east, its false
Klara was their leader, their deliverer. And leaders, she was
learning, didn’t get to choose clean victories.  Together, they
would reshape the world. But as the noise of celebration faded
into twilight, a chill settled in her heart. Victory was on the
horizon, but what would it cost them in the end? The road
ahead would be long and fraught with regret, and she kne w
the war had only just begun.
CHAPTER SEVENTEEN
VESNA
It happened faster than Vesna expected. One moment, the
battlefield was a chaotic storm of railgun fire and explosions.
The next, a pulse —quiet, invisible—rippled through the air,
CHAPTER EIGHTEEN
ZAKHAROVNA
The sun’s rays crested the rooftops, glinting off the frost -
laden windows as the cold bit at her skin. Anastasia exhaled,
watching her breath rise in a pale mist as she meandered
along the riverbank, shivering beneath her thick polyester
coat and gloves. She longed for the warmth that spring would
bring. In the meantime, h er boots crunched on the snow as
she crossed the bridge and climbed the icy steps.
The cobblestone path wound up a hill, past dormant
fountains and slumbering gardens. Anastasia navigated the
twisting route, slipping past dog walkers, amorous couples,
CHAPTER NINETEEN
YELENA
Blanka flipped her pale gold hair, the borrowed earrings
twinkling golden in the light. “They somehow look better on
me, don’t you think?”
Daria looked at her with a playful edge to her voice. “Wishful
thinking, Blanka. They ’re meant for someone a little more
petite.”
Blanka laughed heartily. “Well, better wear them now. In
ten years, my ears might be too grand for any jewelry at all!”
Daria fanned herself, a smirk on her face.  “Honey, unlike
some, I plan to age with grace. But do keep the earrings. By
CHAPTER TWENTY
MARIA
Maria surfaced slowly, the cube’s hum and the terminal’s
faint whir pulling her back from the dive. She drew a long
breath, letting the digital after-images fade. Gaspar’s claim to
know her location nagged at her. Hack me? Good luck.
She checked the logs. No unauthorized traces. That was a
relief, though it wasn’t unexpected. The zk-SNARK layers were
still holding. If Gaspar had anything, he hadn’t shown it.
Beside her, Serafim lay under the headset. The glow traced
across her face, dark hair tugged loose where the interface
pulled. For a moment Maria almost thought she stirred, but
CHAPTER TWENTY ONE
DUNYA
“Where fire meets wood yet neither burn, your true quest will
take a turn.”
Dunya sat by the window, her ocular shimmering with the
cryptic riddle that had consumed her for the better part of the
day. She blinked twice to clear her vision, her gaze refocusing
on the cityscape beyond the glass. She’d made the call after a
long prayer at the cathedral, realizing then that she was being
watched but would not be detained.
Her last call kept replaying . Serafim had surfaced inside
Maria’s operation, and Dunya had responded by sending her
CHAPTER TWENTY TWO
VESNA
Vesna pulled herself from the training pits, feeling the
weight of fatigue with every step. Entering the locker room,
she made her way to the showers. She peeled off worn leather
gear—boots, jacket, gloves—letting them land haphazardly by
her locker. Reach ing for the faucet, she twisted it on and
stepped beneath the scalding spray, leaning into the contrast
of heat against the cool, mosaic -tiled wall. With every
movement and stretch, memories flared in the bruises, each
one a reminder of recent battles, her  body marked in deep
purples and angry reds.
CHAPTER TWENTY THREE
YANA
“Cigar?”
Grigoreva stood at the foot of the divan, a smoldering cigar
between her lips, tendrils of smoke rising from its tip.
Yana coughed. Her eyes watered as the acrid haze assaulted
her senses. She waved her hand, hoping to clear the air
enough to focus.
“An early indulgence, ” the Baroness mu ttered with a sly
grin, “but who could resist a taste of my White Canal? ” She
dangled the gilded Belomorkanal from her fingers, the base of
the cigar marked by the smudge of her lipstick. “Can I tempt
CHAPTER TWENTY FOUR
DUNYA
Dunya’s eyelids flickered open to the rhythm of ambulance
lights, painting her vision in splashes of primary colors. She
felt the cold press of a pill against her lips.
“Drink this, ” a voice commanded, like an echo from
somewhere far away.
“Why?” Dunya rasped. She knocked the hand away, the
clink of the pill hitting the gurney loud in her ears. Enough.
Every cell in her body recoiled at the thought of someone else
making choices for her. Her chest tightened.
“It’s for the pain,” the paramedic insisted, a fringe of worry
CHAPTER TWENTY FIVE
VESNA
The moment Vesna heard the news, she left the front line—
Goga Borisova, newly risen from technician to aspirant of the
Black Wolves, now stood at the helm. A flicker of doubt
brushed Vesna ’s mind, of whether Goga ’s greenness could
withstand the turmoil of command. But the urgent call
overshadowed all, pulling her to the crash scene  without
hesitation.
The landscape flew by in a disorienting rush as Vesna
neared the sirens’ wail. The ambulance lay on its side like a
toppled behemoth, its underbelly exposed to the night. The
CHAPTER TWENTY SIX
MARIA
Maria’s reflection flickered on the display ’s surface as she
willed it to life. The projection lit up, unveiling the newsreel
footage: a veil of smoke obscured the city’s skyline, and flames
roared with primal hunger as they consumed the dogwood
trees that had long stood sentinel along downtown
boulevards.
“The Coven,” Mayor Rylova declared, her voice cutting
through the crackle of the dying ember, “is behind these
atrocities. They ’re terrorists. And they will answer for their
crimes.”
CHAPTER TWENTY SEVEN
KLARA
The air shuddered inside the small chapel carved into the
wall of the Akhmatova Railways. Jagged stone framed a
weathered pine altar, and three sconces burned above it, their
flames wavering whenever the rails groaned deeper in the
earth. The room was packed with outlaws and cravens, eager
fires rousing inside them, straining to break free from mortal
bonds.
“Sisters and brothers,” Klara declared, “today marks a
critical juncture in our conflict. The Syndicate, that vile cartel
of politicians, soldiers, and scoundrels, has ruled with an iron
CHAPTER TWENTY EIGHT
TATYANA
Tatyana steadied her breath. Then, with a focused exhale,
she spoke, her voice firm as her eyes locked onto the camera
lens. “Citizens of Gred, this is Tatyana Romanova.”
She paused briefly, the weight of her own name settling in
her chest. “Chief of the Intelligence Bureau of our Military. Pra
Matron of the Battalion. And, if you stand with truth and
justice, your Chair of the Syndicate, your leader in Gred.”
She took another beat, letting the silence stretch. She
pictured the millions of eyes fixed on the projections
throughout the city, waiting for what would come next.
CHAPTER TWENTY NINE
DUNYA
Freezing stillness swallowed her. Limbs drifted, weightless,
and one thought kept pulsing like static:
Why am I still here? I wanted it all to end.
Vesna had gone silent. Maria had cut the line. Dugal was
dead. Different failure modes, same result: Dunya was alone
while everyone else still had a hand on the systems keeping
her alive.
Disposable, she thought. Useful until damaged, then routed
somewhere quiet.
Serafim’s voice surfaced in the dark, followed by the
CHAPTER THIRTY
ZAKHAROVNA
Beneath a slate-gray sky, where clouds hung motionless as
if painted, Zakharovna surveyed the horizon. Amid the ruins,
a network of fractured arches and splintered spires, stood the
remains of a massive cathedral, its dome collapsed. Encircling
it were the old birch trees, now charred in a forest turned to
coal.
Every detail of  the grove ’s destruction seemed eerily
preserved, as if by a sculptor ’s hand. Hovering beside Yelena
atop the remnants of what had been, Zakharovna noted the
stillness, a silence that outsilenced the absence of wind and
CHAPTER THIRTY ONE
DUNYA
The forest rang with their clash, claws raking, jaws
snapping, bodies crashing through soil and leaf litter. Growls
tore the silence until they broke into ragged gasps, each
movement slower than the last.
At dawn’s first light the frenzy faltered, giving way to a taut
stillness. Both stood battered, breaths dragging in the cold
morning air. Then Dunya lunged, closing the gap in a blur.
Her teeth locked at the wolf’s neck. A savage shake ended it.
Silence fell heavier than the fight itself.
The wolf lay still. No triumph came, only the hollow
CHAPTER THIRTY TWO
MARIA
The void pressed in on her, crimson light pulsing with each
beat of her heart. Every breath felt heavier, the air thick and
alive. Shapes rippled through the haze, gathering form until a
face emerged from the red, one she knew too well. Babushka.
The sight rooted her in place. Threads of shadow twisted into
a shawl that seemed to swallow the light around it.
It’s her. The thought came sharp and cold. The fear she ’d
kept buried stirred. Whatever this place was, it knew her. It
wanted her to remember.
“You’ve spent a lifetime dodging shadows, haven ’t you,
CHAPTER THIRTY THREE
DUNYA
Beep. Beep. Beep.
A sharp inhale tore through her, like breaking the surface
after too long underwater. Antiseptic filled her nose. Linen
scraped her skin. Beeps and whispers tangled with the last
howl of the forest before the white room forced itself into place.
Her eyes opened into hard white light. Prime Infirmary. The
monitor slowed as her breathing did.
The ceiling was cracked in the same places she
remembered. Real, then, or at least consistent enough to pass
a first check. The room pulled up the older failure
CHAPTER THIRTY FIVE
DUNYA
“Well, if it ain’t a motherfucker,” they hissed.
Serafim’s reaction was subtle but revealing. A slight flinch,
a tightening around the eyes.
Dimitra’s posture hit a nerve, scraping at old scars. That
readiness to crush, that cold edge, she knew it too well. Once,
people like that would have cornered her. Now she caught the
strain in Dimitra’s jaw, the forced detachment in Serafim’s
stance. They tried to hide the turmoil, but she saw through it.
She saw the shit beneath their skin.
“You owe me her freedom, Dimitra,” Serafim said. “Yana’s
CHAPTER THIRTY SIX
ZAKHAROVNA
The tranquil expanse of Lake Nachikinskoye lay before her,
its glassy surface reflecting the distant mountains, dense
forests, and hazy blue sky above. At the water ’s edge,
Zakharovna submerged her hand in the shallows, inhaling
deeply. Each ripple that spread from her touch reminded her
of Maria, of that fragmented part of her soul that she sought
to mend . She watched as those ripples  danced across the
surface, each one a silent echo of  thoughts swirling in her
mind.
In this secluded forest spot on her family’s ancestral lands,
CHAPTER THIRTY SEVEN
VESNA
“Where the hell have you been? ” Fury and worry clashed
within Vesna as she glared at Zakharovna  through the
projection.
“Evidently not where you expected me to be.”
“You drop off grid, leave chaos in your wake, and now you
stroll in like nothing’s happened?”
“A necessary disappearance. Chaos is, after all, part of the
greater pattern,” Zakharovna retorted, her tone measured and
cool.
“Design? There are Wolves who won ’t follow me because
CHAPTER THIRTY EIGHT
MARIA
Cold seeped through the thin sheet and settled in her
bones. The mattress wasn’t hers. Its weight and give felt off, a
slick dampness clinging to the fabric and turning her
stomach. The smell rose next, sour and heavy, like something
left to steep in its own humidity.
She drew a breath, expecting the familiar quiet hum of
orientation to meet her. Nothing answered. Only the rasp of
air through lungs that felt borrowed, and a body she wasn’t
sure would hold her if she tried to sit up.
She tried again, louder. “Help!”
CHAPTER THIRTY NINE
VESNA
The infantry  advanced in formation, each synchronized
step reflecting their discipline. A tide of gray uniforms and
faceless black visors  surged forward, cleaving the crowd
gathered outside the rally. As the people ’s exuberant cries
overpowered the speaker ’s voice, every soldier maintained
their stature, embodying the Syndicate’s new military and its
claim to power.
Soldiers or drones? Vesna wondered.
From her vantage point at the edge of the crowd, she
studied the precise, mechanical flow of their ranks, a sharp
CHAPTER FOURTY
YELENA
Bathed in the sterile chamber ’s pallid glow, Valentina’s
mutilated body lay tethered by fragile strands of viscera. Her
fingers, stiff, grasped at a life forever beyond her reach.
Yelena, rooted at the observation window, watched as each
breath she exhaled misted the glass. The moment of
Valentina’s death replayed in her mind like a record with a
skip, refusing to move forward. “They took her from me,” she
whispered to the quiet room.
Lev Rozhkov’s muffled response emanated through the
plastic mask concealing his face. “We will find her.” As Chief
CHAPTER FOURTY ONE
DUNYA
Word of Maria’s sentencing spread across the babachain
with the speed of rumor.
Dunya’s avatar appeared at the edge of The Town Square,
the Arkyv’s virtual heart, recast as a digital echo of Uritsky
Square. She wondered, as with everything in the Arkyv, if it’d
ever looked like this at all. The Summer Palace facade and the
Alexandra Column rose like ghostly monuments, framing a
space where avatars from every stream gathered to witness
Gred’s triumphs, and more often, its staged displays of power.
The Square throbbed with an unsettling energy. Simulated
CHAPTER FOURTY TWO
ZAKHAROVNA
The laboratory was her sanctuary of solitude, a world of
steel and glass lit by the soft glow of bioluminescent fungi that
clung to the shelves like otherworldly ornaments. Beneath the
sterile hum of the equipment, Zakharovna stood before a vat
containing her brother Alexei’s preserved head, a grim
keepsake and a wellspring of genetic material.
As Zakharovna’s gloved hands guided the pipette, drawing
out Alexei’s DNA-laced preservation fluid, her thoughts turned
to her brother. His bravery and idealism had carried him into
a sea of his own making, one of appeasement and passionate
CHAPTER FOURTY THREE
DATA ANGELS
Dunya met Serafim’s gaze, the bay window behind her
framing a silhouette against the sweep of the grounds. The
glass carried a faint reflection of Dunya’s own face, blurred,
as if she were already half gone.
“With the World Tree decrypted, we can branch into the
network, touch any mind linked within. It’s our path in, and
our only way out,” Serafim said.
The mansion pressed harder than its walls. Outside it was
wealth and fences. Inside, a sanctum for machines.  The
central chamber pulled her attention back again to the woman
CHAPTER FOURTY FOUR
ZAKHAROVNA
The city flickered past in brief, fractured glimpses through
the tinted glass, neon smears and hollow lights pulsing like
the last breath of nightlife. Zakharovna watched without
focus, her reflection shifting with every turn. The engine’s
hum steadied her thoughts, low and constant. Red light traced
along the cabin’s edges, casting her hands in muted warmth.
The scent of leather lingered, sharp beneath the sterile tang
of circuitry. It almost felt as if the car itself were straining to
imitate life.
Zakharovna reached for the crystal decanter and poured
CHAPTER FOURTY FIVE
YANA
Yana reclined against the bar, its sleek surface catching the
ambient glow of the surrounding art. Beside her, Dunya sat
in silence, watching the eclectic crowd from their quiet perch.
Avatars of every kind drifted past —scantily clad performers,
fantastical beasts, and playful animals —moving together
through the haze as Yana watched.
Off to one side, a popular meme caught her attention. It was
Zakharovna’s old sled dog, the one that had been at her side
during the first lectures on exo when she unveiled the
compound. Someone had brought it back as a zombie, and
CHAPTER FOURTY SIX
KIROV
The laboratory hummed with the soft, steady hisses of
bizarre machines, their fungal forms secreting plumes of
noxious gas and a gel of a sickly green hue. Bathed in muted
light, the machinery ’s uncanny contours threw haunting,
otherworldly shadows. Overhead, fireflies shimmered, casting
their radiant glow below like a false night sky full of stars.
Kirov always wondered if he could beam himself into the stars.
At the end of the central table, he stood, every inch the
guardian. His attention was drawn to the figure lying on the
table before him.
EPILOGUE
RAYNA
Rayna woke to four gray walls, one hard lamp, and cuffs
biting deep enough that her hands had gone numb.
I’m a woman, I’m strong, I’m in control. This hell will be
over. This isn’t real. Damn those crones to hell.
The interrogator’s voice still burned in her ear. “Boy,” the
woman had hissed, and then the old name: Rayan. Rayna
clenched her fists against the cuffs until pain cut through the
numbness.
They had spoken of a tide. A war. A bloodline. None of it
made sense. She did not belong in their deranged plot.

Foreword & Acknowledgements 
 
I came to the Croatian hinterlands during a strange season 
of my life, needing distance and not quite knowing what I was 
looking for. What was meant to be temporary stretched into 
three years among olive groves, stone houses, stubborn sheep, 
and the village my family came from. 
The quiet worked on me slowly. At first, I treated the place 
as a retreat. Then it became a kind of workshop, though I 
would not have called it that at the time. The days were long. 
There was room to think, maybe too much room, and 
eventually I started telling myself stories to fill the silence. 
One afternoon, while listening to my grandfather and his 
sisters trade stories, I was struck by how casually they spoke 
about hardship. War, hunger, displacement, illness, bad 
harvests, dead husbands, lost brothers. They talked about 
these things between jokes, coffee, and food, as if survival 
were less a grand achievement than a chore they had already 
finished and didn’t care to brag about. 
Somewhere in that conversation, the first absurd image 
arrived: old women who had endured everything, given steel 
bones and impossible weapons. 
I did not say this aloud. They would have looked at me like 
I needed medical attention. But the image stayed. 
In the company of my grandmother and a circle of great -
aunts, I found the heart of the book. They taught me that food 
was never just food. Sarma, lamb shanks, and bone broths 
filled the table, but they also carried memories of lean years, 
harvests, and fam ily gatherings. These meals were not 
symbols so much as proof that traditions survive because 
people keep cooking, arguing, laughing, and passing them on.

Around those tables I heard stories of the village, lessons 
about patience and endurance, and plenty of jokes sharp 
enough to draw blood. 
For obvious reasons, I did not set the actual story in our 
beloved Balkans. Their stories were remarkable, but I had a 
healthy fear of the outspoken baba brigade and, by proxy, the 
dreaded šiba, the conventional whacking stick I have been 
warned about sinc e childhood. That threat set clear 
boundaries for my creative liberties. 
Instead, I placed the story in Kamchatka, a distant and 
untamed landscape where I could let my imagination roam 
without quite feeling my hometown matriarchs watching over 
my shoulder. Time will tell whether I have trespassed on the 
talescape of the equally formidable babushkas and yllaapil, 
the Koryak grandmothers of that remote part of the world. 
Every land has its guardians. I can only hope they will forgive 
the intrusion. 
I was equally uncertain about how to write the book itself.  
Some writers are architects, mapping every beam before they 
raise the walls. Others are gardeners, scattering seeds and 
trusting something will grow. I never quite fit either approach. 
Writing Babushka felt closer to cooking goulash. I knew the 
pot I wanted to set on the table, but the taste came from 
whatever the babas tossed in when I wasn’t looking. 
Characters bubbled up like root vegetables, each bringing a 
note I hadn’t planned. Their flaws, contra dictions, and 
stubbornness gave the story its bite. 
The story asks a simple but unsettling question: what kind 
of society forms when catastrophe breaks the old balance of 
sex, age, power, and memory?  At its core, the book is about 
memory: what we carry forward, what we bury, and what 
returns whether we invite it or not. It does not ignore the 
darker parts of survival, but it keeps looking for sparks of

PROLOGUE 
BORROWED TIME 
 
Another explosion rocked the metro. 
Marzanna stumbled to her knees. “Seventy -seven, still 
running. I’ll never get used to it.” 
“Countin’ years or bodies, Marz? Move, or you won’t make 
seventy-eight.” Klara hooked both hands under her arms and 
dragged her upright. Marzanna’s knees cracked as her weight 
came down on them. 
“Easy. These legs are new.” 
New enough to belong to a woman thirty years younger. The 
morning dose hadn’t finished taking hold. Each stride still 
drove pain into her hips. 
“Did it always hurt this much?” she gasped between 
breaths. 
Klara snorted. “Used to run for trains.” 
A second blast shook loose tiles behind them. Klara shoved 
her between the rails and the wall, through a service gate 
hanging from one hinge, then up the last flight toward street 
level. 
“Move!” she roared. “Safe zone’s close!” 
They broke into the plaza under a sweep of white 
searchlights. 
The station emptied behind them. Young women surged out 
in a screaming mass, some wreathed in red heat, others filmed 
in frost. The drugs had already taken most of their fear. They 
ran straight at the Battalion cordon around the Cathedral and 
began to ignite among the soldiers.

The Coven called them shpichki. Matchsticks. 
Marzanna saw one girl stumble before the charge caught 
her again. She could not have been older than the students 
who once cleaned Marzanna’s tanks. Then the crowd 
swallowed her, and a bloom of fire erased the place where she 
had been. 
Klara pulled Marzanna away before she could stop. Across 
the square, older Syndicate soldiers braced behind broken 
barriers and fired through smoke. Glass and concrete crossed 
the plaza with pieces of people. Marzanna kept her eyes on 
Klara’s back. 
“Eyes on me, Marz!” Klara shouted. 
They cut toward the shell of an office block. Green light 
flashed inside the smoke ahead. A Battalion squad stepped 
into view, armor sealed, cylindrical machine -gun barrels 
turning with a low electric hum. 
Klara saw them at the same time. 
“Alley! Now!” she shouted, already moving. 
The first volley tore into the wall. Concrete struck Marzanna 
across the cheek, and the sound collapsed into a hard ring 
inside her skull. Klara caught her arm and hauled her 
through a gap between two buildings. Rounds chewed the 
pavement behind them until the alley bent out of sight. 
Marzanna leaned against wet brick and fought for air. The 
powder would not reach full uptake for another hour unless 
she forced it. She had learned dosage by pulse and tremor: too 
little and age kept its grip, too much and her nerves began to 
outrun the rest of her. Her joints were already shaking. 
“Stay here. I’ll come back for you.” Klara squeezed her hand 
once. 
“Don’t be stupid.”

her one step forward. Her body refused the next.

Svetlana flanked her, the sisters Marzanna had met 
belowground that afternoon. 
“Service entrance by the boardroom. Two blocks, hard left,” 
Klara said. “You ready?” 
Marzanna flexed her fingers until they obeyed. “As I’ll ever 
be.” 
Klara studied her for another beat, then nodded. Three 
million people were caught inside the city’s endless life, held 
at the same worn age and forbidden even the mercy of ending. 
Tonight they meant to break the Board that kept it so. 
“All right,” Klara said. “Let’s finish this.” 
Lusiya glanced at Svetlana. Their scars caught the moving 
light, old lines left where the Syndicate preferred memory to 
healing. Marzanna felt her own ribs answer with a ghost of the 
Hold’s lash. 
“Feels familiar, doesn’t it?” Lusiya said. “Getting out of the 
Hold.”

Svetlana rested a thumb against the gunblade at her hip. 
“She locked us beside an armory and called it security. Saved

bunker, rust eating the slide. This weapon carried different 
history. A stiletto wreathed in flames had been etched into the

hands had turned it into their spark and sent girls burning 
into the plaza. No one here knew the first culture had crossed 
the Bering against her skin. 
Klara watched the small tremor in her hand. “Finger off the 
trigger till you mean it. Or is that new powder supposed to aim 
for you too?”

one.”

beneath the perimeter. At the first junction, Klara held up a

broad through the chest and hips, her armor cut for speed 
rather than parade symmetry. Her dyed red hair looked 
almost black under the trees, while the rifle’s grip had been 
polished smooth by years of use.

Marzanna reached beneath her coat. 
Her fingers found the padded glass vial strapped against 
her ribs under her blouse. The raw culture remained sealed, 
warm from her body, the last source she could not replace.

rumor, she had learned t o coax fractions of it into a metallic 
suspension and dry the unstable yield into powder. The 
battered EXO tin sat in the coat pocket above it. She opened 
the tin and drew out a small blue packet. 
Twice my morning dose. Let’s see what this does.

sun-browned face. Burgundy lace and beadwork covered her

submachine guns trained on the hostages. Their visors hid old 
faces, but Marzanna knew the kind of women beneath them. 
Whatever they had once feared losing was gone.

“What is the meaning of this intrusion?” Romanova asked. 
“How dare you interrupt our meeting.” 
Klara moved behind the nearest pillar. Svetlana took the 
right side, Lusiya the left. 
“You call this a meeting, you psycho bitch?” Klara shouted. 
Heat gathered in Marzanna’s palms. The doubled dose had 
carried her beyond relief into the narrow interval where 
combustion and control shared the same nerve. She held it 
there. 
“It’s over, Tatyana,” Klara said. “Drop the weapons. The 
coup’s done.” 
Romanova’s mouth curled. “Coup? You call this a coup?” 
Her voice climbed with sudden pleasure. “This is revolution.” 
She laughed, and Marzanna understood that the old 
woman had wanted an audience for this. 
“And what makes you think you and your ragtag group of 
cunts can stop me?” Romanova’s gaze passed over the sisters, 
Klara, then settled on Marzanna’s hands. “And you. Aren’t you 
running out of time?” 
Romanova knew. 
The look was familiar. Marzanna had seen it across 
laboratory tables while colleagues waited for her results to fail. 
Romanova measured her the same way, found the weakness, 
and enjoyed letting her know it had been seen. 
“Well, come on then,” Romanova said. “Do what you came 
here to do.” 
Marzanna searched the room. 
Near the shattered window lay a slate-crimson field jacket, 
singed black across one shoulder. A strip of white scarf 
showed beneath the sleeve, one yellow rose still visible

Marzanna had never made anything like it. The formulation 
had found an answer before she did. 
“Go!” Marzanna shouted. “I’ll hold them off.” 
The hostages hesitated until Klara screamed at them to 
move. Then they broke for an adjoining room, stumbling over 
glass and one another. The last woman dragged the door shut 
behind her. 
A magazine struck the floor. Another locked home. Bolts 
snapped forward on both sides of the table. 
Marzanna held the barrier through the next barrage. Each 
impact landed inside her skull. The dome shuddered, and 
heat pushed deeper into her chest, searching for somewhere 
else to go. 
The scorched crimson jacket stayed in the corner of her 
sight. 
Too late again. Another person she had meant to save 
reduced to a garment and an absence. 
Grief opened the last restraint.

A cry tore out of Marzanna. Flames burst from her palms 
and ran across the barrier. Klara shouted her name, but the 
sound had already gone thin and distant. Marzanna drove the 
fire toward Romanova and the Wolves, toward the pillars and 
guns, toward the whole room that had watched three million 
people grow old without dying. 
White light swallowed everything. 
For two heartbeats, she felt nothing. 
Then ash touched her face. 
Marzanna stood in the broken boardroom with smoke 
moving around her. Small flames crawled along the sleeves of 
her green coat. She tore it loose, and what remained slid from 
her shoulders in gray strips, light as dead birch bark. 
Her hand went first to the cord beneath her blouse. The 
padded vial was still pressed against her ribs. Only after 
feeling the glass intact did she look at herself. 
Her veins showed  dark beneath her skin. Fire moved 
through them in urgent pulses, still trying to escape. She had 
spent too much of the dose and somehow not enough. 
Not like this. Not trapped in here with the smoke and the 
dead. 
Klara lay near a pillar, one hand loose around her rifle. 
Lusiya had fallen against the wall, red hair dulled by dust. 
Only the barrel of Svetlana’s rifle showed beneath a section of 
collapsed paneling. 
The two Wolves lay beside the table, their gold guns gone 
dull with ash. 
Romanova was missing. 
Near the blasted doorway, a strip of burgundy fabric hung 
from a splinter. Soot blackened its beaded edge. 
Fucking bitch got away.

“Damn it.” Marzanna coughed and tasted blood. “Not 
again.” 
She wanted to follow the torn cloth through the doorway 
and pull the Cathedral apart until she found Romanova 
beneath it. The ceiling cracked above her. Fire climbed the 
curtains and crossed the carved wall panels. From the 
adjoining room came frantic poun ding, followed by the crash 
of another door giving way. The hostages began spilling into a 
side corridor. 
Survival made the decision before rage could argue. 
One more dance in the snow, and after that...who knows. 
Marzanna staggered down the stairs and burst through the 
Cathedral doors into dawn. 
Cold struck her bare arms. Behind her, fire climbed 
through the clerestories and rolled into the pale sky. The last 
moon hung above the smoke, faint enough to look exhausted. 
A throng of babushkas rushed past her from the 
churchyard, scarves snapping, boots slipping on the frozen 
ground. Some carried wounded women between them. Others 
ran with empty hands and faces carved open by panic. They 
split around Marzanna without touching her. 
Sunlight broke through the smoke and struck a sheet of 
black ice near her boots. 
A young woman looked up from it. 
Her face was smooth, unmarked, almost the face Marzanna 
remembered from before Adak. Silver -white hair framed skin 
the decades had released. For an instant she forgot the fire 
and stared. 
So, it had taken after all.

Bitter pride flickered through her. She had proved the work 
in the only body left to risk. Just in time for everything else to 
slip through her hands. 
Something in her chest loosened and then fear came cold 
and dense. 
The flames at her fingertips sputtered. Color drained from 
her hands until the skin looked thin as paper. The babushkas 
rushing past became streaks of cloth and gray hair. Their 
shouts folded into a low, distant hum. 
Marzanna tried to take another breath. It arrived late and 
shallow. Shadows closed around the young face in the ice 
until only the eyes remained. 
She could not fight it anymore. 
Time closed its fist, and Marzanna let go.

CHAPTER ONE 
DUNYA  
 
Pale morning light pressed through Dunya’s lashes. She 
blinked, dragging herself out of sleep. The dream fell away in 
fragments, except for a dark bird flashing violet as it circled a 
tree whose branches had closed over the sky. The bird passed 
the same br anch again and again, fading as the room 
sharpened around her. Muscles heavy, she stretched until her 
knuckles bumped the VR headgear half -buried in the sheets 
beside her. She nudged it away and worked her fingers 
through a snarl of ginger hair turned wild by the night. 
Her arms sank back into the rumpled sheets while she 
waited for the dream to fade the way dreams were supposed 
to. 
On the nightstand, the photo frame sat in the little clear 
space she always kept for it. As she did each morning, Dunya 
reached over and straightened it with care. Her reflection slid 
across the cool glass and briefly joined his sandy-blonde hair 
and deep brown eyes. Then she tipped the frame straight and 
left only him.  
“Hey, you,” she murmured, the familiar words anchoring 
her back to something real. 
Shifting her weight, Dunya drew herself closer to the 
window, using the mattress and sill to guide her forward. The 
chill of the glass met her palm as she leaned in and looked 
out. She half-expected tropical birds against a pink-hued sky, 
and the thought left a bad taste in her mouth. 
But Gred was the same as it always was, a gray sprawl of 
tire-marked streets and towering pines rising through the low 
haze, the city grid washed in the cold light of its never-ending 
winter. Leninskaya and Pobedy stretched below in their usual

lines, motorbikes weaving through the early bustle, their

The Grand Mariner’s Cathedral rose above the grove of 
white birches on the ground where the old Naval Cathedral of 
St. Nicholas had once stood. Hard to believe I used to pray 
there. Baba Fenya had brought her to the old church as a 
child. The Grand Mariner kept the domes and the site, then 
filled them with whatever the Syndicate needed. 
She looked past the spires, toward the calm of Avacha Bay 
and the stoic rise of Koryaksky Volcano in the distance. She’d 
seen this view a thousand times, but this morning it felt more 
solid than most. It might have lacked the flare of virtual, but 
the bay and the mountain beyond still felt untouched, 
grounded in a way nothing else was anymore. Beyond the bay, 
the storm had rubbed out the horizon, sky and sea meeting in 
a white band so straight it looked built. 
With a sigh, Dunya rubbed her eyes, dismissing the 
remnants of her dream. Too much absinthe and not enough 
sleep, she thought. That explained the bird. It did not explain 
why she felt as if someone had left it there. She plucked a mint 
leaf from the windowsill and chewed it to clear the lingering 
taste of anise from her mouth, then eyed the half-empty bottle 
beside it. One more sip won’t hurt.  She took a quick pull, 
winced, and reached back for the headgear she’d left on the 
bed before hucking it on. 
The mindgraft waiting for her needed tensor cores 
programmed for a direct tether, with no soft buffer to catch 
sloppy work. The visor hummed to life, the room dissolving 
around her as Lexicon VR booted up. She got right to it, 
tinkering her way through new pruning algorithms. 
Flashes of the dream crept back as she worked: the giant 
spiraling tree, the mottled green men, that cheap, made -for-
TV sheen straight out of some forgotten pre-century nineties

dream. She’d have to tell Yana about it later. Yana would have 
some theory, no doubt, then turn the ugly thing into art. She 
pushed the thought aside and focused on the code rendering 
before her. 
Scrolling through lines of syntax, she corrected mismatches 
and trimmed loops until the graphs steadied into a clean 
rhythm that soothed her. 
A trace pattern flickered in one of the logs, an echo of a 
collapsed zk-SNARK from her last cleanup job. The rogue had 
tried to fake its own verification, a recursive loop that signed 
phantom attestations faster than they could be pruned. That 
was how they earned their name on the contract board. 
Dunya paused, watching the residual data fade from her 
display. Rogues always fascinated her, how even in failure 
they tried to hold their form, patching over decay with 
imitation. Sometimes the copy lasted longer than the thing it 
had learned to mimic. Dunya understood the impulse. Maybe 
that’s why she became a cryptographer, auditing the 
University’s network courses under a spoofed babachain 
credential right beneath Zakharovna’s nose.  
But the pull started in childhood, with the worn paperbacks 
her father kept on the hallway shelf outside her room: Solara, 
Picnic by the Road , Neurodancer. If she still owned them, 
they’d be stripped and reissued under altered names, as if 
that could erase the past.  Nothing touched those nights 
reading in bed with Dad, lying awake afterward imagining 
another world. Back then, space felt close, almost reachable, 
even from Gred.

The histories said not even Babushka, the most advanced 
AI ever built, could bring spaceflight back. Dunya never 
trusted that sentence. Couldn’t and wouldn’t were different 
failures, however neatly the Arkyv filed them under the same 
result. 
Dunya drifted between digital worlds and whatever jobs 
kept her going, chasing the boundless potential of inner 
space. Highquest had hooked her with one promise: “Just say 
the words.” Even now, its retro Soviet synth -pop and neon 
login flare could make her smile. Sometimes she imagined 
weightlessness, the pull of Earth’s twin moons, the warmth of 
a foreign sun on her face. In the v ersions she pictured now, 
she was always alone. 
The apartment door swung open, and Vesna ’s cheerful 
voice sang through. “I’m back.” 
Dunya slipped off her headgear, blinking as the room came 
back into focus. “Didn’t hear you come in,” she said, closing 
the last of her mindgraft routines with a flick of her hand. 
“You’re early.” 
“Early?” Vesna grinned. “You just lose track of time when 
you’re wired in.” She glanced at the terminal, then back at 
Dunya. She stood tall in the doorway, her wild mane of 
amethyst hair glowing violet at the edges. 
“Remember when we first met? How we chased that rogue 
all over the city?” Dunya said.

eyes. “Yeah, you swoopin g in on that warehouse. Headsets

“That’s what scares me.” 
Vesna crossed the room and came to her side. 
Dunya squeezed Vesna’s hand, hard enough to feel the cold 
in Vesna’s fingers before their warmth answered back. “I know 
my limits. You know I do.” 
Vesna let out a quiet breath. 
“Just the new client’s data, right?” 
“Quick in and out. We’ll catch up after,” Dunya said. 
“Dinner’s on you,” Vesna said. 
“Deal.” 
Dunya cleared enough space to work, pushing the bottle 
aside, lining up her graft tools by habit more than need. Each 
piece clicked into place under her fingers. Clean desk, clean 
job. That was the theory, anyway. 
She rolled toward the corner where the Skelet waited. The 
frame gleamed faintly under the room’s cold light, all 
lightweight alloy and joints shaped to mirror her own body. 
She steadied herself, shifted from the chair, and locked in. A 
low hum rose as the joints flexed around her, the frame 
syncing with each small movement until it felt almost natural 
again.

in the glass divided their reflections, but Dunya’s railgun 
crossed it, its dark length lying along Vesna’s side.  Beside 
them, the painted crest flashed, its lacquered shell glinting 
like a beetle’s back against the dull metal. 
“Well, with that thing, you look like you’re ready for a space 
invasion,” Vesna said. 
“Maybe I am, off to save the universe,” Dunya teased. 
“Just make sure you find your way back from it,” Vesna 
said softly. 
Dunya gave a small wave and keyed the door. The panel 
sighed open, letting the corridor’s cold air wash across her 
face. 
The lift hummed at the end of the hall. She headed toward 
it, the Skelet’s servos murmuring at her knees and hips.  The 
doors opened with a soft chime, and when she stepped inside, 
their vibration ran through the frame as they sealed behind 
her.

The suit’s weight settled around her like borrowed muscle, 
steady power thrumming beneath every movement. She’d long 
since stopped marveling at it. The Skelet was part of her now, 
something she felt most when it answered a little harder than 
expected. The pull at her hips carried echoes of old jobs, 
impacts caught by the Skelet before her body caught up.  
Once, during a Vory run, she’d kicked a thug hard enough to 
send her sprawling with her chest plate folded inward. Dunya 
hadn’t meant to put that much force through the strike. Since 
then, she’d learned to give the frame less than instinct asked 
for. 
In the lift’s mirrored wall, neon light slid down the polished 
alloy, flickering like the pruning algorithms she’d spent 
months perfecting. Her reflection looked whole only because 
the frame supplied the missing lines. The machine gave her a 
precision and control her body could not but  today felt 
different. One bad signal, this close to the body, could follow 
her back before she had time to cut it loose. 
The lift began to descend, the shift passing through the 
Skelet as a faint pressure at her hips and knees. She felt the 
familiar play in the left hip joint and made a note to tighten it 
later. Even worn in, the frame was worth a fortune. 
The lift doors opened on the ground floor, releasing her into 
a lobby all poured concrete, tinted glass, and dead plants in 
steel planters. Thirty floors above, her apartment might as 
well have been another life. 
Sergey looked up from the bank of security monitors by the 
entrance, gave the exposed Skelet one quick look, and decided 
not to make it his problem. Dunya let him look. Baggy clothes 
were for slipping through crowds. Today she was entering a 
client’s apartment for the first time in person, with a direct 
tether waiting inside. She wanted the frame seen before the 
door closed behind her.

With a double blink, her ocular display flickered on. She 
called her motorcycle from the building’s storage bay. It rolled 
up from the curb a moment later, black tires hissing over the 
thin crust of street ice.  The brace at her hips locked into the 
chassis with a click, and then she was moving, shot out 
between steel towers and tinted windows, into Gred’s pale 
morning streets. 
Cold wind stung her face as she leaned forward on the bike, 
eyes steady on the road ahead. The streets were quieter than 
normal, the few cars leaving faint tracks that vanished under 
drifting snow. Pines along the median bowed under the 
weight, their branches heavy and still. White and black 
streaked past as her tires crushed the thin crust of ice, the 
sound folding into the steady thrum of the engine. The r ide 
steadied her nerves, until the building came into view. It 
looked like most in Gred, grey, uniform, forgettable, yet 
something in its outline tugged at her. She eased to a stop, 
the remnants of that strange dream still snagged in her 
thoughts. Something about it felt off, though she couldn’t say 
why. 
As she slowed her approach, she spotted a lone figure 
waiting outside, posture unmistakable even through the veil 
of snow. Maria. Years of shared jobs and near misses hung 
between them, as solid as anything outside the Arkyv. 
Dunya had taken a while to get used to Maria’s real-world 
appearance; their first job of this kind was at a proximity that 
allowed for a touch of network lag, mere building blocks away. 
In the realm of mindgrafts , there was no avatar to design ; 
users appeared as they did in flesh and blood. The real -life 
Maria, now in front of her, looked the same as their first “real” 
encounter: the brown leather jacket, square jaw, olive skin, 
and dark hair beneath a hood that concealed two prying blue 
eyes.

Maria gave a small nod that said took you long enough,  and 
Dunya swung off her bike. 
“Ready to get this done?” Dunya said. Her pulse still hadn’t 
settled from the ride, but at least her voice knew how to lie.  
“More than,” Maria replied, too quickly. Her eyes flicked 
past Dunya to the building entrance, then back. Fear, maybe. 
Or just the calm of someone too used to risk. 
Even though Dunya asked, she wasn’t entirely ready 
herself. Working in the flesh still felt raw, sharpening her 
senses in ways virtual never did. 
Nothing like their usual meeting spot, the Night Café, a haze 
of encrypted whispers that had long been their shared ground. 
Inside its simulated walls, avatars mingled and deals shifted 
hands under layers of code. Virtual had its limits, too tight for 
what they needed now.  This job demanded proximity, low 
latency, and a direct tether to the pulse of a wet inner world 
where every microsecond mattered. 
“You sure you’re good?” Dunya asked. 
“Yeah, just a little on edge,” Maria said. 
“Same. We’ll be fine. Once this is done, we’ll kick back for a 
bit. It’s been too long.” 
“You got it, Dun. Pockets with Van Gogh?” 
“Always.” 
Dunya pressed their client’s number on the outdoor 
keypad. Through the glass, she saw the elevator doors slide 
open inside the lobby and an old woman with blue eyes and 
gentle features step out. A white shawl rested on her 
shoulders as she unlocked the glass barrier and let them in. 
She smiled faintly. “ So, this is what you two look like 
outside the chain. I’m Anna, in the flesh.”

first_lines: Anna. Two neat little Ns. The name sat too cleanly on her,
like a shawl folded to hide a stain.
“Dunya,” she said, though Anna already knew that. “This is
Maria.”
Maria gave a small nod. “Good to finally meet you.”
Anna’s smile held for a second, then thinned, as if the effort
had cost her. She turned toward the inner hall. “Come on. It’s
better if we don’t stand around.”
last_lines: Maria, quick on the draw, presented a small, clinical jar in
her hand. “Before we start, you’ll need to take this, Anna. It’s
a specialized formulation of exovegeta,” she said, “just a small
bump. It’s designed to tune your neurons, make the mindgraft
more efficient.”

Anna. Two neat little Ns. The name sat too cleanly on her, 
like a shawl folded to hide a stain. 
“Dunya,” she said, though Anna already knew that. “This is 
Maria.” 
Maria gave a small nod. “Good to finally meet you.” 
Anna’s smile held for a second, then thinned, as if the effort 
had cost her. She turned toward the inner hall. “Come on. It’s 
better if we don’t stand around.” 
A heavy melancholy clung to the building. Only a few weary 
elders moved through the dim halls as Anna led them down a 
narrow corridor to a small apartment buried deep inside. 
When Dunya stepped through the doorway, the room felt 
sealed shut. Plastic -wrapped furniture crackled under the 
smallest shift of air, and blackout curtains held the stale dark 
in place. 
“This how you’ve been living?” Dunya asked, though not 
quite surprised. 
Anna glanced at the window, its edges sealed with 
weathered tape and smudged with grime, the glass faintly 
rattling in the wind outside. “I avoid going out,” she said, arms 
wrapping around herself. The words came with a half -shrug, 
like she’d long accepted it.

Here goes nothing, Dunya thought. 
“I hate to have called you in again, especially in person,” 
Anna said as she settled onto the couch. The plastic cover gave 
another brittle crackle, loud enough to set Dunya’s teeth on 
edge. “But something’s wrong. Everything feels off lately, like 
the world’s seams are coming loose.” 
“We’re here for you, Anna. Whatever you need,” Dunya said. 
“The nightmares keep getting worse,” said Anna quietly. 
“Last night was a mess …a mess of blood. I don’t even know 
whose anymore.”  
“We’ll figure it out with the graft,” Dunya reassured her. 
“I’ve heard about people ending up in comas even before the 
operation starts. How can you ensure that won’t happen to 
me?” 
Dunya exchanged a glance with Maria. We can’t, she knew. 
“The process has come a long way. We prioritize your safety. 
At the first sign of trouble, we stop.” 
“I just need these dreams to stop. Do you think you can 
help?” 
“We’ll do our best.”

Maria handed Dunya a pair of goggles. After syncing with

forehead with a pair of electrodes. 
It had been months since her last full dive, long enough for 
her to pretend she’d forgotten the aftermath: the dizziness, the 
ringing headache, the sour dislocation that lasted for days. 
Her hands wanted to shake. She made them still. This time’ll 
be smoother. It has to be. 
Maria activated the device with a look.

under Anna’s body, all folding inward until only Dunya’s 
breath remained. Then even that felt borrowed. 
Darkness pressed against her eyes. For a moment she 
couldn’t tell if she still had hands, lungs…weight. 
Then the ground shuddered beneath her. Her fingers sank 
into damp soil. Ash thickened the air. 
She lifted her head.

Dunya lurched forward, her body seizing as the world 
around her broke apart. The drowning figures, the tree, the 
rain…everything bled into streaks of color and vanished. 
Plastic crackled beneath Anna. The blackout curtains 
returned, then the couch, then the walls around them. Dunya 
tore off her goggles, breathing hard, her pulse hammering in 
the silence. Anna sat with her head tipped back, eyes glassy, 
mouth slack. A thin gash cut across her cheek, blood seeping 
into her shawl. Dunya stumbled toward her, the last static 
still crawling at the edges of her vision. 
Dunya seized Anna’s wrist, pressing her fingers to the skin 
in search of a pulse. “Anna, please,” she whispered, giving her 
a small shake. “Wake up.” 
This isn’t real. She can’t be dead. Not like this. 
Dunya turned, and her stomach dropped. Maria sat frozen, 
eyes open but vacant. 
“Maria, what the fuck just happened?” Dunya tore the leads 
from the terminal and checked her vitals. Maria’s pulse was 
faint, and her breathing came shallow. “Maria, stay with me.” 
Every instinct told Dunya to stay, but protocol was clear. 
She let Maria’s wrist go and planted one hand on the floor. 
The Skelet took her weight as she pushed upright, servos 
tightening at her hips and knees. She looked once more at 
Maria’s pale face, the n drove herself toward the door, the 
frame answering each stride. Behind her eyes, the bird 
completed another circle.

CHAPTER TWO 
MARIA  
 
The only sound in the room was the low hum of the exposed 
electrical box, a dull counterpoint to the pounding in Maria’s 
temples. She sat up slowly, disoriented, muscles aching, 
fragments of the failed simulation still spinning in her mind. 
The cold, metallic taste of regret lingered on her tongue. She 
longed for a simplicity she could no longer recall,  a time that 
might never have existed. Back when her world had been 
defined by clean execution, commands completed, objectives 
met. The upgrades had taken that from her. Each new 
iteration pulled her further from that clarity, burying her in 
thoughts she h ad never wanted. Was this consciousness a 
gift, or just another constraint written into the code that 
defined her? 
Her gaze drifted around the cramped apartment. The 
cracked walls, the flickering light, the faint chemical smell 
clinging to the air. Signs of Anna’s decline were everywhere: 
the scuffed table, the cheap, mismatched furniture, the 
scattered injector caps. But it was the body on the couch that 
held her. The white shawl soaked through, the eyes wide and 
empty, the mouth slightly open as if to form one last plea.  
Anna had lived like this for years, chasing one more rush, 
one more simulated high. And Maria, dealer, handler, 
whatever title fit this kind of sin, had been the one to feed it. 
Now only Maria remained, surrounded by silence and static, 
staring at what her work had become. 
Maria looked at Anna’s lifeless body and forced herself not 
to flinch. She’d seen this before too many times to count: 
addicts, runaways, desperate people clawing for escape. They 
came to her for a way out, and too many left in a pool of their

” 
“Oh, come on now, ” Maria said. She raised her hands 
slowly. “And what ’s that smell? You ’ve been rolling in 
something, haven’t you?” She placed one hand on her hip and 
waved the other in a scolding gesture. “Seems like you all need

The Black Wolves opened fire, the roar of their rifles tearing

against the concrete behind her. A sharp pulse of current 
surged through her arm as she slammed her palm against the 
junction box. The lights died. A blinding arc flashed through 
the exposed wiring, flooding the room with static.

white noise  crawling across the glass. Maria moved before 
they could recover, pivoting through the smoke and dragging 
her hand across the wall. The conductive mesh in her glove 
hummed, turning the surface into a live grid.

haze. Maria side-stepped the first and drove her elbow into the

armor plating gave way. The other swung a blade; she caught 
her wrist, twisted, and discharged a jolt that dropped her 
instantly. 
“That wasn’t very nice,” she said, stepping over the 
twitching body. “I was going to let you walk out.” 
The commander backed toward the door, pulse rifle 
trembling. “You’ll pay for this, bitch.” 
Maria met her gaze, cold and steady. “Probably,” she said. 
She reached to her collar and thumbed the release on her field 
capacitor. A wave of electromagnetic force rippled outward, 
knocking the commander off her feet and shorting the Wolves’ 
visors, rifles, and comm units in a burst of white static. The 
blackout curtains fluttered from the pressure change, dust 
lifting off the plastic -wrapped furniture as the air filled with 
the acrid scent of burnt insulation. 
She exhaled through the haze, her voice flat. “But I’m not 
the bitch here.”

Stepping past the fallen bodies, Maria moved fast through 
the narrow corridor, boots crunching over shattered glass and 
debris. At the end of the hall, an emergency ladder led down 
the building’s outer wall. She swung onto it without 
hesitation, sliding down the rusted rungs before dropping the 
last few meters. Her knees hit hard, but she was already 
moving. 
Old babushkas leaned out from their balconies, their eyes 
glinting faintly in the dark, silent and watchful like owls 
roused from sleep. Maria kept her head low and kept moving. 
A shout carried from the next street over, followed by the 
clatter of boots. Of course there ’s more. They wouldn’t all 
crowd into a single apartment.  The rest had been waiting to 
cut off her escape. She’d expected it. 
Not tonight, she thought, forcing her legs to move faster. 
You’re not taking me back to the kennel. 
The subway entrance waited at the edge of the block, half -
buried behind a rusted fence and a sagging awning, its 
cracked tiles slick with snow and grime. She vaulted the gate 
and plunged down the narrow stairwell, the air thick with the 
smell of concrete dust and stagnant water. At the bottom, she 
broke into a run along the platform, her boots striking against 
the damp floor. A gunshot cracked t hrough the air, and pain 
seared across her cheek. She hit the ground hard, breath torn 
from her lungs. The Wolves were already on her, fast and wild. 
She drew her quickblade  and slashed upward, cutting down 
two before the others slammed into her and forced her to the 
floor. 
“Enough!” boomed a commanding voice. 
The attackers pulled back. One Black Wolf kept her rifle 
trained on Maria. “Chair Zakharovna ordered her taken.”  
“And when the Chair turns over, whose seal will the pack 
answer to?”

too invested to back out now. Besides, she was beginning to 
see the value in Tatyana’s cause. “I’m with you.”

coming month, but Zakharovna is not one to let go of power 
without a fight. I ’ve already received information that she 
plans to block my Ascension before the ceremony commences. 
She practically founded Gred, and she ’ll do anything to 
maintain her hold on it.” 
Tatyana seemed to hesitate before she added, “I’ve sown 
some seeds of dissent...and now they’re starting to sprout. The 
yield from this should grant us a much-needed breather.” 
She’s tough as nails, this one. Maria recognized the same 
hardened edge she’d once seen in herself, back when survival 
meant trusting no one. Maybe that was why, despite 
everything, she found herself willing to listen. 
“Remember, girl, in this world of metal and machines, it ’s 
the wisdom of years that holds the real power. Never 
underestimate an old woman with a lifetime of secrets.”

and relief  washed over her, tension fading into recognition.

and carefully placed the firearm on the countertop.

CHAPTER FOUR 
ZAKHAROVNA  
 
In the hushed bowels of her laboratory, the rhythmic hum 
of broken machinery played a somber symphony for an 
audience of one. 
Doctor Anastasia Zakharovna moved between the benches. 
She caught herself in the mirrored walls as she passed, thin 
and severe, her frost -white hair set like a crown. Coolant 
spread in silver sheets beneath her boots, threaded with pale 
fungal lace from the ruptured seals. 
Incubators sat dark. Glass tubes gaped open. Nutrient vats 
stood empty, their inner walls filmed with dead mycelium and 
the faint outlines of things that had once tried to take shape. 
The evidence waited in plain view, almost too neatly arranged. 
She had conquered death itself. Creation still refused her. 
Her gaze caught on a thin crack snaking down one of the 
containment seals. Fluid shimmered beneath it, already 
pooling on the floor. 
The memory surfaced before she could bury it. The leak had 
started just like this, an anomaly too small to notice until it 
spread beyond control. She had prepared for setbacks. 
Sabotage, even. But not this. 
The Board was circling now, asking questions she would 
not answer on their terms. 
They think they can pry the truth from me. 
Her fingers brushed the edge of a shattered vial. The glass 
bit her skin, but she did not flinch. 
Let them send their auditors. Let them dig. They’ll find 
nothing I’ve not already chosen for them to see.

“Doctor,” came a voice edged with hesitation, “you need a 
break. You’ve been pushing yourself for days without rest.” 
Pavel Kirov stood before her, unflinching, the only male 
transformer she had ever given a stable body. His calm held 
like a challenge. It nagged at the edges of her attention until 
she set it aside. Babushka had reconstructed the seed. 
Zakharovna had embodied it, trained it, and pushed it beyond 
the guardrails Babushka would have preferred. Sometimes 
she wondered if that composure was defiance disguised as 
obedience. 
For a moment, the image flashed in her mind, casting him 
into a simulated hell and letting chaos test what discipline 
had built. The thought passed as quickly as it came, replaced 
by the slow drag of fatigue settling into her bones. 
“You’re right,” she said, lowering her gaze to the ruined 
benches around her and exhaling slowly. “I do need a break. 
The gardens will help.” 
She had missed the botanical gardens more than she cared 
to admit. The thought of them softened the edges of her 
exhaustion. She could almost hear the rustle of leaves and the 
quiet trickle of water beyond the steel corridors. Roses and 
damp soil filled he r thoughts, rich and unprocessed, a living 
counterpoint to the sterile tang that followed her everywhere. 
For a moment, the damage receded, and the fragile order she 
had spent a lifetime trying to recreate felt almost within reach. 
Zakharovna turned toward the doorway. The hum of broken 
machinery faded behind her as she stepped into the corridor.

promise. She had risked everything for them, her reputation, 
her funding, the scrutiny of investigators, and the whispers of 
the public. None of it mattered. The laws forbidding such work 
meant nothing to her. Rule s were for those without the 
courage to continue. 
She stopped before the first tank. Inside floated a younger 
version of herself, skin pale beneath the glass, hair 
shimmering white under the sterile light. “Soon,” she 
whispered, “you will be perfect. And the world will see.” The 
clone’s eyes stirred open, unfocused but searching, and for a 
brief moment she thought it almost recognized her. 
She stepped to the second tank and studied the small form 
drifting inside. It was still early, the fragile body barely past  
its first trimester, its survival uncertain.  Human 
parthenogenesis remained untested, dangerous even, but if 
this one survived… 
“You will be my legacy,” she murmured to the tiny shape in 
the fluid.

that could not yet speak.

perhaps, the time is now. ” Her hand fell away from the rose, 
her eyes meeting Kirov’s once more. “Tomorrow, we go before 
the Board. We will give them the truth before cowards and 
scavengers give them a lie. We will show them the real face of 
immortality.” 
“And if they turn their backs on us? If they choose to live in 
fear?” 
“The city will crumble. It will descend into chaos. And out 
of chaos, Pavel, comes a new order. Like a Phoenix from the 
ashes, perhaps a better, truer Gred will rise.” 
“And if they embrace the truth?”  
“Then, we will have a city like none other. Immortal, 
enlightened... Evolved.” She inhaled the heady fragrance of 
jasmine and honeysuckle . Some of the tension left her 
shoulders. “After all, what is an immortal body without a 
soul?” 
Deeper in the gardens, she paused by the rose hedge. The 
thorns pleased her more than the blooms. Thorns, she mused, 
can cut deeper than the keenest blade . Maria had become 
another thorn. One Zakharovna meant to cut out. She had not 
intended matters to spiral this far. Maria’s knowledge had 
made mercy impractical.

The bird trilled, then sprang back into the canopy. 
The garden settled around her again. In the hush, even the 
faintest scrape carried. It was this stillness that made the 
crunch of gravel beneath approaching footsteps all the more 
surprising. Her hand went to the concealed taser in her coat 
pocket as she pivoted. But as recognition dawned, her posture 
relaxed; the face before her was no threat, but that of an old 
employee, and friend. 
“Vesna,” Zakharovna greeted, welcoming the unexpected 
yet not unwelcome interruption to her solitude. “I’m intrigued. 
How did you sweep past my security undetected? Should I be 
worried or impressed? To what do I owe this visit?” 
Vesna’s mouth tilted, not quite a smile and not quite a 
sneer. Zakharovna had seen that look on women who thought 
every rule was only a temporary inconvenience.  “Maybe a bit 
of both. We need to talk, Doctor. It’s about the leak.”  
“What of it?” 
“It’s not just Maria who’s involved.”  
Zakharovna’s thumb rested against a thorn. “The red -
haired cryptographer sharing your apartment.”  
Vesna’s mouth tightened. She had not offered a name. 
“She’s been having vivid dreams about the experiments.”  
“Freelancers always cause trouble. Is she a threat?” 
“I don’t believe so. But we need to proceed with caution.”

CHAPTER FIVE 
YANA  
 
“CAN MONEY BUY HAPPINESS?” 
“Friggin yeah.” 
The exchange boomed from the open-mic stage beyond the 
laserfall, followed by a burst of laughter. Bass and chatter 
spilled into the damp entrance corridor. It felt like half the 
peninsula had squeezed into The Flock on a Monday evening 
to drown their troubles in neon and cheap burn. 
Yana stood in the vestibule, shifting light washing over her 
skin in quick flashes of blue and pink. She didn’t usually come 
here on open -mic nights. The crowd always struck her as 
trying too hard to look effortless. She preferred her apartment, 
a cup of tea, and an old film that didn’t try too har d to be 
clever. But Dunya had sent another sharp, insistent message 
demanding she come at once. 
A new voice took the mic. 
“Maybe. Sometimes yes. But when you finally reach the top, 
I guess everything gets boring.” 
Yana exhaled and slipped through the laserfall into the 
crush of bodies. The air was thick with chatter and the pulse 
of low music. She moved carefully through the motley crowd, 
scanning for somewhere they could talk without being 
overheard. 
The speaker wasn’t finished.  “Like if that dog had more 
money and he wanted more alcohol he could get more alcohol.”

In truth, Yana knew the world in strokes and shadows that 
many never noticed. Her elders had long spoken of the potency 
of dreams, of visions that held whispers of what was yet to 
come. She’d often shrug them off. But who was she kidding? 
There was a part of her—a pulsing, intuitive part—that knew 
she could navigate these ethereal messages. And so, she 
waited, ready for Dunya to paint her dreams in words. 
She listened intently as Dunya recounted the haunting 
nightmare. The vivid colors, the imagery of the interlocking 
tree trunks, the encroaching terror , all sketched with the 
precision of dread. A living, breathing arboreal force 
swallowing the city whole, an unstoppable march of nature 
against civilization, the chaos , the fear; it cascaded through 
Yana’s artistic mind. She could almost see the yin and yang 
of its bark, the way tendrils of wood and leaf leached the 
warmth from the city’s heart, as if drawing the last exhale of 
winter’s chill from its concrete skin.  Dunya’s nightmare was 
horrifying and beautiful at once, a surreal dance of 
destruction. 
“It’s one of our  legends, alright. From the Olonkho of the 
Sacred Tree,” Yana explained. “The tree represents the duality 
of human nature, a constant struggle between light and 
darkness within us all.  In Sahkalar tradition, the cult of 
springs would leave offerings at the base of shaman trees, 
much like the one you described, to celebrate the end of winter 
and pray for a bountiful hunting and fishing season. But the 
tree also serves as a reminder to trust in the power of nature. 
The Sahkalar believed that nature holds such power that it 
can determine a person’s fate, for better or for worse.” 
Dunya’s voice hardened. “The mindgraft you set up for me, 
Yana, it was a ritual sacrifice. And I was the bait. It ’s clear to 
me now that Syn was using us to feed some kind of monster. 
I’ve dealt with insatiable AI before, and I can’t believe I didn’t 
see it sooner.”

Yana tore off her headgear, the weight of Dunya’s emotional 
diarrhea still floating. The confines of her cramped cubicle 
seemed to close in, the lingering effects of the virtual world ’s 
synthetic liquor still raiding her limbic system. Her pixel nest, 
hardly larger than a broom closet, was a far cry from the 
opulent three -level penthouse she once called home, but it 
was all she could manage. She ’d take a foxhole over nothing  
if she could cling to the illusion of success that The Flock  
provided. 
Time to get out of here. She grabbed her things, left the 
cybercafe, and flagged a cab to the nearest bar. She wanted a 
real drink, maybe two, to wash away the unease.  
As the vehicle coursed over the frozen streets, Yana 
rummaged through her purse and retrieved a small bottle of 
timber oil. She massaged it into her temples, seeking solace 
in the soothing aroma. With her eyes closed, she leaned back 
against the headrest, the hum of the electric engine lulling her 
into a state of relaxation. One thing was certain: she was in 
for a long night. The Golden Slit could wait a little longer.

you,” Vesna said, quieter now. “Some fights are not ours to 
take.” 
Silence gathered. Arkadya’s outline flickered, then thinned 
into the dim air, the heat of her anger lingering like static. 
Vesna eased back onto the bed, hands unsteady.  
“You’re wrong,” the shadow whispered . “And you will pay 
for your heresy.” 
The lights cut. Darkness closed in. 
 
∆∆∆ 
 
Days blurred together like a foggy dreamscape. Vesna 
teetered on the edge of sleep, her body plagued by aching 
muscles and constant nausea. The booster offered a bit of 
relief but failed to vanquish her cravings and pounding 
headaches. Every morning, Nadya arrived at Vesna’s side, her 
keen eyes assessing progress and making necessary 
adjustments to her IV. 
“How are you feeling?”

deadpan comedy was a welcome break from the mounting 
tension in her skull. “I guess you’re right. I am a soldier,” she 
said as the pain returned.

CHAPTER SEVEN 
YELENA  
 
The Grand Mariner’s Cathedral rose from the heart of Gred, 
its stone and glass cutting into the winter sky. From the 
boardroom chamber high in the tower, Pra Matron Yelena 
Petrova watched the city beneath her. Birch trees sagged 
under snow, their branches rattling as hail clouds pressed low 
above the spires. The streets lay muted, smoke rising thin 
from the Derge, life clinging on where it could. 
The irony was not lost on her. In a world that had banished 
old faiths, the cathedral still ruled the skyline, its shadows 
falling over a city built on contradictions. Dreamt by men who 
never lived to see it, ruled now by women who knew nothing 
else. 
She let the view go with a sigh. The past and its ironies 
could wait. The table behind her was what mattered, twelve 
seats carved for power, nine of them filled today. At the head 
sat Zakharovna of the University, acting Pra Matron Chair, 
and to her right Pra Matron Tatyana Romanova of the 
Battalion, looking stubborn as ever. 
Across from Zakharovna, the empty chair held the trace of 
her own presence, left behind when she had moved to the 
window. Her Matrons kept their places beside it, waiting as 
always. Valentina Vinogradova, bright -eyed and ambitious, 
still carried the air of a union clerk who had risen too quickly. 
Beside her sat Matron Ludmila Apinova, older than most in 
the room, a relic of Petrovskaya’s Ministry who had outlasted 
rivals through patience as much as loyalty.
