A quartet of hands raised in favor, a trio dissenting, and one 
taking refuge in the safety of abstention. The specter of 
deadlock loomed large and unsettling. In times past, the third 
Matron of the candidate ’s party held the honor of the ninth 
vote, the pivot point  between victory and defeat. Matron 
General Irina Nikitin, the chosen third for Romanova, folded 
her arms. Her vote held the potential to quell the motion or 
leave it to gasp in the chill of her indifference. 
Yelena understood Nikitin ’s unpredictable nature 
demanded caution in future dealings. The General of Gred ’s 
army was a formidable woman, wielding immense power and 
influence that should never be underestimated. Though 
Nikitin might not wish to appear complicit in a conspiracy, 
Yelena sensed she would be unable to resist the temptation 
for long. 
With Zakharovna ousted before the Ascension, the 
University would stand defenseless, its vulnerabilities laid 
bare, a tantalizing prize for the Battalion, who were hungry for 
accountability. For Zakharovna, shorn of her authority, the 
sands of time would run out, the specter of self-pardon fading 
into the shadows of her once mighty reign. 
Yelena’s eyes collided with General Nikitin’s in an exchange 
of silent electricity, yet Nikitin deflected the charge, her gaze 
veering away. 
“Nikitin?” Zakharovna’s eyebrow scaled her forehead in 
trepidation. 
The general lifted her hand.  
Zakharovna’s face contorted, a battle of emotions playing 
out in her eyes before she surrendered with a bitterness that 
seeped into every word, the icy edge of her voice melting into 
a pool of defeat. “Very well. The motion is carried.  If there is 
nothing else, this meeting is adjourned,” Zakharovna said, her 
authority all but vanished.

its people, first and foremost. They’ve earned the right to live

over, testing the limits of her self-control.

Zakharovna’s tone. It was always the same , a self-indulgent

woman thrived on these stories, each more tiresome than the 
last, and yet, Yelena could do little but wait as Zakharovna

Zakharovna leaned back, a wistful smile forming as she 
began recounting. “She overthrew the rooster and took his 
place, with the other chickens following her because of her 
strength and ability to lay the most eggs. She was the empress 
of the barnyard and strutted around like she owned the place. 
But one day, the farmers left th e hennery unguarded, and a 
hawk swooped down and snatched her up. The other chickens 
were left to fend for themselves and eventually became prey to 
foxes and coyotes.” 
“The rooster, exiled and scorned, waited until the farmers 
returned and repaired the hennery. He then took his rightful 
place as leader, watching the skies closely and giving the

CHAPTER EIGHT 
DUNYA  
 
Dunya crossed the quad, her wheelchair’s tires whispering 
over the concrete. Students loitered beneath the Temple of 
Gamayun, whose stone wings enclosed a laurel wreath with 
all the subtlety of a state seal. 
Vesna had been gone for days. Dunya’s messages showed 
delivered and nothing else. Yana had stopped replying too. 
Two dead channels made a pattern, and patterns were 
supposed to be Dunya’s thing. 
Had she pushed too hard? Probably. She had once sat 
through an Arkyv therapy module about personal boundaries 
and come away convinced that boundaries were what people 
invoked when they wanted you to stop asking questions. 
She paused beside a bench, locked one wheel, and used the 
backrest to lift and reposition herself. Her arms shook by the 
time she settled again. Vesna had told her to take a break, so 
Dunya would leave the apartment, drink a coffee, and pretend 
this counted.  
She pushed her wheels forward, the motion a temporary 
reprieve from her darker thoughts. At the edge of the quad, 
she veered onto the path that led to the Graduate Society 
Building, a squat red -brick affair housing a cafeteria, a 
bookstore, and a smatterin g of shops. It was one of the few 
campus locations that remained student -free, a sanctuary 
where she could escape the chaos of her online life and its 
relentless mysteries and intrusions. 
Entering the cafeteria, Dunya ordered a coffee and found a 
waist-high table by the window, angling her chair for an easy 
reach and clear view of the entrance. As she inhaled the rich 
aroma of her drink, she couldn’t help but half -hope Vesna

wanting something that was not another problem to solve. 
Serafim leaned close enough that Dunya forgot the room for 
one dangerous second. Her hand found the edge of Dunya’s 
vest, then stopped there. The touch was light, but it carried 
intent. 
“I want you,” Serafim whispered. 
Dunya’s eyes widened as guilt cut through the heat. 
“Vesna,” she stammered. “I... I can’t.” 
“I’m taken, too.” 
“We shouldn’t.” Dunya forced herself back from the edge of 
the moment. “Thank you. I just... I need to find her.” 
“She wouldn’t want you to stress. You’ve been through a lot 
lately. How far are you from home? I can take you.” 
The offer should have felt kind. Instead, it tightened 
something in Dunya’s stomach. Serafim’s concern had begun 
to feel placed rather than given. “That’s kind of you, but I’m 
fine.” The truth was that  she’d left her braces back at the 
apartment. They were heavy and awkward, and tonight she 
didn’t have the strength for any of it. Not the walking, not the 
pretense, and certainly not whatever Serafim was offering. 
“Well, at least let me help you to the door.” Serafim stood 
and extended her hand.

through a fog-drenched forest, its eyes glinting like shards of 
glass. Fire swept across a ruined city, devouring the skyline 
as bodies lined the streets. A young woman struggled against 
her bindings, terror frozen on her face. A Matron watched from 
the shadows, a yellow rose tucked in her hair. Then came the 
tree, vast and alive, its branches twisting toward the heavens. 
Dunya saw herself at its peak, looking down on the chaos 
spreading below, unable to move, unable to turn away as the 
vision swallowed her whole. 
“No. I don’t think I am.” Dunya said. 
The visions dissolved as quickly as they had come, leaving 
her trembling and unsteady.  
“What is it? What’s wrong?” Serafim’s voice sounded 
distant, muffled by the ringing in Dunya’s ears. 
She tried to speak, but the words tangled and fell apart 
before reaching her lips. “I... I’m not sure.” The images still 
burned in her mind, too vivid to be dreams yet too strange to 
be memories. 
“It’s all right,” Serafim whispered. “Just breathe.” 
Dunya inhaled sharply and leaned back, her body heavy 
with exhaustion. The motion sent her coffee cup teetering off 
the table. It should have fallen, but instead it froze midair,

“What did you do to me?” Dunya choked out, her voice 
hoarse with panic.  
Serafim stood over her, expression calm, eyes cold. “Only 
what you allowed. Now, where is the key?” 
Dunya writhed on the floor, her muscles seizing as the 
liquid scorched its path through her veins. She could feel it, 
like fire spreading through every nerve, searing her from the 
inside out. “I told you. I don’t know. I don’t know what you’re 
talking about,” she gasped, her voice breaking with the effort.  
She tried to push herself up, but her limbs were limp, 
betraying her. The floor felt like quicksand, dragging her 
down. “Please,” she whimpered, desperation clawing at her 
throat. “Just let me go.” 
“I can’t do that. Not until you give me what I need.” Serafim 
knelt and grabbed Dunya’s chin, forcing their eyes to meet. 
“Where is the key?”  
“I... I think I gave it to Vesna.” 
The room’s brightness suddenly flared, a blinding light 
stabbing through Dunya’s vision. She squinted, instinctively 
shielding her eyes, her pulse quickening with dread. From 
across the bay, flames tore into the sky, and a mushroom 
cloud bloomed, growing l arger, devouring the horizon as it 
spread. It swallowed the city’s gleaming lights, veiling them 
beneath a cloud of destruction.

The roar of the explosion overwhelmed her, forcing her 
hands instinctively to her ears, though it did little to muffle 
the sound. She watched in horror as windows shattered 
around her. Out of the corner of her eye, she saw Serafim 
crash to the ground, arms raised defensively over her head 
against the rain of glass and debris. Suddenly, the room 
plunged into darkness, and all Dunya could hear was the 
ragged rhythm of her own breathing. 
And then she shot up in bed, her eyes scanning the room. 
A deep breath of relief escaped her as she realized she was 
safe at home. Her headgear rested on a desk across from her, 
code-locked and charged. So, I didn’t fall asleep at the roll... 
With swift movements, Dunya pivoted into her wheelchair, 
gliding over to her workstation. She slipped the neural rig over 
her head, the crown tightening as sensors aligned along her 
scalp. A faint hum filled her ears. As she pulled on the device, 
she winced at the sting of the electrodes piercing her skin. The 
hardlight display materialized before her, layered with 
translucent panels hovering in the air. Streams of data 
scrolled in vertical columns, shifting as her eyes tracked them. 
She sifted through them  at a breakneck pace, searching for 
anomalies. 
A flash of memory cut through the fog. The campus visit. 
Dunya focused, straining to pull another fragment into view. 
A new face, a conversation, then nothing. The rest slipped 
away into darkness no matter how tightly she tried to hold it. 
Her breathing hitched as she pushed deeper into the neural 
feed, drawn toward a faint signal pulsing within her own data 
stream. It glowed in the haze of her thoughts like a beacon, 
an energy patte rn in her hippocampus that shouldn’t have 
been there. A cognitive implant she couldn’t remember ever 
having installed.  
Her ocular buzzed with a new message.

The panels flickered, reorganizing into a compact 
notification window: 
SENDER: SYNDICATE/UNIVERSITY. 
SUBJECT: NEW CONTRACT. 
PRIORITY: HIGH. 
She didn’t want to take on any new work, not with Vesna 
still missing, but she considered her options. She recalled 
what Yana had said at The Flock: 
“Wouldn’t that make us the delivery crew?” 
A part of her clung to the hope that each new contract might 
actually bring her closer to Vesna, even though she resisted 
the thought. She hated to think that Yana’s omen might be 
true, but with few leads left and fewer people she could trust, 
the contracts were her best chance. 
She curled her lips in anticipation and opened the message. 
The panels expanded, lines of encrypted text unraveling into 
readable format: 
SEARCH AND LOCATE. 
Dunya didn’t get tangled up in her targets ’ biologics; their 
physical identifiers were just noise that could cloud her 
mission’s clarity. The real hunt was in the web of VR, tracking 
their unique signatures through data streams, laying the 
groundwork for a real-world capture. It was cleaner that way, 
less personal. 
It’s better not to know, she reminded herself. But this time… 
Expanding the contract details, she scrutinized the extra 
data: 
SERAFIM SOROKIN 
BIO AGE: 22 
HEIGHT: 5’9”

to be. Her gaze lingered on the flickering name, her hand 
trembling as she hovered over the command to proceed. The 
interface pulsed faintly, waiting for confirmation. 
She read the data again, disbelief hollowing her out. Maybe 
it was a glitch, some database error, or a cruel coincidence. 
That had to be it. And yet the details were exact. 
She closed her eyes and pressed her fingers to her temples. 
The pain, the sleepless nights, the visions, they all blurred 
together. When she opened her eyes again, the interface 
hovered expectantly, its faint blue glow washing over her face. 
Her hand drifted toward the confirm  command. She exhaled 
slowly, caught between fear and exhaustion, wishing more 
than anything for the nightmares to stop.

CHAPTER NINE 
KLARA  
 
The Derge had once tried to rival Gred, prosperous and 
loud, its markets packed with traders, repair stalls, and 
engine smoke. Now it sat on the horizon as a ruin, a nest of 
outlaws and scavengers tearing each other apart over scraps 
of metal and warmth. T he approach was worse, a corridor of 
dead haulers, cracked pylons, and ice -swallowed road 
markers. She pushed through the elfin cedar and waist -deep 
snow, each drift collapsing under her weight with a muffled 
groan. The cold gnawed through her coat, sharp and familiar. 
It was the same kind of cold that had nearly killed her once. 
That storm still lived in her bones. The cold pulled the 
memory out of her, raw and bright: the sky splitting open, the 
wind howling like a wounded animal, the world turning white. 
The Vachka had struck in that chaos, overrunning the 
Syndicate outpost at Zavoyko while half the garrison froze in 
their trenches. They wanted the springs. Everyone did. Out 
there, heat and running water meant survival, and the 
geothermal wells were worth dying for. 
Her mission then had been to support the Syndicate troops 
dug in among the basalt crags to the east, defending what 
remained of Zavoyko at all costs. The ARRT Antenna had 
fallen years earlier, but the spring line, repair sheds, trenches, 
and Avacha approaches still fed the Yelizovo-Zavoyko defense 
system. If those fell, the southern approaches would open and 
Petropavlovsk would lose the last defensive ring between the 
city and the hills. The old saying still held true: no roads led 
to Kamchatka. The last plane had taken off thirty years before 
that. 
Driven by duty, Klara had abandoned her post at the radio 
station and joined the fighting along the ruined tower line,

and deliberate, drew closer. A shadow loomed over her, vast 
enough to blot the light. She forced her eyes open and saw the 
bear standing above her, chest rising and falling like a 
bellows.

finish her, but instead she felt the brush of a paw against her

steady, impossibly calm. The beast studied her, then leaned

turned to heat, then to something else. The bleeding stopped. 
The torn flesh sealed. Breath came easier. 
When the pain finally ebbed, so did her strength. She 
sagged into the snow, vision swimming, the bear still watching 
her as darkness gathered at the edges of her sight. 
The bear rose and lumbered away, vanishing into the 
swirling ice and snow that enclosed them like a guardian 
shield. As the storm eased, Klara found herself alone. She 
longed to follow the creature but couldn’t move. Cold crept 
back into her limbs, and her  sight began to dim when a 
shadowed figure emerged from the haze, lifting her gently and 
carrying her away. 
Through the haze, a figure took shape, moving toward her 
with measured steps. At first, Klara thought it was another 
vision, a trick of exhaustion. Then the wind shifted, revealing 
a familiar outline, the curve of the shoulders, the stride. A 
faint glow ca ught her attention, two points of red cutting 
through the dimness. Her breath hitched as recognition 
settled in. Vatraliyna. 
She was flanked by three women, two nursing fresh 
wounds. They must have crossed countless snowbanks, 
ravines, and frozen rivers to reach her. As night deepened, the 
cold’s grip tightened, gnawing at Klara’s very marrow. She 
pulled her cloak closer, seeking shelter from the wind. Her lips 
parted, the words of gratitude forming but never finding 
breath. Each time she surfaced from the blur of exhaustion, 
she noticed the ibexes’ packs growing lighter, the hours 
stretching longer.

saddles, silent and spent. When the outline of a cave finally 
emerged through the blowing snow, a ripple of relief passed 
through the group . They slowed to a stop, and with her 
strength failing, Klara leaned on Vatraliyna for support as she 
dismounted. Wrapped in a fur blanket, she sank into its 
warmth, grateful for even that small comfort.  
“We’ll make camp here, ” Vatraliyna declared. “I’ll start a 
fire.” 
Klara attempted to sit up but faltered, weakened by the loss 
of blood and the aftershock of their harrowing experience. 
“Rest,” Vatraliyna urged, her tone gentle but firm. “You 
need to rest.” 
“Did we win?” Klara asked. 
Vatraliyna shook her head. “No. But we live. That is 
enough.” 
Klara wanted to argue. It was an ugly answer, and 
Vatraliyna had made it sound like discipline. The fire blurred 
before Klara could find the strength. 
She awoke to the soft urgency of Vatraliyna’s voice. 
“Klara, wake up.” 
Blinking her eyes open, Klara found Vatraliyna ’s face 
looming over her, lit by the soft glow of firelight. Although 
night still enveloped the world and she hadn’t rested for long, 
she felt a renewed sense of energy. 
“What is it? ” she asked, her fingers brushing the tender, 
healing flesh where the bear had licked her wounds. 
“I’m not sure, ” Vatraliyna said, “but I saw something out 
there, watching us. We need to be cautious. I don’t think we’re 
alone.”

CHAPTER TEN 
VESNA  
 
Something was building, low and steady, and Vesna wasn’t 
sure she’d come back from it. The machines surrounded her 
with a slow, resonant hum that worked its way into her chest. 
Light shifted across the walls in fluid motion, the colors 
folding into one another like waves. She kept her hands on the 
armrests, resisting the urge to move, to break the rhythm that 
held the room together. 
Nadya drifted through the glow, her fingers shaping quick 
commands that scattered the colors into new patterns. She 
glanced back with a measured calm. “Nervous?” 
A chill ran through Vesna at the question. The lights 
seemed to draw closer, brushing her arms with static. Nerves 
she understood. This was different, something alive in the 
light that held her attention and wouldn’t let go. 
“Maybe. A little,” she said. 
Nadya’s gaze lingered, calm and unblinking. “It’s okay to be 
nervous,” she said softly, her voice almost swallowed by the 
hum of the machines. “But more importantly, are you ready?” 
“Got nothing better to do,” Vesna muttered. Her gaze drifted 
to the wires spreading across the floor, twisting like veins 
through the concrete. Nadya  had said the machine would 
reach through her memories, and already fragments were 
stirring at the edges of thought, faces half-forgotten, moments 
she’d tried to bury. The machinery droned in time with her 
breathing, steady and patient, as if waiting for permission to 
dig deeper. Nadya called it training, but the way she had said 
it left Vesna guessing what that really meant.

Relax, Vesna. It’s just sizing you up. Checking out your brain 
patterns, your DNA. Nothing scary.” 
“I get it, but... What if it finds something bad, you know?” 
“Seriously, Vesna, we’re not scanning for a secret evil gene. 
It’s about understanding you better, not digging up skeletons. 
Think of it as setting the stage before the real work begins.” 
“No surprise supervillain origin story,” Vesna mused. “Still 
feels like standing on the edge of the world  though, looking 
down.” 
“Most people feel that way before the shift. Once it starts, 
the fear turns into focus.” 
The thought of backing out flickered and passed. She gave 
a quick nod before she could change her mind. The chair was 
cool under her palms, grounding her. “Alright. Let’s do this. 
Show me what this thing can do.” 
Nadya gave a small nod of her own and reached for the 
controls. “Hold still.” 
A soft hiss came from beneath the chair as it adjusted, 
cradling Vesna’s weight.

seemed to shift around her. Lights pulsed in sync, the hum 
deepening until it filled her chest. The air carried a faint

shapes bending with each flicker of light. At the center of the 
alcove waited a sleek, obsidian headset resting on a pedestal, 
its surface catching the glow like polished glass. 
“Once you put that on, the real work begins,” Nadya said. 
“The serum doesn’t activate on its own. It responds to what 
we call cellular command sentences,  patterns formed in the 
language centers of your brain. In simple terms, your 
thoughts guide the rewrite. Your memories will keep you 
anchored and give you control over the process.” 
Vesna’s eyes shifted to the headset. The sight of it drew her 
in, sharp and magnetic. Nadya’s words stayed with her, 
echoing in a way that felt almost physical. Rewriting her own 
code and using memories as anchors felt less like science and 
more like stepping into something alive, something waiting for 
her to cross the line. 
Nadya gestured to the machine. “She’ll guide you through 
it. Trust her.”

∆∆∆ 
 
The darkness pressed close, humming low beneath her 
skin. Then, almost imperceptibly, it began to change. Color 
seeped outward, sketching a world into being. What had been 
empty space gained weight and texture, the surface beneath 
her feet hardening into s hifting layers of soil and stone. The 
void was painting itself, learning what it wanted to be. 
She turned slowly. Luminous trees rose at the edge of sight, 
their branches threading together across the sky. The sight 
was beautiful in a way that made her uneasy, as if the world 
had been arranged with care not for wonder, but for control. 
A faint drizzle began to fall between the trees, the drops 
catching light as they descended. Each droplet stretched, 
elongating midair until it became a shape, a silhouette, a 
movement. The rain gathered into bodies that began to turn 
and sway, their garme nts glimmering with pale color. 
Dancers. Their motions were measured, synchronized, as 
though the storm itself had learned choreography. She didn’t 
know the ritual, but something inside her did. 
Vesna tried to stay still, but her body moved anyway, 
muscles finding the rhythm on their own. Patterns rippled 
across the dancers’ garments, spirals, waves, and creatures 
she recognized. Brown bears. Amur tigers. Snow sheep. The 
symbols changed as they ci rcled her, flickering between 
meanings she couldn’t grasp, half warning, half invitation.

body moved without consent. The dance consumed her,  
rhythm and breath merging into one. A distant chorus rose, 
pulling her toward its center. Then the melody twisted, 
harmony giving way to noise that surged and broke apart. The

dream. Shapes resolved into steel towers clawing at a winter 
sky. Shadows stretched across the snow like scars. A familiar 
weight settled in her gut. She knew this battlefield. 
Vesna looked down, her breath catching. The void of 
dreamlight hardened into the matte gleam of armor. She 
flexed her fingers, the movement triggering a faint metallic 
whisper as carbon fiber plates shifted with her. Black, light, 
and impenetrable. Her old lieutenant’s uniform. 
She turned her hands over, the faint frost catching on the 
polished edge of her gauntlet. The rifle rested against her 
shoulder, its familiar weight anchoring her to the moment. 
The weapon’s surface was scarred and dull in places, each 
mark a story she wis hed she could forget. At her hip, a thin 
scarf fluttered in the icy wind, blue and red against the 
washed-out landscape, the emblem of the wolf barely visible 
through the frost. 
The world around her flattened into a stark wash of whites 
and grays, a winter battlefield drawn in rough, uncertain 
strokes. Through the drifting smoke, the outline of a burning 
bus emerged, its metal frame groaning in the heat. In its 
shadow, an old woman crouched low, her head wrapped in a 
worn babushka still carrying the faint blush of yellow roses 
long faded. Firelight wavered across her face, tracing every 
line and hollow, making her look carved from the same ash 
that filled the air.

beneath her, Vesna’s instincts took over. She snapped down 
her visor, her vision shifting to thermal signatures and target 
vectors. In one swift motion , she pulled the elderly woman 
down, shielding her as they hit the ground. 
For a moment, silence held. Only the crackle of fire and 
Zakharovna’s faint whimper cut through it. Vesna pushed 
herself upright, muscles trembling as she steadied her breath.

together in the wind.

steady, unhurried. Silver hair spilled over her shoulders, 
catching the firelight like molten wire. For an instant, Vesna 
thought she was seeing a ghost. Then the woman lifted her 
gaze, and the world seemed to narrow to that single look.

CHAPTER ELEVEN 
YANA  
 
Yana tossed back another shot of spudka, the authentic 
burn igniting her throat like wildfire. She was surprised they 
even served it here—real spudka meant someone, somewhere, 
was growing potatoes off the record —but she embraced it. It 
was her third in as many minutes, and the barroom’s edges 
started to smudge and blend. But that didn’t matter. She only 
craved the numbing embrace of oblivion. Cheap alc ohol was 
better than cheap synth, she mused. After all, what’s a fat 
liver to a fried brain? As she chased the burn with memories 
that haunted her, she couldn’t help but wonder if she’d ever 
escape her vices and ghosts. 
And as if on cue, one such ghost stirred. Mikhail, her trusty 
housekeeper, echoed through her cups. “Yana, this isn’t you,” 
she could almost hear his old voice say, just as she’d listlessly 
lined up another dose of laced exo. That fine white powder 
always promised an escape. Hours would blur into days as 
she lost herself in virtual, drifting . M eals had become an 
afterthought. 
Now, she wondered where Mikhail was, how he was doing. 
She could still picture him tapping his cane against the 
kitchen tile and calling it temporary whenever she offered to 
buy him a better one. Had he found work in one of the other 
gold suites among the towering marble spires of Almaznyy 
Gorizont? Or, she feared, was he enduring hardships, possibly 
mistreated by less compassionate matrons? In Gred ’s 
wealthiest district, the harsh reality was that reality wasn’t 
kind to old men. Those like Mikhail, remnants of a time long 
forgotten, were almost always  relegated to the most menial 
and thankless of servant roles. The thought twisted in her 
heart. I promised to protect him, and I failed . In a city where

Yana turned, the motion slow and unsteady. Behind her 
stood Dimitra, a freakishly tall and imposing figure with a 
severe expression. Their wispy pink hair and half-shaved head 
caught the neon glow flashing from the bottles of alcohol that 
lined the shelves behind the bar. 
The Baraka Lounge was a high-end establishment, the kind 
of place where people went to see and be seen. If it wasn ’t 
winter, the outdoor patio would be teeming with old women 
smoking hookah and sipping overpriced cocktails, while the 
indoor café would be bustling with patrons enjoying 
cappuccinos and croissants. But it had been winter for a 
decade now , and only those with business to conduct 
frequented these kinds of establishments. 
“I’ve learned that you ’re a heartless bitch, ” Yana slurred. 
“And I’m going to murder you.” 
She swung, a sloppy, desperate strike. Dimitra moved like 
a shadow, fingers clamping at her throat before she could 
draw a breath. Panic surged through her, sharp and animal. 
Through the haze of alcohol and her dwindling air supply, 
Yana caught sight of the tattoos winding across Dimitra’s 
forearms. The familiar swirls of black, swamp green, and pink 
ink sparked a deep, visceral loathing. Even through the blur, 
she couldn’t miss the serpent glowing neon against the skin, 
coiled around a dagger, a twin to the mark on their neck. The 
sight confirmed what she already knew: Dimitra bore the 
notorious sigil of the Vory, along with the reputation of one of 
their deadliest assassins. 
“You’re going to help me get to Grigoreva. If you don ’t, I’ll 
make sure your little secret is exposed. Do you understand? ” 
Dimitra’s grip tightened around Yana’s neck, constricting her 
airway for another heartbeat before releasing her. 
Yana gasped, her vision swimming as she fought to regain 
her breath. “I…understand.”

Yana navigated the throng, her movements hindered by the 
pressing crowd. Street vendors vied for attention, their calls 
mingling with the sizzle and pop of skewers on open grills. The 
air was thick with the scent of kebabs, each spear glazed in 
tangy Yuzhno sauce, a specialty of wild berries and volcanic 
spices. She half-smiled at the thought; however tempting the 
aroma, she knew the only real meat in danger of sizzling was 
her own if she didn’t do this job quickly. 
Oktyabrya Prospekt pulsed as the lifeblood of Gred, its eight 
lanes teeming with vehicles and pedestrians. Even in the icy 
grip of winter, this vibrant artery refused to freeze. The 
expansive sidewalks, peppered with dogwood trees and cafés, 
embraced the bustling cityscape. A blend of old Soviet 
architecture, reimagined with ostentatious Art Deco flair, 
juxtaposed against sleek glass -and-steel behemoths, their 
lofty spires piercing the cloud-veiled sky. 
She halted before an imposing structure, its facade a 
marriage of marble and glass. Cyrillic letters spelled out 
Усадьба Григорьева, with the English translation, Grigoreva 
Estates, just beneath. The use of Cyrillic was more about 
status than communication these days. Yana paused, 
checking that the translations matched. 
Nestled between two towering skyscrapers, a thirteen-story 
mansion loomed, its red-tiled roof standing out boldly against 
its monolithic neighbors.  A high concrete wall concealed the 
estate’s grounds from prying eyes. 
Yana’s entrance through the revolving door marked her 
passage from the chaos outside to the hushed, grand interior. 
This shit really hits different, she thought, her gaze lifting to 
the ornate atrium as she stepped in. Intertwining vines crept

With purpose in her stride, Yana crossed the opulent lobby,

together like ash and ice. She liked to imagine it told the story 
of the penin sula—its eruptions, its long winters —but she 
knew it was just another designer’s flourish. As she neared 
the elevators, the bellhop’s eyes narrowed with suspicion. She 
caught the look, understood it for what it was, and kept 
moving. 
Yana glanced at the young man who held the elevator door 
open for her. Pity stirred in her chest, recognizing the invisible 
chains that bound him to servitude. His tense shoulders  
mirrored a resigned acceptance, and Yana’s heart ached with 
the helplessness of their shared situation. 
As she stepped out of the elevator, an exquisite silken 
runner stretched down the corridor, its pattern of entwined 
figures traced in fluid, suggestive red lines. It led her toward 
an imposing wooden door dominated by an ornate brass 
knocker. Before her fi ngers could touch the cold metal, the 
door groaned open to reveal a striking young woman. 
Her raven hair cascaded like a silken waterfall down her 
back, and a sheer robe, hugging her thin frame, whispered 
secrets of her form beneath. The woman ’s voice carried a 
disinterested lilt as she inquired, “Yes?”

gold buttons that seemed to amplify the chaise’s opulence. In

focus. After knocking, she announced, “Baroness Grigoreva,

surpassed the splendor of the penthouse. An ornate four -
poster bed dominated the space, and a stately desk faced a 
bay window that offered a breathtaking view of the bustling 
street below. Rich details fi lled the room, from the plush 
carpet underfoot to the intricate moldings along the walls, 
instilling a sense of wonder in Yana as she absorbed her 
surroundings.

key. Inserting it into a concealed slot, the elevator started its 
descent. After a few moments, it halted three floors below the 
lobby, its level unmarked on the panel. The doors parted, 
revealing a dim, stretched -out corridor. Grigoreva marched 
onward, her heels clacking against the concrete floor. Yana 
followed, struggling somewhat to maintain her poise in her 
new six-inch pumps. 
At the hallway’s end, double doors required another key to 
unlock. Yana ’s skin prickled with apprehension as she 
entered, her eyes scrutinizing the shadows for any indication 
of movement. A large pod, suspended from the ceiling in the 
center of the room, was enveloped by wires and tubes that 
snaked off in every direction, vanishing into darkness. Yana’s 
instinct was to flee, but the Baroness pressed a hand on her 
back forcing her forward. 
“Where are we?” Yana asked. 
“This is a private transportation network. It’s how we 
traverse the city unseen,” the Baroness explained, gently 
guiding Yana with a hand as they stepped into the pod 
together. Once inside, the pod began to move, slowly at first, 
then rapidly accelerating.  Gripping the guardrails, Yana’s 
knuckles whitened as the tubes and wires attached to the 
vehicle whipped wildly around. Shutting her eyes, she tried to 
ignore the disorienting sight of sparks flying past as the pod 
raced through the tunnel network.

Taking a moment to compose herself, Yana suddenly 
became aware of the stark simplicity of her plain black attire. 
Quite the setup,  she thought. With renewed resolve, she 
quickened her pace to match the confident stride of her host, 
determined not to be outdone in presence or purpose. 
Yet as she surveyed the room further, an unsettling feeling 
crept in. She felt exposed among the sea of masked faces. The 
Baroness caught her fleeting unease with a glance. “No need 
to hide your face here, my dear. No one will recognize you.” 
Seen but unknown, another realm of her making. She had 
no need for encryption here. Reassured, Yana straightened, 
adopting an air of poise she didn’t quite feel but knew she 
could pull off. 
Before she could get carried away, the Baroness, now only 
a few steps ahead, beckoned her over to a lively group. “Ah, 
Grigoreva,” a tall woman with a chiseled jawline greeted, icy 
eyes peering out from behind a porcelain mask depicting 
Morana, the goddess  of death. “You’ve brought us a 
new…friend.” 
The Baroness smiled and nodded. “Yes, this is Ms. Kuular. 
Yana, these are some of my closest colleagues.” 
The women eyed Yana with interest, and anxiety surged 
within her. Forcing a smile, she said, “It’s nice to meet you 
all.” 
The tallest woman extended her hand. “I am Baroness 
Rostova,” she said, her voice warm. As Yana shook her hand, 
a bit of tension eased.

“Let’s start with your family. What can you tell me about 
them?” 
Yana hesitated, her gaze dropping briefly. “It’s not all that 
glamorous. My mother was a dancer, but she passed away 
when I was young. I don’t have many memories of her. My 
father was from Tuva. They met in Yakutsk, where he worked 
as a miner after the Great War. He brought us here for work, 
but he died in the Strangers’ Revolt. He was an alcoholic.” She 
paused, the weight of it settling over her. “I suppose my life 
hasn’t strayed far from theirs.” 
The Baroness took another sip, leaning back in her chair. 
“In my opinion, it was a mistake to keep the men in this city 
alive. I’d have my bellhops electrocuted if they ever dared to 
touch me or my girls. You’re not like the others, Yana. I can 
sense you’re different.” 
“Is that a positive or negative development?” 
“It’s difficult to say. But I believe it could be quite 
intriguing.” 
As the opening strains of “Moon River” filled the air, the 
Baroness rose gracefully. “Would you care to dance?” Yana’s 
heart raced, but she found herself standing before she could 
reconsider. 
The Baroness took her hand, leading her onto the dance 
floor. The familiar melody of Breakfast at Tiffany’s played in 
her ears, a favorite of Yana’s, though in this moment, she 
barely had time to savor it. 
The Flock occasionally hosted old movie nights on a large 
digital screen in their common room. Yana would sit and 
watch while other patrons ERPed around her, lost in their 
virtual fantasies. As the familiar melody of “Moon River ” 
played, she suddenly realized she preferred The Flock’s 
carefree, hedonistic atmosphere to the gala’s stilted opulence.

CHAPTER TWELVE 
ZAKHAROVNA  
 
In the greasy light of a Vilnius night, they lingered beneath 
flickering neon, faces rippling in the reflected glow. Rain fell 
steady, never enough to wash the city clean. The scent of 
seared fat and cigarette haze hung heavy, settling deep into 
coats and hair. Zakharovna moved through it as if she 
belonged there. These streets had shaped her, every alley and 
doorway etched into memory. The mingled reek of meat and 
exhaust was the perfume of a city that never stopped feeding 
on itself. 
Between lab sessions, she drifted to the brothels. They had 
become her second laboratory, a place to study the chemistry 
of desire and to test the limits of what could be altered in flesh 
and mind. At twenty-five, the work had already taken its toll. 
Synthetic nucleotides, forbidden compounds, and long nights 
spent reprogramming cellular pathways had left their traces 
in her skin and in the lifeless ends of her hair. The women 
there never judged her for it; they touched her like she was 
still whole. Each en counter offered something she could 
measure—heart rate, hormone shift, a momentary flicker of 
trust—before she lost herself in the pulse of other lives. The 
brothels offered both data and escape, one experiment feeding 
the other. 
The days soon blurred together. The intoxication was part 
chemical, part human. She found solace in fleeting warmth, 
in strangers who asked no questions. It was during one of 
those evenings that Vair entered her orbit. Virginia Attrae, 
psychologist and mad am to the city’s elite, quickly became 
more than an acquaintance. She was the only person who 
seemed to understand Zakharovna’s hunger for knowledge 
and ruin in equal measure.

leave the artificial intelligence lab in Vilnius University’s 
psychiatric department. The research was revolutionary, yet 
it felt small compared to the questions clawing at her mind. 
Academia had boundaries, and she had begun to see beyond 
them. Still, she needed its tools a little longer. The dissertation 
could wait. 
She accepted a position as a research assistant, a 
compromise that kept her close to what mattered most: the 
machines, the data, and the human subjects. The lab had just 
begun the Artificial Dreams Project, developing full -body 
virtual reality suits for ps ychotherapy trials. Immersed in 
these simulations, she interacted with generated 
personalities, observing how they navigated pleasure, fear, 
and attachment in a world built entirely from code. 
As her focus deepened, the thought of home slipped away, 
replaced by the pull of uncharted territory and the strange 
comfort she found at the edge of the known. 
In the aftermath of the Great War, the landscape shifted, 
and the United Federation of Europe rose as a formidable 
power. Zakharovna’s artificial intelligence lab, positioned at 
the forefront of post-war innovation, turned its efforts toward 
the psychologi cal scars left behind. The most promising 
creation to emerge from that work was V.A.I.R. —Virtual 
Augmented Intimate Relations—a psychotherapist and virtual 
environment hostess conceived as a tribute to a departed 
friend.

V.A.I.R. had been designed to ease the trauma of returning 
soldiers. Its ability to calm fractured minds was extraordinary, 
yet the University soon recognized the limits of such progress. 
Peace brought sc arcity. The system’s therapy protocols 
demanded immense computational resources, and as civilian 
networks strained under constant demand, there was little 
power left for indulgence. 
The collapse began quietly. Data centers went dark, virtual 
worlds blinked out, and the global net fractured. Humanity 
survived, but its great digital architecture did not. Historians 
would call it the Divergence, an age of decline whose origins 
no one cou ld fully explain. Amid the ruin, Zakharovna 
preserved what she could, sealing a fragment of V.A.I.R.’s code 
on a hidden drive, a relic from a vanished world she had 
helped create. 
Her reverie was abruptly shattered by the sudden swell of 
music, signaling the start of the evening’s burlesque show. 
The vibrant energy of the performance and the dazzling 
costumes jolted her back to this alternate life, the low hum of 
conversation and the occasional clinking of glasses filling the 
dimly lit cabaret.

CHAPTER THIRTEEN 
VESNA  
 
It had been Nadya who first introduced her to Marfa and 
Gala. “They’re the best we have from the University’s training 
program,” Nadya had said flatly. Vesna had been skeptical at 
first, fresh from the rigorous combat sims. She was still 
adjusting to the fact that she would soon be leading flesh-and-
blood soldiers again. 
Nadya had assured her of their physical and mental 
readiness, listing their records as if they were gospel. Marfa, 
the detonations expert, could supposedly dismantle any 
explosive device. Gala, meanwhile, was a prodigy with the 
sniper rifle, her precision and calm under pressure evident in 
the University’s files with sub -half-second target acquisition, 
perfect shot groupings, and no failed simulations on record. 
In the days that followed their introduction, Vesna observed 
them through the unit’s training rotations and readiness 
drills. She watched how they moved, how they adapted under 
pressure, how they seemed to anticipate one another’s rhythm 
without a word. Th eir focus impressed her, their precision 
almost mechanical in its consistency. They weren’t just 
soldiers; they were survivors, each carrying their own silent 
battles, their own reasons for joining this fight. In their eyes, 
Vesna saw reflections of her ow n resolve and her own 
unspoken vows, along with the faint echo of something colder, 
something shaped by the same machinery that had once 
forged her. They too were weapons, she knew. 
Recalling the details from their dossiers, Vesna’s mind 
wandered back to her earliest days with the Black Wolves.

against the University, when she had skulked  the hallowed,

into the open. We do this clean. Make it count.”

they needed to veer off the main thoroughfares. The command 
center lay beyond the plaza,  accessible only through a

shadows around them thickened. The walls of the buildings 
loomed high above, creating a claustrophobic corridor that 
muffled the sounds of the city  behind them.  Here, in these 
confined spaces, every footstep echoed, every breath seemed 
louder.

air, and Vesna’s hand shot up, signaling Marfa and Gala to 
stop. Her heart thumped against her ribs, adrenaline 
sharpening her focus. Even with their precautions, the drone’s 
thermal imaging and sophisticated sensors could compromise 
them.

Quickly, Vesna motioned for cover. They pressed against a 
shadowed wall, their painted faces blending into the darkness. 
In a hushed tone, she relayed her plan through her earpiece. 
Marfa pulled a compact signal jammer from her pack. With 
a deft flick of her finger, she activated the device. Almost 
immediately, the drone ’s steady hum stuttered, its smooth 
flight turning erratic. The lights on its underbelly flickered 
briefly, betraying its momentary confusion. 
Seizing the window of opportunity, Vesna darted across the 
street. Marfa and Gala followed in perfect sync behind. 
As they reached the opposite side, the drone recovered, 
resuming its patrol over the area they had just vacated. Vesna 
exhaled silently, a momentary relief washing over her. They  
pressed forward, blending into the shadows as they closed in 
on their target. 
The kebab shop’s bustling exterior blended into the urban 
landscape, hiding something far more dangerous. Behind its 
weathered sign and faded awnings was a large, vertically 
sliding garage door —a covert gateway to the command post. 
Vesna signaled Marfa and Gala, the command clear without a 
word. Marfa approached the discreet service entrance and 
placed small charges around the perimeter. Meanwhile, Gala 
positioned herself on a hanging staircase, with a clear line of 
sight to the entrance. 
Vesna crouched near the main gate, her titanium alloy 
pistol resting in her hand with its familiar weight —light yet 
formidable, like an old friend. It was as if the years since her 
lieutenant days had melted away. 
Marfa detonated the explosives. 
With no sound or smoke, the air around the command 
post’s entrance subtly shuddered. The door remained intact, 
but the pressure wave had done its job.

of the room settled around her. Their shared space, doubling 
as kitchen and meeting area, offered a brief pause from the 
mission’s relentless pace. On the kitchen island sat a loaf of 
bread, some cheese, and a bowl of apples. Most would call it 
luxury in a city surviving on mealworm paste, but to Vesna, it 
was just fuel. After years away from the force, she’d already 
adjusted to the basic proteins and fibers that kept her going.  
The walls were sparse but held a few paintings, each telling 
its own quiet story in the room’s dim lighting. Vesna’s gaze 
lingered on one—a barren landscape, all gray lines and muted 
browns, capturing a deep sense of desolation. Another showed 
a stormy sea, the brush strokes turbulent, as if trying to trap 
the chaos of the waves. 
Turning her attention back to Marfa, Vesna watched as she 
casually enjoyed a cigar while activating the hardlight 
projection system. The room shifted as the device hummed to 
life, a three -dimensional map materializing above the table. 
Vesna leaned in, her focus locking onto the dynamic display 
of Arkadya’s movements. The hologram flickered, revealing

CHAPTER FOURTEEN 
MARIA  
 
Maria breathed into the frigid air as she surveyed the 
warehouse. The outskirts of Gred had always whispered of a 
forlorn past, but here in the shadows of this dilapidated 
structure, the whispers roared. This was a place forgotten by 
time, remembered only by those who danced with danger. 
Tatyana’s instructions had been clear, a stark command 
that cut through the haze of Maria ’s thoughts. “Trust in the 
skills that have kept you alive. Serafim is a tool; use her.” 
Maria replayed Tatyana ’s warning in her mind as she 
stepped carefully over the scattered debris on the warehouse 
floor. Her previous ventures with Serafim had always unfolded 
in the cryptic realms of cyberspace, their identities shrouded, 
their collaboration a carefully orchestr ated dance in the 
shadows of encryption. With Dunya, there had been a 
predictable rhythm, an established familiarity in their 
exchanges. But Serafim was different; she was an enigma, her 
methods, and motives less clear. 
The tension curled inside Maria like a tight spring. Every 
step she took here was a conversation with the ghosts of her 
failed exploits, the memories pulsing in her cybernetic veins. 
Yet, with each heartbeat, the hunger for redemption forged her 
resolve. She couldn’t afford to drown in the quicksand of her 
past—too much was at stake. 
A silhouette emerged from the gloom, its edges blurred by 
the uncertain light. Serafim. Even as she stood still, there was 
an undeniable presence about her, like a storm cloud 
promising havoc.

into the depth of her eyes —a tumultuous mix of secrets and

Maria glanced at Serafim, finding a flicker of curiosity in 
her companion’s expression. For a moment, she wondered if 
Serafim saw this not just as an infiltration but as an 
experiment. 
As they approached the entrance, the vast archway 
captured Maria’s attention.  It seemed almost alive, the ivy 
intertwining with the stonework in a slow, hypnotic rhythm 
that gave the illusion of breathing. To her, it appeared less like 
a doorway and more like an enormous mouth, poised and 
ready to consume all who dared to enter. 
Her eyes drifted across the room’s expanse, the sheen on 
the walls drawing her in a slow, meandering sweep of the 
glossy black surfaces. The dim glow from the Spire’s core cast 
elongated shadows that stretched across the floor, softening 
the edges where darkness met light. Her ears, attuned to the 
silence, picked up the faintest disruption —a whisper of 
movement, or perhaps fabric against the cool, polished stone. 
A chill traced up her spine as her eyes adjusted, began to 
discern forms within the shadows. There was a presence, she 
realized, something or someone anchoring the weight of the 
room. The sense of another ’s breath seemed to mingle with 
the sterile air. 
Serafim remained close, a reassuring presence, her spectral 
image a mere wisp against the somber backdrop. Maria ’s 
focus narrowed, the periphery fading, as the figure slowly 
came into view. 
A man. As out of place as those old images in the Arkyv of 
Earth’s single moon, a piece of history discordant with the 
known reality of its twin.

Leaning on a cane, his long brown trench coat swept the 
polished floor with each subtle shift of his weight. His bucket 
hat cast his eyes in shadow, yet as they came into the light, 
they glowed with the artificial luminescence of screens, 
scrolling with streams of code. 
Droplets of a viscous substance glistened at the rim of his 
nostrils, catching the light from the lantern he held in his left 
hand—an incongruous note of the organic in a domain of 
silicon and circuits. 
“Welcome,” his voice emerged, an assemblage of diverse 
tones stitched seamlessly together.  His gaze lingered on 
Maria. “I am Gaspar, the warden of the gateway. Do you 
possess the fortitude to delve deeper into this enigma, or do 
the shadows already grip your spirits?” 
Here stood the Spire’s initial guardian, an entity crafted to 
test the psyches of intruders with its bizarre appearance and 
unnerving presence. Maria couldn’t shake the feeling that 
they were trying to freak them out before the real game even 
began. 
Gaspar gestured toward a dim corridor, his eyes never 
leaving Maria’s. “Follow me,” he instructed, turning with an 
air of finality. 
As they stepped through the archway, the door behind them 
sealed shut with a thud that echoed Maria’s racing heart, an 
unspoken cue that retreat was off the table. She exhaled 
quietly, grounding herself in the vast chamber that began to 
materialize before them. The library’s core cast a dim glow, 
causing shelves of ancient, leather-bound books to gradually 
emerge from the shadows. 
“No pressure,” Maria muttered, half -ironic, pushing 
forward into the sea of untold stories that this ancient library 
offered.

“The book that doesn ’t belong,” Gaspar said. “Seek it out. 
But beware, the tomes are sibylline . They reveal themselves 
only to the seeker. No other eyes will discern their titles or 
stories. Not even mine.” 
He paused briefly, his gaze shifting to each of them. “You 
will have to find your respective volume,” he said. “It’s a piece 
of the puzzle, crucial to completing our combined cipher. Be 
diligent. The answer you seek resides within its pages or 
perhaps even hidden in plain sight off it. ” He added with a 
measured seriousness, “Choose wisely—each of you gets only 
one chance. A misstep not only fails your own trial but also 
seals the fate of your ally.” 
Seraphim smirked, glancing at Maria. “Just another day on 
the babachain, huh?” 
“Yeah, we’ve danced this dance before.” 
Maria moved along the aisles, her fingers hovering over the 
spines. Not unsurprisingly, each appeared to be  a glowing 
chronicle of Zakharovna’s life—triumphs, failures, intimacies, 
betrayals. Her own existence felt alien in this mausoleum of 
her mentor’s past; a cyborg, a fused being, an echo not merely 
of flesh but of ambition and will. 
What if she chose wrong? The thought flickered through her 
mind like static. Constructs had threatened her before; at 
worst, she could initiate an emergency override and jack 
themselves out. If that failed, they’d fight off some digital 
demon or another. Still, the stakes felt unnervingly high this 
time. She couldn’t afford to let doubt creep in. 
The titles danced before her eyes, ancient and obscure, 
until the dance slowed, focused, and stopped. One spine 
seemed to stand out against the multitude, a subtle beacon in 
the dim. “The Progeny’s Path: Artificial Minds and the Transfer 
of Consciousness.”

I didn’t spill innocent blood then, and I refuse to spill it now. 
Is this trial a measure of conscience or brutality? What does the 
Spire want—my redemption or my relapse? The moral algebra 
of monsters held no sway over her now. Whether a test of heart 
or a trial by combat, she knew she would endure. Onto the 
next challenge.

thickened with anticipation. Gaspar’s form began to dissolve.

convergence of all that you are, all that you have been, and all 
that you may yet become.” 
He shimmered, and the colors from the sky bled into his 
form. “And that truth, ” he said, “will be found neither here,

headache suddenly erupted, its intensity like a relentless vice 
gripping her skull. The industrial outlines of the warehouse—

way, an d she collapsed to the cold concrete floor. The last 
thing she saw before she began to slip away was Serafim ’s 
worried face fade into the encroaching darkness.

CHAPTER FIFTEEN 
DUNYA  
 
The doors to the Grand Mariner’s Cathedral loomed over 
her. Dunya paused beneath them, tracing the joints where the 
panels met, too precise for human work. Of course, they 
weren’t. In the Arkyv, she had studied the Aquilonian  
Pantheon, raised on the ruins of older temples by hands that 
never worshiped there. A society that thought its monuments 
eternal, blind to the labor buried beneath them. The thought 
lingered as she rested her palm against the door, the chill 
seeping into her skin and settling somewhere deeper, where 
memory and doubt met. The wood was coarse and cold, the 
carvings deep but uniform, every imperfection accounted for. 
She knew this feeling, the quiet weight before a door that never 
truly stays shut. They never do, she thought. 
The pressure built under her palms. For a moment nothing 
moved, then the weight shifted, a slow give that felt almost 
alive. A sigh escaped the seam as cool air spilled through the 
widening gap. 
Snow swirled in after her as she crossed the threshold into 
the narthex, curling around her boots before settling on the 
stone. The air inside was still and sharp, the storm’s roar 
outside fading to a low hum through the outer walls and vents, 
softer still beneath it the steadier hum of her Skelet concealed 
under her cargo pants. 
The light changed as the doors closed behind her. The 
storm’s pale glare gave way to a softer amber wash that bled 
from the seams in the walls.  Her eyes adjusted slowly. 
Columns lined the nave ahead, their surfaces catching faint, 
shifting reflections from candles or maybe screens hidden 
deeper in the alcoves. The air tasted faintly of resin and dust.

across the floor in slow, uneven bands of color, giving bodies 
to names Baba Fenya had taught her in childhood, long before 
Gred arranged them into a single pantheon. Back then they 
had been household stories and scraps of old folklore, always 
followed by her grandmother’s reminder that stories were not 
gods. Now Slavic goddesses shimmered in ribbons of neon and 
violet, their circuitry halos pulsing in faint, uneven intervals. 
The entire window see med to breathe. The glow pressed

whether it was their watchfulness that unsettled her or the 
thought that someone had programmed them to look back.

waters, and dark forests, now sanctified in glass. She was 
portrayed as a shepherd with a serene expression, her staff 
twined with vibrant green ivy. The Black Wolves prayed to

cycle,” she would say, “but these are no goddesses; there is

The cathedral, however, was now nearly empty. The harsh 
winter made travel difficult, and most people preferred to 
stream mass from the warmth of their apartments. Dunya 
counted a few priestesses in their candlelit niches and a 
handful of worshippers scattered among the pews. The Grand 
Mariner’s Cathedral had been built to hold three thousand 
after the old Naval Cathedral of St. Nicholas was absorbed into 
its larger shell, yet now it felt cavernous, its silence pressing 
heavier than the cold outside. 
Gred had sold immortality as an upgrade. In practice it 
looked like this: old bodies kept online, younger voices missing 
from the room, everyone retreating into virtual because the 
physical city had stopped offering anything new. Even the 
cathedral ran at low occupancy. 
Baba Fenya’s faith belonged to the Petropavlovsk of 
Dunya’s childhood, when St. Nicholas still held Orthodox 
services on this ground. The Grand Mariner had preserved 
pieces of the building while changing what the building was 
for. Dunya could still find pieces of the old faith in the cache. 
Dunya found a secluded pew and sat, the cool oak steady 
beneath her. She closed her eyes and drew a slow breath, 
feeling the weight of her body and the stillness of the cathedral 
around her. Her mind buzzed with questions she couldn’t 
quiet. 
She leaned forward, elbows on her knees, the metal in her 
joints creaking softly under the strain. Her head bowed, 
tension coiling through her frame. Vesna filled her thoughts. 
Her absence had outlasted the usual cycles of silence and 
return, leaving a gap  that felt wrong. Dunya had sent 
hundreds of messages and heard nothing back. 
The evidence of her frustration was still there. She had 
kicked a hole in her apartment wall, the plaster giving way

steadied her when everything else blurred. Together they ’d 
pulled off virtual jobs and data runs that should have broken 
them, yet somehow, they’d  always come out laughing. That 
bond had been enough to keep the loneliness at bay. 
Those shared runs had been a welcome distraction from a 
life that felt smaller with each passing year. Vesna had worn 
the colors of the women who hunted her father down, and 
Dunya had never let either of them pretend otherwise. The 
Yelagin log absolved no one. It proved only that Vesna had 
handed her a truth that implicated her own pack, then stayed 
when Dunya refused to turn it into gratitude. Trust 
accumulated through smaller things after that: a voice in the 
earpiece, a door opened after midnight, a tran sfer handled 
without pity, a meal left warm. By the time Vesna lost her 
barracks room and moved in, they already knew each other’s 
medicines, passwords, and bad nights. They had become 
necessary to each other before either called it affection, and 
the two never separated cleanly. Vesna was her only real 
companion, a woman twenty years older, and sometimes 
Dunya caught herself feeling like she’d skipped ahead to the 
end of her own story. Time had stopped in Gred anyway; no 
one aged here, not really. Maria’s absence still pressed on her, 
the final moment in the mindgraft looping in her head with a 
clarity that felt like her own betrayal.

The guilt of leaving Maria in that critical state weighed on 
her as she sat in the pew. She’d made a split-second decision 
to evacuate, to save herself, but the image of Maria’s still body 
wouldn’t fade. The questions that followed pressed hard 
against her thoughts. Could she have done something 
different? Missed a signal that might have changed th e 
outcome? 
What unsettled her most was the calm that had settled in 
since. It felt wrong, as if her mind had gone quiet only because 
it didn’t know where else to go. 
It felt almost suicidal, sitting so openly in the Grand 
Mariner’s Cathedral, the heart of the Syndicate’s power. 
The campus visit survived only in fragments. Still, she had 
checked the warrant channels twice before leaving home. No 
detainer, biometric flag, or University hold carried her name. 
If she’d crossed a line with the mindgrafts , if Maria had been 
taken by Syn, why was there no pursuit? Either the whole 
thing had remained off -ledger, or someone had broken the 
trace before it spread. The silence was unnerving, almost 
unreal. They should just come and arrest me now. I’ll show 
them, she thought, a flicker of defiance lighting inside her. But 
the feeling faded as quickly as it came. Do I really have the 
nerve to face them? 
Her life felt empty. Friends gone, family long dead, Vesna 
missing. The space left behind kept widening until it was all 
she could see. The thought that maybe nothing she did 
mattered anymore, that she had slipped beneath notice, was 
worse than the fear of  being caught. She sat in the stillness, 
surrounded by a silence that felt like judgment. 
She felt useless now, an operator without an assignment, a 
shadow moving through enemy ground unseen and 
unchallenged. The strange contracts she’d been getting only 
deepened the feeling, each one twisting into another dead end.

CHAPTER SIXTEEN 
KLARA  
 
As the memory of the blizzard faded, Klara pressed on 
through the Derge’s endless white. The wind clawed at her 
hood and the snow hissed beneath her boots. She knew the 
price of survival, had paid it more than once, and would pay 
it again if she had to. Not dying isn’t the same as living,  she 
thought, lifting her flask and taking a long pull of spiced 
brandy. She had learned that lesson in field tents long before 
she ever learned how to kill.  The burn steadied her, a small, 
defiant flame against the cold. 
The western snow lay heavier than in the east, its false 
purity hiding what it had already claimed. Klara had found 
three bodies so far, old women who had lived alone on the 
outskirts of the Rustbelt, where the last gnarled trees gave 
way to open tundra. E ach had faltered for only a moment, 
taken by the cold or by something worse before they could cry 
out. 
Demons… 
The kikimora, tricksters of old tales, were said to feed on the 
souls of the dead, leaving their bodies shriveled and hollow. 
Or so the elders claimed. Yet the faces before her looked more 
like the work of failed exo treatments, skin drawn tight and 
veins dark with residue. The cold just finished what the drugs 
started. Klara turned the blood -stained handkerchief in her 
hand, pity rising despite herself. As she laid it over the last 
woman’s face, the air around her seemed to still. For a 
moment, she felt her release, a mercy she preferred to the 
thought of demons gnawing at what remained . It was the 
closest thing to healing she still allowed herself.

likely. She steadied her breath and pressed the damp 
handkerchief to her lips, tasting iron as she studied the trees. 
The forest held its breath with her. Then a twig cracked to her 
left, sharp and close, and every muscle in her body tightened.  
“Who’s there?” Her voice quivered as she called out. “If you 
mean no harm, show yourself.” 
The bushes rustled. Klara held her ground, eyes fixed on 
the sound. Predator or prey? Either way, they’ll want warmth 
soon. Shelter —or their blood, if it comes to that.  The choice 
came quicker now than it used to, and that frightened her 
more than the dark. 
As the wind eased, the presence faded into the trees, leaving 
no trace behind. Klara let out a long breath and turned back 
to the old woman lying still in the snow. She brushed frost 
from the woman’s lashes and closed her eyes. 
A small wooden totem caught her attention beside the body, 
a carved babushka wrapped in dark etchings, meant for luck. 
She turned it in her glove, feeling the grooves of the design. A 
charm like this could get you questioned in Gred.  With a faint 
sigh, she dropped it back into the snow. Maybe someone else 
would find it. Someone who still believed.  Belief had once 
come easy to her, before it started costing lives.

Vatraliyna’s face appeared in them, stern but illuminated by 
warmth, the memory of her voice whispering through the 
years. “Control the spark, Klara, or it will control you.” Another

eased, just slightly.

behind the words.

Her own surname struck harder than she expected.  There 
was no one left to carry it but her, and no version of her left 
that would have made them proud. Chaban. A word erased 
from the Arkyv, scrubbed clean after the uprising that birthed 
the new Board. Her clan had vanished with it, consumed in 
the city’s reshaping. Once, the Chabans had ruled the Derge

line. Now, only ghosts. 
She pictured the Cathedral, the three empty seats at the 
high oak table. They were always there above her, unfilled and 
unmoving, silent witnesses to what had been erased. 
The old woman’s gaze pulled her back. Sharp and 
appraising. Klara knew what she saw: no living kin to prove 
her claim, no lineage left to speak her name. A gap too 
convenient for doubters. Yet behind that scrutiny, Klara 
caught something else, calculation and curiosity. The woman 
was measuring her, not as an imposter, but as someone who 
might still matter. 
Klara held that gaze. Whatever she said next would tip the 
balance. The story she carried  was thin, worn, and 
unprovable, but it was hers alone, the one truth she refused 
to let die. 
“I hail from the peninsula, just like all of you,” Klara said. 
Her voice carried over the rising jeers. “I once swore myself to 
the Syndicate, believing they wanted what I wanted —to heal, 
to protect. I was wrong. The Syndicate doesn’t care for the 
people. It only feeds on power. And when it had e nough, it 
turned on its own.”

above the crowd’s chant. “Yet they require our aid. With our 
combined strength, we can reclaim what’s rightfully ours—our 
liberty, our dignity, our very lives. The Syndicate may possess 
power and weaponry, but they lack our will, our heart, and 
our soul.”

echoing her call. “To the Coven! To the Coven!”

Feeling a surge of inspiration, Klara turned to face the 
assembled outlaws. The shift in the air hadn’t gone unnoticed, 
and a new energy pulsed through the crowd. “Brothers and 
sisters!” Klara’s voice echoed across the square. “This is our 
moment. Now is the time to fight! ” The outlaws roared in 
approval. Grinning, she raised her sword once again. “For our 
future!” she cried, striking down on the nearest riot shield. 
As the two factions clashed, the air became a storm of fire 
and lead. Klara surged through the battlefield like a blaze 
unchecked. Her blade, a comet of silver arcing through the 
mayhem, ignited the air with its ferocity. The discord of war 
raged around her, but she was the flame at its heart —a 
symbol of rebellion incarnate for the outlaws, the Coven, and 
her own unquenchable thirst for freedom. 
The Black Wolves found themselves overwhelmed, their 
ranks breaking before Klara ’s unyielding advance. Forced to 
retreat, they were pursued by the outlaws’ fury, hurled stones, 
and the incendiary rage of Molotov cocktails. This place, once 
part of their wretched domain, was slipping from their grasp , 
Klara knew. 
As the sound of  their victory diminished into the jubilant 
roars of the once -oppressed, Klara reached for the flask of 
spiced brandy that clung to her side through the dance of 
battle. Unscrewing the cap, she raised it high and took a long, 
satisfying swig. 
The warmth of the drink coursed through her, as 
invigorating as the triumph itself. Not content with savoring it 
alone, she passed the flask to the nearest fighter, a nod to the 
unspoken warrior’s code of sharing both the spoils and the 
spirits. 
The flask traveled from hand to hand, the outlaws’ weapons 
clinking in makeshift toasts. Each turn at the liquor seemed 
to fortify the bond now linking their destinies.

VESNA  
 
It happened faster than Vesna expected. One moment, the 
battlefield was a chaotic storm of railgun fire and explosions. 
The next, a pulse —quiet, invisible—rippled through the air, 
snuffing out the roar of the Black Wolves ’ weapons as if the 
world had drawn a sharp breath and held it. They’d trusted 
Fort Ivan’s defenses to protect their railguns, but now they 
were forced into the close combat they craved. The University 
Marines held the flanks, their Gauss rifles cracking in bursts 
behind her, only targeting those in Vesna’s way. 
Her opponents barreled toward her with terrifying 
momentum, their massive frames bearing down on her. 
Freakishly large in pitch-black, fur-lined puffer jackets, veins 
bulging from their necks, they charged like an unstoppable 
force. Vesna had to be nimble, precise, darting between their 
swings. Bloodshot eyes glared at her, snarls twisting their 
faces. She brandished her gunblades, driving one into flesh 
with a sharp jab before slicing across the tor so of another. 
More of them surged forward, their heavy boots pounding the 
earth, the scent of sweat and blood thickening the air as she 
fought to stay ahead of the berserked pack.

shouted back. “But I’m not going to apologize for anything.”

factions in a truce. It was here that the Black Wolves first 
pledged their allegiance to the city. 
Vesna pressed her fingertips against her temples, easing 
the last remnants of a splitting headache. As the fog of pain 
finally lifted, her focus sharpened, and she gazed up at the 
monolithic statue. Though she had visited Fort Ivan many 
times before, today something was different, a deep conviction 
that her destiny was bound with this place: twelve thousand 
tons of foundation stones sprawled across twenty forested 
hectares, shaped by the relentless Rus winter and the white -
capped waters of Fort Ivan’s deity, the goddess Velun. 
The towering red jasper figure, cloaked in moss and etched 
with frost scars, seemed more alive than ever. Vesna bowed to 
Velun, her breath forming misty clouds in the chilly air. She 
felt the eternal guardian watching over her and her pack, 
ready to fight alongside them when needed.

meeting each soldier’s eyes with cold, unwavering focus. Her

ignore the silent authority she projected. She was here to 
solidify her position, to remind them all that she was their 
Alpha and protector of their cause.

behind her like chastened pups.

CHAPTER EIGHTEEN 
ZAKHAROVNA  
 
The sun’s rays crested the rooftops, glinting off the frost -
laden windows as the cold bit at her skin. Anastasia exhaled, 
watching her breath rise in a pale mist as she meandered 
along the riverbank, shivering beneath her thick polyester 
coat and gloves. She longed for the warmth that spring would 
bring. In the meantime, h er boots crunched on the snow as 
she crossed the bridge and climbed the icy steps. 
The cobblestone path wound up a hill, past dormant 
fountains and slumbering gardens. Anastasia navigated the 
twisting route, slipping past dog walkers, amorous couples, 
and hurried workers. Gripping the guardrails, she moved 
carefully, aware that a single misstep could send her 
tumbling. Her breaths grew heavier with each step, but the 
sight ahead gave her pause: a grand neoclassical edifice, 
towering over the landscape. Her thoughts drifted to centuries 
past, imagining robed  clerics and lavish gatherings beneath 
the enduring stonework. For a heartbeat, she let herself 
believe in it, in the weight of history pressing close, even if 
none of it truly existed. 
Approaching the cathedral, Anastasia observed a steady 
stream of visitors, some pausing to pray while others hurried 
across the grounds. She halted before the grand doors, 
catching her reflection in the fountain’s polished surface. 
Standing tall, she studi ed the high sweep of her cheekbones 
and the clear blue of her eyes in the watery mirror. The firm 
line of her jaw and the fullness of her lips felt distant now. A 
gust of winter wind tousled her cinnamon brown hair, sending 
it dancing around her face. She gazed deeper into the 
reflection, searching for the young woman she once knew.

ceiling, its intricate stonework and vivid murals casting a 
quiet majesty over the space. The air was calm, though the 
scattered presence of others reminded her of the sanctuary 
this place had become in  the wake of the war. She hadn’t 
expected such a crowd. Dozens filled the pews, their faces lit 
by candlelight, gathered for the memorial. Some were familiar, 
others not. A few still wore traces of night makeup, a reminder 
of the world Virginia had once ru led. The scent of wax and 
wilted flowers lingered in the air. Anastasia watched them in 
silence, uncertain whether they had come to mourn her or to 
ease their own guilt. 
At the altar, she knelt, murmuring prayers into the silence 
before rising, a quiet unease stirring within her. She paused, 
sensing a faint change in the stillness, a presence she hadn’t 
noticed before. Turning, her gaze settled on a figure cloaked 
in shado w, their face hidden beneath the heavy folds of a 
woolen cloak.  
“Anastasia,” the woman whispered, “you were always there 
for her.” The words caught Anastasia off guard. It took a 
moment for the name to settle as she took in the dim glow of 
candles around the altar, realizing she had arrived later than 
she meant to. 
The woman lowered her hood, revealing a face half lost to 
shadow, uncannily familiar. The same blue eyes and the same 
gentle curve of the mouth made it feel as though Virginia had 
returned from the grave. “My sister spoke so fondly of you,” 
the woman said softly.

crease. Anastasia stared at it, her mind struggling to place 
what she already knew too well. The memory came back to 
her as she pictured the cold morning by the Neris River, the 
two of the m wrapped in that same scarf while hail clattered 
over the cobblestones. 
Anastasia lifted the scarf and draped it around her neck, 
the faint scent still the same after all these years. She 
remembered giving it up once, leaving it behind in a moment 
of anger she could no longer justify. “I thought I’d forgotten 
this,” she murmured, her fingers brushing the label where her 
name was scripted in elegant lettering. 
Clutching the scarf, Anastasia’s eyes filled with tears. “I 
never should have let it go,” she whispered.  
“My name is Vilka. I’ll be outside. I’m glad you’re here,” the 
woman said softly before turning to leave. 
“I know,” Anastasia said quietly, but Vilka had already 
slipped through the door. 
Left alone, Anastasia turned toward the altar. Tears 
streamed down her cheeks as she knelt, eyes closed, praying 
aloud. Her words echoed in the quiet, but the silence within 
her heart remained unbroken. “I commend you, my dear 
friend, to Almighty God and entrust you to your Creator. May 
you rest in the arms of the Lord who formed you from the dust 
of the earth.”

Anastasia rose from her knees, the echo of her whispered 
prayers lingering in the sacred stillness. Stepping outside the 
cathedral, she saw Vilka standing as a silhouette against the 
sunlight. 
They linked arms, and as they walked, the space between 
them seemed to fade away. Vilka, once distant and 
unknown—a sister Anastasia had only heard of in passing, 
mentioned rarely by Virginia—now brought her a quiet sense 
of comfort. 
As they made their way toward the park, Vilka’s voice broke 
the silence. “You must be wondering why I’ve been absent all 
this time,” she said. “I couldn’t even bring myself to go to the 
funeral. I told myself there was no point, but the truth is, I 
was afraid. I didn’t want to see her like that.” 
Anastasia looked at her, her voice low. “I almost didn’t come 
here today.”  
Vilka nodded, her gaze fixed ahead. “Then maybe coming 
now means we’re both ready to stop running from her.”  
Anastasia felt the weight of Vilka’s words settle in. Virginia’s 
illness had carved deep wounds within the family. Vilka, 
Anastasia had learned, had kept the darkest truths from their 
ailing parents, sparing them further anguish when they were 
already consumed by their own battles with termi nal illness. 
Anastasia saw it in her eyes, the kind of pain that came only 
from love held too long in silence. It was a choice made out of 
care, now edged with the sharpness of regret. Grief, Anastasia 
realized through Vilka’s  quiet confession, followed no rules. 
And in her silence, Vilka had endured that heartache alone.

conversation flowing easily as they shared stories of their 
families. Vilka spoke of choosing Oxford for her studies, while

outstretched like futile pleas for renewal. Gray maples, too, 
were leafless, and Zakharovna’s thoughts drifted to distant 
memories of the blue siberica flowers that once adorned the 
graveyard each spring, a recollection buried under the weight 
of decades. The absence of those blooms struck her with a 
sharp pang of loss. 
As the boundary between virtual reality and memory 
blurred, Zakharovna found herself sitting on the ground 
beside Vilka, her mind heavy with the question of whether to 
stay. It felt as if a forgotten shard of her soul was calling her 
to linger, to remain among the echoes of her past.

CHAPTER NINETEEN 
YELENA  
 
Blanka flipped her pale gold hair, the borrowed earrings 
twinkling golden in the light. “They somehow look better on 
me, don’t you think?” 
Daria looked at her with a playful edge to her voice. “Wishful 
thinking, Blanka. They ’re meant for someone a little more 
petite.” 
Blanka laughed heartily. “Well, better wear them now. In 
ten years, my ears might be too grand for any jewelry at all!” 
Daria fanned herself, a smirk on her face.  “Honey, unlike 
some, I plan to age with grace. But do keep the earrings. By 
then, they might be the only thing not sagging on you … 
Speaking of changes, is it me or is this room turning into a 
sauna?” 
Just then, Roza walked in, looking around in confusion. 
“Where did I leave my ice pack? These hot flashes make me 
feel like I’m in the Valley of Geysers!” 
Daria chuckled. “Roza, if hot flashes were frequent flyer 
miles, we’d have left this planet years ago. But unfortunately, 
we’re stuck with menopause, forever.” 
Roza rolled her eyes, chuckling. “Well, I’m just grateful that 
‘ol Gred is as cold as an Eskimo ’s outhouse. If our city ever 
lost its frosty charm, I’d probably end up melted into a puddle 
like a discarded ice cream cone!” 
Blanka smirked, adjusting her new earrings. “And heavens 
forbid if that stubborn ice cloud over the Pacific ever decides 
to call it quits! I’d miss the winter galas! But knowing my luck, 
that’s when my fluffy fur coat would decide to come back in 
style!”

ceremony, were you?”

people see the power of their votes. The first ballot in our new 
war has already been cast, and soon, they will join you.” 
“Understood,” Valentina said. Yelena caught the quick nod, 
that familiar gesture signaling Valentina’s sharp intellect, 
always quick to grasp even the most complex situations. With 
her usual confident stride, Valentina rose and left the room. 
As Valentina’s footsteps faded, Yelena turned to the window 
overlooking the plaza. The time -worn shell of the once -grand 
Hotel Kamchatsky  stood rigid at the corner, while in the 
distance, Avachinsky Volcano loomed over snow -dusted 
fields. The bare skeletons of aspen and rowan trees dotted the 
landscape, their yellow -gray branches cutting stark 
silhouettes against the pale winter sky. They p unctuated the 
snow’s quiet, like muted declarations of resilience against the 
grip of winter. 
She redirected her gaze to the plaza. Among the buildings 
and the bustling crowd, Yelena ’s eyes searched for someone 
absent—Zakharovna. 
Where is she? What is she plotting?

the silence in the lectures, where she usually reveled in praise, 
was glaring. It wasn’t like Zakharovna to step away from the 
spotlight—especially now, free from the political constraints

mercy.

stranglehold of office. But her silence now, in these crucial

creeping in with every thought of her old adversary’s quiet 
retreat into the shadows. 
And Romanova’s stillness was equally unsettling. Would 
she not seize the chance to fill the power vacuum left by 
Zakharovna’s absence?  Leveling more accusations of 
misconduct wasn’t an option now; Yelena had initiated

growing list of problems . It smacked of Zakharovna ’s

rebellion needed to be crushed, quickly , effectively. And

she thought, her mind already working on a new public
