CHAPTER TWENTY 
MARIA  
 
Maria surfaced slowly, the cube’s hum and the terminal’s 
faint whir pulling her back from the dive. She drew a long 
breath, letting the digital after-images fade. Gaspar’s claim to 
know her location nagged at her. Hack me? Good luck. 
She checked the logs. No unauthorized traces. That was a 
relief, though it wasn’t unexpected. The zk-SNARK layers were 
still holding. If Gaspar had anything, he hadn’t shown it. 
Beside her, Serafim lay under the headset. The glow traced 
across her face, dark hair tugged loose where the interface  
pulled. For a moment Maria almost thought she stirred, but 
the stillness held. 
How long’s she been under? How long was I out? 
Maria was wiped. A yawn caught halfway and snapped into 
a sneeze as her system pinged. SOVA again, the Sentient 
Ocular Virtual Assistant she usually kept muted. Nearly every 
ocular carried some descendant of the old chatbots. They 
translated speech, searched local archives, summarized feeds, 
and watched the body wearing them. Routine replies wrote 
themselves. People had stopped calling any of that a chatbot 
years ago. It was interface plumbing, useful enough to 
disappear. Most kept the functions and muted the voice. Some 
alerts still forced their way through. This one carried its usual 
impatience. “Maria, time to wake up.”  
“What do you think I’m doing?” 
She blinked hard, trying to steady herself, when SOVA 
pushed again, voice softened with a simulated sigh. “I know 
it’s not easy, but we need you back.”

“Working on it,” Maria muttered. She braced as static 
crawled across her nerves, the disconnect rippling through 
her implants. 
“Efficiency’s the trade-off,” SOVA said, fading with the link. 
Maria let the silence settle. Her head throbbed with the 
unavoidable weight, the price of diving direct. The others’  
headsets spread the load, splitting fragments of thought 
across mirrored substrates. They’ll never feel this. Only me.  
Her dives forced everything through her own cortex, no 
buffers, burning it in raw.  It wore her down faster, but it cut 
deeper and struck quicker than anything else. That edge had 
saved her friends before. When Shatterveil’s gambit turned 
out to be a ruse, Dunya, dazed but breathing, had stumbled 
out laughing, grateful for croissants and billiards that night 
like never before. 
A fresh ping cut across the quiet, sharper than SOVA’s fade. 
Matron Romanova’s voice pressed through the new link, stern 
and close. “Maria, are you still with us? You’ve been out of 
touch for too long.” 
Maria blinked into the warehouse gloom, the broken 
windows letting in only scraps of moonslight. With a thought, 
she brought her ocular online. 
Romanova resolved in her vision, sharp lines of light 
coalescing into a spectral figure. The contours flickered with

find a new way in.” 
“Never underestimate Zakharovna. That trap was skillfully 
hidden.” 
Maria blinked, trying to clear the shimmering distortions 
across her vision. In the corner of her ocular feed a diagram 
of her occipital lobe pulsed red. The flash grenade from the 
Spire sim had cut deeper than she’d allowed herself to admit. 
She tapped her forehead and pulled up her HUD. Neural 
pathways to the optic nerve glowed with interference, 
nanobots swarming through the field. They began repairs, 
dosing her with painkillers as they released enzymes and 
cellular regenerators. 
“My fault, ” she admitted, eyes scanning the sensory 
diagnostics. Core processors steady, no critical faults, no 
system glitches. “I miscalculated.” 
“You weren ’t alone in that, ” Romanova reassured her. 
“Perhaps if we had disabled some non-essential systems first, 
we could have evaded detection.” 
“Maybe. But hitting the Spire was necessary,” Maria said. 
“We needed a vantage point. From up there, I could have seen 
Zakharovna’s whole lattice, traced every link, every choke. 
That was how we were supposed to break it apart, layer by 
layer.” She exhaled, the frustration still there. “Instead, we got 
dumped the second we reached the top. The climb was back-
encrypted. We start from further out this time. Find the soft 
nodes. Work our way back in.” 
“Agreed,” Romanova said. “So, let’s bring Dunya into the 
fold. I want the three of you to evaluate your options before 
another breach.” 
Maria hesitated. “After Vesna...”

smile. “How about you, Matron? With all that’s happening, 
how are you holding up?”

overshadows everything else right now . The thought of what 
those agents might have done had they  trapped you in 
virtual... It’s unnerving. As for the University ’s primary 
observatory hub, infiltrating it was always a gamble.” 
“Doesn’t make it hurt any less. I’m sick of taking losses.”

interpreted as sympathy. “We’ll try again. Let me devise a new 
plan.”

“I’ve been out of touch,” she began. That felt like an 
understatement. Her mind stretched back to Anna’s 
apartment, the failed graft, and the confusion that had split 
them afterward. “I wish I could say it was all part of the plan, 
but we hit a roadblock.”  
“I wasn’t captured,” she wrote, her own skepticism tugging 
at the words. She knew it must have looked like she had been. 
The silence, her sudden disappearance after the mission. All 
she could do now was hope Dunya would take it as truth. 
“Our first assault fell flat. The Syndicate ’s security is more 
advanced than we’d imagined.” Maria refrained from adding, 
more than I ’d imagined, her ego wincing at the implication. 
“But it’s far from a lost cause. We’re regrouping, searching for 
fresh entry points.” 
She paused, reading the message once more. “Stay sharp. 
Hold the line. We’ll find a way in.” 
Her message sent, Maria watched as the words 
disintegrated into a swarm of voxels, vanishing into the neon 
dreams of the babachain. She exhaled slowly, allowing herself 
a brief respite in the silence of the warehouse.

Battalion now? How can you expect me to trust a play straight 
out of a Pra Matron’s book, with you suddenly under her 
wing? I’ve heard the stories, Maria. She’s not one of us. This 
isn’t just about the job. It’s about where you stand . You’ve 
always walked a thin line, but with Romanova? That’s a leap 
I’m not ready to take with you.” 
The message faded, leaving the warehouse air heavy. Maria 
sat with it, the weight of Dunya’s reproach hanging in the 
quiet. 
Serafim started. “I...” 
Maria held up a hand, silencing her. “Not now.” She knew 
Dunya’s trust had been shattered, their alliance strained 
beyond repair. The question lingered unspoken: Where do we 
go from here?

hadn’t stepped in. The cut lit up the Wolves, Maria. I f you

off then and there. You were lucky. Lucky Romanova had eyes 
on you.”

everything she’s been through… Zakharovna won’t see her 
coming.”

anymore. They were courting chaos, pretending they could 
contain it.

Old babas clutched their bags tightly, their weathered faces 
and scarves imbued with a sense of permanence. Every so 
often, a young woman would rush by, a glimpse of change in 
a mostly static  urban tapestry. A small group in gray work 
attire leaned nonchalantly against the pillars, an emblem of a 
black honeycomb against a field of yellow sewn onto patches 
on their arms. She wondered, in a different life, if she might 
have enjoyed manual labor, if Dugal had sti ll been around to 
poke fun at her whenever she worked up the confidence to try 
smithing something on his old CNC. 
The distant murmur of steel meeting steel crescendoed, 
filling the air until it coalesced into a resplendent train. Its 
head was adorned with a sculpted metallic fox, eyes inset with 
amber, a harmonious melding of Art Deco flair and Soviet 
robustness. The doors hissed open, inviting the crowd to enter 
as if beckoned by the fox’s taciturn gaze. 
Inside, Dunya found herself standing, back against the cold 
wall of the metro car. Her eyes met those of an older woman 
across the aisle. Crow ’s feet framed the woman ’s pale blue 
eyes. Self-consciously, Dunya fluffed the fabric of her baggy 
pants with her free hand, creating a slight bulge to obscure 
the outline of her Skelet.

Dunya stepped back, her hand on her holstered pistol as 
the metro car came to a stop. “Devils you know, witches you 
don’t. Better stay out of the fire.” 
As she moved toward the door, whisked along by the quiet 
efficiency of her braces, Dunya cast a final glance at the 
wayward psycho who had tried to kill her without cause. The 
metro doors sealed shut with a pneumatic hiss. For a moment, 
their eyes met through the glass, and a subtle pang of regret 
flickered within her. 
She watched the train pull away, contemplating the circular 
nature of the metro route. It would bring the girl back to the 
city’s heart, give her another shot at chaos. The thought 
stung, but Dunya shook it off. 
Still, the encounter gnawed at her. A lone, mid -level Vory 
wasn’t the kind of assassin the Syndicate would send if they 
truly wanted her dead. There were far more effective ways to 
eliminate her than some knife -wielding thug on the metro. 
Was it a coincide nce, or had her former employers grown 
sloppy? No, she doubted it. The Syndicate rarely made 
mistakes, and this attack felt too amateurish. More likely, the 
Vory had seen the faint glow of her Skelet beneath her sleeve 
and assumed she was still tied to a field contract. Most 
operators kept their rigs after severance if they survived the 
work. She had too, and maybe that was enough to paint a 
target on her back. 
She’d been to her apartment twice since the mindgraft had 
gone to shit, and no one had come for her. Her guards were 
never tipped off. Maybe none of it mattered. Maybe the 
mindgraft, like Yana had said, was just another bum gray-hat 
job that held no significance whatsoever, and Maria was just 
a lying bitch playing with her generosity. Either way, she knew 
the Syndicate could —and likely would —do better if they 
wanted her silenced for good.

The corridor narrowed. Dunya marked the exits, signal 
strength, and distance back to the platform. Whatever the Veil 
was, it did not get to decide whether she was worthy. It was a 
location, and locations had access rules. 
Her eyes adjusted to the limited light, the path barely 
illuminated by her Skelet’s subtle display. She had expected 
to find a flame , rumors and coded messages had led her to 
expect it. But as she drew nearer, she discovered a small 
chapel carved directly into the tunnel wall, as though a drill 
bot had attacked the stone and stopped midway, leaving the 
jagged edges raw and unfinished. The chapel’s rough exterior 
contrasted sharply with th e intricate wooden carvings of the 
altar inside, where an ancient tome rested on a stone pedestal, 
seemingly untouched by time. 
A shiver danced through her body as her eyes swept across 
the wooden walls and altar of the chapel. Where fire meets 
wood, the thought pulsed in her mind. No flames flickered in 
sconces, no ember glowed in a brazier. She’d found something 
pivotal, she was sure, but it felt like a riddle waiting for its 
other half. 
Intrigued and cautious, she approached the pedestal and 
flipped open the book ’s pages. The inked symbols and 
diagrams seemed to animate, glowing faintly in the gloom.

Squinting in the dim light, she leaned closer to the ancient 
text, the words barely more than whispers on the worn page. 
She traced the letters with her fingertips, coaxing them into 
clarity. She broke the silence, carefully pronouncing each 
word: “In shadow’s depth, the secret lies.” 
As her voice resonated in the stone chamber, a sconce on 
the wall flickered to life. Its sudden light made her gasp, and 
her heartbeat quickened. She continued: “Where eyes perceive 
yet still defy.” 
Her eyes widened as another sconce ignited, its light joining 
the first to dance on the pages of the tome.  A deluge of data 
flooded her ocular —numbers, images, and indecipherable 
warnings—she managed to focus on the text and read the final 
line: “Embrace the flame yet fear the burn.” 
With the third sconce lit, her ocular caught the pattern the 
room had been building: three spoken lines, three active 
lights, one strand of her hair highlighted across the display. 
An input sequence. Stupidly theatrical, but clear enough. 
She drew the butterfly knife, cut a lock, and laid it on the 
page. 
White light detonated through the chapel. Her ocular 
blanked, the Skelet threw balance warnings, and every sensor 
returned garbage for two seconds. 
When the feed recovered, someone was standing behind 
her. 
A hooded silhouette blocked the pine wall. Its face remained 
hidden, and her sensors found neither a thermal profile nor a 
readable device signature. Dunya held still, counting the 
distance to her knife. 
Whatever she had authenticated, it had answered.

CHAPTER TWENTY TWO 
VESNA  
 
Vesna pulled herself from the training pits, feeling the 
weight of fatigue with every step. Entering the locker room, 
she made her way to the showers. She peeled off worn leather 
gear—boots, jacket, gloves—letting them land haphazardly by 
her locker. Reach ing for the faucet, she twisted it on and 
stepped beneath the scalding spray, leaning into the contrast 
of heat against the cool, mosaic -tiled wall. With every 
movement and stretch, memories flared in the bruises, each 
one a reminder of recent battles, her  body marked in deep 
purples and angry reds. 
Steam wafted around her. A slight turn of her head revealed 
the source: an auburn-haired woman bathed in the shimmer 
of the water, her porcelain skin glistening. The woman’s lips 
moved in a low, haunting melody, like an ancient prayer. 
Though Vesna had never set foot in a church, not even before 
the faith was outlawed, the sound stirred something deep 
within her. But as the melody held her in its grip, the steam 
surged, thickening, and the vision dissolved, leaving her with 
only the echo of the tune and the rhythmic patter of water 
bouncing off the tiles like soft rainfall. 
The scalding water cascaded over her back, but it did little 
to quell the firestorm raging in her mind. The damp smell of 
mildew clung to the air, sour and suffocating, mixing with the 
sting of abandonment that twisted inside her. Friends had 
turned foes, now wearing  the yellow scarves of the Hive or 
rallying behind Tatyana Romanova in open defiance. Each 
desertion left a venomous sting, and in the shower’s seclusion, 
she allowed herself to feel the slash of every loss. 
As leader of the Wolves, she had to project unyielding

murmur of conversations blurred with the steady patter of

Ivan—a violation that scraped at the Wolves’ honor, tainting 
their space. Zakharovna’s absence hung over her like a 
shadow, leaving her alone to navigate this crucial moment. 
The hot water flowed, but it couldn’t chase away  the cold 
dread coiling inside her. She couldn’t allow treachery to seep

pack, to prepare them for the inevitable clash ahead.

heap of discarded clothes by her locker. Bare -skinned, she 
crossed the room and grabbed her phone, flicking it open. Her 
eyes settled on a days -old message from Dunya: “Are you 
coming home?” She hadn’t found the will to respond, not to 
this one or the others. The day they’d first traded contacts felt 
like a distant memory, and now Dunya’s neediness clung to 
her like something foul. 
With a sigh, Vesna bundled her damp purple hair into a 
messy bun, tugging on her boots as the cold leather gripped 
her bare feet. Dunya’s message clung to her thoughts, her lip 
caught between her teeth as she mulled it over. She tossed 
the phone onto the bench and finished dressing, the weight of 
unanswered words still hanging in the air. 
Sharp footsteps echoed behind her. Vesna turned to see a 
familiar figure in uniform —tall, slender, with cropped silver 
hair and a face set in stern lines.

Vesna recalled seeing her at the Research Center—brilliant, 
but untested in the field. “I know you’re sharp in the labs, 
Goga. But this isn’t about smarts. It’s about grit, about facing 
the enemy head-on. Out there, it’s different.” 
Goga’s tone hardened. “You killed my sister. Now I’m 
standing here, asking to be part of your game. And let’s be 
real—you’re not exactly swimming in recruits with all the 
defections. Think of this as a chance to settle the score.” 
Vesna felt a chill at the mention of their former pack leader. 
The underlying threat, the veiled accusation, was clear, but 
she shoved it aside. In the ranks of the Black Wolves, death 
was always lurking. Goga should’ve known her sister wasn’t 
exempt—not from me, not from anyone. 
“Alright, you’re in,” Vesna said firmly. “But this isn’t about 
settling scores. It’s about doing the work. Can you handle 
that?” 
Goga met her gaze, a flicker of satisfaction crossing her 
face, darkened by something else. “I can handle it. Just give 
the word.” 
Vesna nodded. “Wait for my call. Be ready.” 
As Goga turned to leave, she paused, glancing back with a 
half-smile that never touched her eyes. “Oh, and by the way,” 
she said casually, “I don’t buy the rumors. I know you took 
down Arkadya yourself.”

mouthed the passphrase, the lock clicked, and the engine 
roared to life beneath her, vibrations rippling through her 
body.

her wake. The wind whipped against her face, a brief reprieve 
from the storm in her mind. Each mile swallowed by the bike’s 
tires stretched the distance between her and the weight of 
command, offering a fleeting escape.

the cool lake air from Kultuchnoye drifting by. Sweat trickled 
down her neck, and she let out a quiet chuckle —she’d 
forgotten her helmet in the rush. Pushing the bike faster, she 
gained speed, the familiar streets of town unfolding around 
her. The road widened, flanked by towering buildings on either 
side, closing in as she raced through the dark.

She shifted her focus inward, bypassing the subtle mental 
interface that typically guided the bike. Now she felt the raw 
power beneath her, the engine’s snarl unfiltered and fierce. 
This sensation, this wild intensity, brought her back to her 
cadet days. T he cityscape stretched before her, skyscrapers 
standing like silent giants as she sliced through their 
shadows. Neon lights flickered across the streets, casting a 
wash of colors. She wove through the dense traffic with ease,  
instincts honed from years of chasing criminals sharpening 
her every move. 
The city blurred in a cascade of motion as she raced 
onward. Ahead, the silhouette of the Grand Mariner’s 
Cathedral cleaved the sky, towering over everything around it, 
its grandeur unmistakable even from a distance. Nearing it, 
the silvery trunks of white birches stood out in stark contrast 
against the cathedral’s shadow, their leaves whispering softly, 
as if in deference to the towering structure behind them. 
As she approached the city’s core, a flicker of light in the 
distance drew her eye —a fire. A dogwood tree stood at its 
center, its blossoms ablaze like embers. The sight held her for 
a moment, and she eased off the throttle, transfixed. 
A woman stood in the heart of the flames, her haunting eyes 
locking onto Vesna’s from afar. Clad in a form -fitting black 
robe, a gnarled wooden staff  in hand, she seemed to control 
the fire with nothing but a thought. Adrenaline spiked 
through Vesna as she gunned the throttle, her bike roaring 
beneath her. This woman needed to be stopped. 
Vesna skidded to a screeching halt, jumping off the bike as 
its engine rumbled, the heat radiating off its frame. In the 
smoky haze around the tree, the flickering firelight revealed 
stacks of leather -bound books, their presence unsettling 
against the crackling flames.

matrons in fur coats held their usual spaces in the evening 
bustle, while a group of young professionals marched by, their 
stares vacant, guided by digital trails in their ocular implants.

concealed in the shadows. A year ago, a garbage fire on a busy 
street would have been nothing more than a nuisance, just 
another flicker in the urban sprawl. But now, with the city 
teetering on the edge, every fire glowed with potential danger, 
every alley murmured of hidden threats. She tightened her 
grip on her gun as she neared the flames, her eyes scanning 
for the elusive woman in black.

free hand. “Stop right there!” 
The woman’s figure flickered for a moment in the light, her 
green eyes wild and frantic. But as Vesna moved closer, the 
robed figure dissolved into the smoke, leaving no trace of her 
presence. 
Vesna hesitated for a heartbeat, then moved cautiously 
forward. As the fire’s glow revealed the face of the fallen figure, 
memories surged through her, almost knocking the breath 
from her lungs. “Dunya.” The name slipped out in a whisper. 
Without thinking,  her pace quickened, each step feeling 
heavier, burdened what felt like  the years between them. 
Dropping to her knees, Vesna brushed away the soot and ash 
from Dunya’s face. “Dunya, what have you gotten yourself 
into?” she choked, the shock mixing with a wave of guilt for 
the time they’d lost. 
Dunya’s eyes locked onto hers, cutting through the dim 
light. “You shouldn’t be here.” 
Vesna gripped Dunya’s shoulders, her voice urgent. “Spill 
it. What happened to you?”

something in the city, Vesna. An anomaly, something that 
defies nature. And I think... I think it’s connected to Syn.” 
Vesna’s irritation flared, her whirl of guilt and concern 
suddenly sharpening into anger. “The Syndicate? You’re still 
tangled up with them? After everything we’ve been through?” 
Dunya’s face tightened. “Aren’t you? I take the contracts I 
need to survive. You’re not here to make those calls anymore, 
Vesna.” 
“You think I wanted this? You think I wanted to leave you? 
We’re in this mess because you couldn’t let go —because you 
didn’t—” 
“I didn’t what? You left me, Vesna! You saved yourself and 
left me to pick up the pieces!” 
“I did it to protect you,” Vesna said, the words raw and 
jagged as they ripped from her throat. “But we can’t do this 
now. I’ll explain later, I promise. Right now, we need to move.”  
“Oh, like how you promised last time?” 
Vesna’s jaw clenched. “I had no choice. Things were 
different—” 
“Things are always different with you.” 
Before Vesna could respond, a shuddering cough broke the 
tension. The ancient trees hissed as their gray -brown bark 
crackled, dense plumes of smoke curling into the air. Then, 
like a phantom rising from the smoke, the robed figure 
reappeared.

desperate force of a cornered animal. “I’m done with your 
games. I want the truth.”

of a smirk. A chill crept down her spine, unbidden and 
unwelcome. “Oh, Commander,” the woman said, her voice 
dripping with mockery. “The truth is, we’re all just pawns in 
this grand game. And the city”—she spread her arms wide as 
the flames licked at her—“is our board.” 
In an instant, the robed  figure was swallowed by fire. The 
flames consumed the fabric, revealing hair that shimmered 
like molten silver. Her pale skin caught the glow, almost 
ethereal in the shifting light. Then, she flickered and 
dissolved, scattering into ash that spiraled away on the wind.  
The low rumble jolted Vesna from her frozen state. For a 
moment, it could have been distant thunder—until the second 
blast roared closer.  Vesna’s gaze remained fixed on the spot 
where the robed woman had vanished when the second blast 
erupted, closer, unmistakable as anything but a detonation. 
The third shook the ground beneath her, the force rippling 
through the air as glass rained down from high windows, 
shards catching the firelight as they fell. 
Only then did Vesna register the crowd —no longer distant 
figures but a panicked mass. Screams cut through the smoke 
as the women who had been wandering aimlessly moments 
before now scrambled, their terror palpable. The realization 
hit hard: it was a coordinated strike, and they were caught in 
the heart of it.

The Wolves, unshaken, tightened their defensive cordon, 
creating a fortified space where chaos swirled just outside the 
perimeter. 
Vesna watched as Dunya was hoisted between two towering 
Black Wolves—both gargantuan women who looked like they 
hadn’t slept in days. Even in their grip, Dunya strained, her 
eyes searching for Vesna. She pushed weakly against their 
support, her focus solely on closing the distance. 
As they brought her closer, Dunya’s legs buckled, and she 
leaned heavily into Vesna. “Vesna,” she rasped, her voice raw 
from shock, “I... I can’t...” Her body sagged, and Vesna quickly 
steadied her, becoming the pillar Dunya’s waterlogged braces 
and battered frame could no longer provide. 
Vesna’s chest tightened as they lifted Dunya onto the 
gurney at the back of the ambulance. Seeing her like this—so 
fragile, so far from the Dunya she remembered —it hit harder 
than anything she could have said. 
“Don’t—” Dunya gasped as they carefully strapped her in. 
“Don’t leave me.” 
“You’ll pull through,” Vesna said. “You’re tough—tougher 
than any of us.” As she squeezed Dunya’s hand, her grip was 
a facade, a shield against a sudden, crushing wave of 
responsibility. I should have answered your calls. I should 
have been there before it came to this. 
The slam of the ambulance doors felt like a gavel, closing 
one ordeal and ushering in another. Vesna’s hand lingered on 
the hot glass, her forehead resting against the pane for a brief 
moment as the vehicle pulled away, its sirens wailing over the 
distant rumble of explosions. 
She turned back to the chaos, her fists tightening like steel, 
every muscle primed for action. The city was under siege. As 
long as she had breath, as long as blood pulsed through her 
veins, she would fight—for Dunya, for everyone caught in the

CHAPTER TWENTY THREE 
YANA  
 
“Cigar?” 
Grigoreva stood at the foot of the divan, a smoldering cigar 
between her lips, tendrils of smoke rising from its tip. 
Yana coughed. Her eyes watered as the acrid haze assaulted 
her senses. She waved her hand, hoping to clear the air 
enough to focus. 
“An early indulgence, ” the Baroness mu ttered with a sly 
grin, “but who could resist a taste of my White Canal? ” She 
dangled the gilded Belomorkanal from her fingers, the base of 
the cigar marked by the smudge of her lipstick. “Can I tempt 
you?” 
Grigoreva’s free hand caressed Yana’s tousled mane, her 
fingers weaving through the strands. “You appear in need of 
something to ease the tension.” 
Yana withdrew, fatigue weighing down her limbs. “No, 
thank you.” She rubbed her temples, the ghost of a headache 
lingering from a night of decadence and excess. “I’ll be fine.” 
She turned toward the mirror and studied the damage to 
her mascara. Dark streaks marked her cheeks. She dabbed 
with a tissue, but the smears held fast. Some stains, she 
thought, were not so easily erased. 
As she stared at her reflection, a troubling thought 
surfaced. No way they just happen to share the same name. Is 
this a setup?  Something was off. The mission had turned, 
twisting into lies she hadn’t anticipated.

hollow. So much for the con artist. Looks like I only lived up to

Aleksandr, hulking and jaw-scarred, stood sentinel on a thick 
column of neck. His hint of a smirk read as amusement when

It was the fifth consecutive night the Baroness had 
summoned her to the bedchamber.  The previous encounters 
had been almost enjoyable; the Baroness had a deft touch, 
her caresses and tantalizing teases unraveling Yana in her 
arms. After hours spent writhing under Grigoreva ’s 
ministrations, Yana could not deny her skill. 
Then Grigoreva started talking about her son as if he were 
still moving through the city under another name. 
Noblewomen from the Battalion had shared nights with 
him, she said. They praised him afterward. Grigoreva sounded 
proud in a way that made Yana’s skin tighten, proud the way 
someone might be proud of a weapon that had performed 
exactly as designed. 
Yana tried to read the angle. Where is he?  She had never 
seen a son in any brief or scrap of intel. 
Then the daughter from the gala slipped back into the 
thought. Serafim had not felt like a daughter being shown off.

She had felt like a mask worn badly. The possibility sat cold 
in Yana’s stomach. Maybe Grigoreva was not hinting at a 
hidden man at all. Maybe she was telling the truth in the only 
form she allowed herself. 
“You’ve grown quiet. Is something amiss?” She reached for 
Yana’s hand, her grip firm and possessive. 
Yana hesitated before responding, then squeezed back, 
attempting to infuse warmth into the chilly contact. “I’m 
alright,” she said, though she doubted it was what the 
Baroness wanted to hear. She caught the skepticism in the 
older woman’s eyes and steadied herself, careful to keep the 
brittle balance between them. She mustered a smile, praying 
it would appease her. 
“I’m pleased,” the Baroness replied, her smirk reclaiming its 
place. “For the record, you are extraordinary.” She opened the 
bedroom door, motioning for Yana to precede her. “You hold 
an unjust advantage over my son ’s other dalliances, you 
know.” 
Yana was disturbed by the tasteless comment. “And what’s 
that?” she asked, feigning a smile. 
The Baroness dismissed her bodyguard with a flick of her 
wrist as they entered the bedroom. As Yana closed the door, 
she turned to face Grigoreva and took her hands, drawing 
them to her chest. She forced a wave of feigned affection. 
The Baroness returned her smile and drew her in for a 
fervent kiss. “Because you’re young,” she murmured, parting 
before their lips met once more. Grigoreva’s hands roamed 
Yana’s body. 
“I trained him myself,” the Baroness said. “But he’s not as 
adept as you.” She leaned in again, one hand caressing Yana’s 
breast. The Baroness’s moan melded with their kiss, and Yana 
withdrew, hands still linked.

amusement at the edge of her eyes. “Not everyone is captivated

Yana had prodded too close. 
Closing the distance between them, Yana encircled 
Grigoreva’s waist from behind, pressing herself against the 
older woman ’s back. She placed a tender kiss on a bare 
shoulder, and made her voice low and intimate , “Like him, I 
too have my own concerns, despite enjoying 
these...distractions. I trust you ’ll uphold your end of our 
arrangement.” 
Yana paused, catching the  warmth of her own breath 
against Grigoreva ’s skin. “What I ’m after is simple —the 
freedom to call my own shots, to live life how I see fit. I ’m no 
one’s puppet, not to be pulled by strings or played like a game. 
And that includes you,” Yana said, lacing her words with a coy 
assertiveness. 
The Baroness stiffened but remained in her embrace. She 
regarded their reflection in the mirror. “You’re an enigma,” she 
mused. “I can’t quite decipher you.” 
Yana maintained the closeness. “Me, an enigma? ” she 
teased. “Cracking codes can be liberating, can ’t it? Perhaps 
there’s freedom in the revelations to come, for both of us.”

The Baroness lifted the cigar from the crystal ashtray. 
Facets threw small prisms across her hand. She drew a slow 
puff and set it back, smoke unwinding between them.  She 
turned and touched Yana’s cheek. “Courageous,” she said. “I 
appreciate that. Beware. Freedom can be treacherous, and not 
all who venture survive.” She kissed Yana again. “We will get 
there,” she said, voice low as she drew back. “Stay by my side, 
and I promise you’ll attain what you believe you desire.” 
Yana’s fingers moved over the Baroness’s shoulders. She 
untied the emerald sash, silk catching the low light. The robe 
slipped, and the nightgown’s straps gave. Fabric whispered to 
the floor, leaving skin to the candlelight. 
Grigoreva gestured for Yana to lie down, and she complied, 
her pulse quickening with anticipation. The older woman ’s 
hands trailed Yana ’s body, resting on her hips before 
encircling her waist and drawing her nearer. But as Yana lay 
down, her heart began to race with an undercurrent of 
repulsion she couldn’t quite stifle. 
“True power is freedom, ” Yana said. “The liberty to act, to 
be who you choose, without constraint. Don ’t you ever feel 
confined by your wealth, your power?” 
“And true freedom is perilous, ” the Baroness warned. “It 
can unleash chaos, incite insurrection. Tread carefully with 
your desires, Ms. Kuular. Freedom bears great responsibility, 
and not all are equipped to manage it.” 
Yana’s hips swayed as she grinned. “Not everyone can 
handle me,” she said in her sultriest voice, “but the challenge 
is always worth the while.” 
Grigoreva glanced briefly toward the door. “We shall see.” 
Her gaze returned to Yana, accompanied by a smile. 
“Promise me one thing,” she said, her tone softer now. 
“What’s that?”

The heavy oak door groaned as it opened, its latch clicking 
shut with a resolute thud. Yana’s gaze shifted to the doorway, 
where Grigoreva’s bodyguard ushered in the newcomer.  He 
escorted a slender young woman inside, carrying herself with 
the easy assurance of nobility Yana knew too well. 
She wore a sheer black top, delicate and airy, with ruffled 
trims that danced at the edges. Through the translucent 
fabric, her tender figure was hinted at, an embodiment of both 
sharp grace and soft ambiguity. Cascades of long, black 
ringlets framed her features, playing off the light that danced 
in her hazel eyes. Her skin was unblemished, smooth, almost 
porcelain in its appearance, a striking contrast to the black 
that contoured her form. 
Grigoreva’s eyes followed the elegant arrival, a subtle nod 
acknowledging her entrance. Her voice, edged with sternness 
and a trace of affection, broke the silence. “Ah, my beloved 
joins us. Now, the time has come to wash away the echoes of 
our revelries, to cleanse the remnants of our indulgences.” 
It was during the previous days of debauchery, amid the 
whispered secrets and veiled half-truths, that Yana realized 
she had nearly pieced together the puzzle of this Serafim’s 
identity. They had shared a table for hours, but the dim 
lighting of the ballroom had obscured the young woman ’s 
features, leaving Yana with only a nebulous impression. Now, 
observing this delicate figure more closely, memories flooded 
back—the subtle hints, the almost imperceptible slips in their 
behavior, the way their eyes danced with mischief whenever 
the topic of Grigoreva’s son was broached.

The first hints of that realization had been jarring, but now, 
as she took in this boyish grace, it became clear. The person 
she had taken for Grigoreva’s daughter wasn’t a daughter at 
all. Whoever he was, he had played the part well enough to 
fool her too. 
Yana couldn’t help but marvel at his audacity and the skill 
with which he ’d maintained his charade. The depth of the 
deception was profound, and as she met his gaze, Yana felt a 
mix of admiration and wariness. 
A nagging thought tugged at the back of her mind: Where 
is the real Serafim? What the hell did she lead me into? 
“I hope I ’m not too late, ” he greeted, acknowledging the 
Baroness with a nod. When his penetrating gaze turned to 
Yana, he apologized with a bow of his head and a soft click of 
his heels. 
The sweep of his long dark hair, the sharpness of his 
features, and those piercing  hazel eyes. Confidence bled 
through his posture, edged with something unpredictable 
Yana couldn’t quite name.  She watched as Grigoreva, 
seemingly enchanted, murmured, “Divine,” and sprang from 
the bed to thread her fingers through those rich black ringlets. 
“You could have any woman you want, ” Grigoreva 
remarked, eyeing her son with a mix of amusement and 
exasperation. 
This imposter before her  straightened, sweeping a casual 
hand through his curly hair as he met his mother’s gaze. “How 
tedious,” he replied with swift dismissal. 
“Besides,” he added, the smirk on his lips deepening as his 
gaze lingered on Yana, “take a look at this one. ..” It was a  
provocative insinuation wrapped in the subtlety of his words. 
Grigoreva’s laughter rang out. “Indeed, you do,” she agreed, 
her eyes twinkling as she looked between the two of them.

Serafim turned to Yana then, the smirk on his face a silent 
challenge. “Do you find me captivating, Yana? ” he asked. 
Without pausing, he gestured towards Grigoreva. “What of my 
mother? Does she captivate you too?” 
Yana met his stare unflinchingly. “She has her charms ,” 
she replied coolly. 
“Charms, you say? How delightfully modest of you, ” the 
Baroness drawled. “But tell me, dear Yana, do you know what 
is truly captivating? Power. And purity of purpose, which you 
shall witness here tonight.” 
Grigoreva signaled, and two robed women slipped from the 
corners to draw the drapes. At an ornate cabinet they lifted 
carved black candles and set  them in a rough circle on the 
plush carpet. A match cracked. Wicks caught. Inky blue 
flames rose and the walls danced with convulsive shadow. 
“The time has come to cleanse and to reaffirm command 
over flesh and spirit. In my child we invoke the bridge between 
binaries. In their form we see the alchemy that absolves and 
sanctifies. As they are consecrated, so are we. Let this be our 
mirror and our crucible.” 
Yana’s heartbeat climbed while he undressed. As each layer 
fell, she took in the mix of hard angles and yielding curves, a 
shape she couldn’t easily name.  With the last layer gone, 
candlelight traced lines across the body and held her eye. In 
the shifting shadows, soft and hard crossed in ways she could 
not name. 
In the quiet, the Baroness went to a hidden alcove. Her 
fingers moved over arranged tools and settled on a slender 
ceremonial blade. 
The blade Grigoreva lifted caught the candlelight. Etched 
scrollwork and saints ran its length, a church relic turned to 
this rite.

As the incantations gathered, she held to the stakes. This 
was not only the Battalion’s rot. It was her ticket out. The 
proof was close. Just a little longer. 
The women gathered and sipped from the blade. Is this 
what you wanted me to see? Pity flickered for the imposter in 
front of her. Being a pawn in Grigoreva’s charade was 
unthinkable. 
As the Baroness broke what the Battalion sold in public, 
iron rules and clean hands, Yana sneered at the irony. A week 
of tactics and a fake smile had dragged her deep into this filth. 
Grigoreva’s appetites had only made the work easier. The 
thought hardened her resolve to watch the whole masquerade 
fall under its own rot. 
Her thoughts roiled. She caught the youth’s eyes, searching 
for truth in the staged rite. Regret. A plea. Or the flat look of 
someone already resigned? 
As Grigoreva leaned in toward Serafim, her fingers finding 
the exposed skin of her nipples, there was a tender cruelty to 
it, a possessive claiming that made Yana’s stomach tighten. It 
was then that Yana saw it. Something flickered in those eyes, 
a crack in the mask that made Yana’s chest clench. 
Pity struck, sharp and sudden, slicing through her mission-
driven focus. Was that a cry for help, a plea for forgiveness 
from the farce this existence had become under Grigoreva’s 
control? Whatever it was, it pushed Yana over the edge. She 
could play her part no longer; the charade had gone too far,

The old women stayed silent, eyes fixed on Yana, as if 
waiting for a last piece to click. 
Candlelight flickered, shadows quivering across faces and 
walls. Everything held a moment. Her heartbeat thudded hard 
against her ribs. 
The cool brush of metal at her scalp snapped her back. The 
steel pin had stayed through all of it, a small link to the night 
she first stepped into that closet and let Grigoreva dress her 
like a toy. 
Her fingers trembled as she reached up and drew out the 
pin, her eyes catching her reflection in the grand mirror above 
the bed’s headboard. She clasped it tight, heartbeat steadying 
against the solid feel of the metal, her only ally. But as she 
handled its pointed end , she pricked her skin, and she 
watched, almost detached, as a small bead of blood welled up 
and began its slow descent along her wrist. 
The Serafim she had met in virtual, who had shown an 
almost desperate need for her to engage with Grigoreva, even 
enlisting her loan shark Dimitra’s assistance—what was the 
purpose behind urging this encounter with the mother of the 
woman who now appeared to be her twin? 
Could this entire scenario be nothing more than a drug -
induced illusion or a virtual manipulation planted by the real 
Serafim during their digital correspondence days prior? 
Yana fixed on the hairpin. Steel caught a stray beam and 
split her reflection into shards. The idea hit clean and sharp. 
Yana leapt and drove the serrated edge into Grigoreva’s 
thigh.  
Grigoreva screamed as blood ran. Yana ripped the pin free, 
set it to the throat, and shoved her out of the candles. The 
Baroness fell back.

“I’m not one of you ,” Yana hissed, feeling a  grin spread 
across her face as she watched the Baroness  cower, blood 
trickling at her feet. 
As if summoned by the chaos, one of the women robed in 
black darted forward, a desperate cry issuing from her lips. 
But Yana was faster. She sidestepped the woman ’s charge, 
then deftly hooked her foot behind the cultist ’s ankle while 
simultaneously driving her elbow into the woman ’s sternum. 
The combined force sent the woman crashing onto her back, 
breathless, against the marble floor with a solid thud. 
Her gaze caught the electrical cord of an unlit lamp. She 
tore it free, the sheath smooth under her fingers, and cut it 
with the hairpin. It would serve as a rope.  
Moving with a precision born from necessity, Yana firmly 
grasped the makeshift dirk, a grim deterrent for any would-be 
heroes. Without hesitating, she pressed it against the 
Baroness’s side, her eyes fiercely locking onto the Baroness ’s 
own wide, frightened gaze, ensuring there was no 
misunderstanding of her intent. 
She twisted the cord around the wrists and tied to the 
bedpost. The one-handed suture knot she had learned on an 
Okhotsk trawler bit down and held. 
A glint of emerald and gold caught her eye. The party 
emblem on the headscarf felt almost funny now. She grabbed 
it from the chair, rolled the fabric, and pressed it between the 
Baroness’s teeth. The next sound came out dull.  
With the Baroness secured, she turned to Serafim. The 
cultist she had dropped was rising, fists closing for another 
rush, until her gaze snagged on the bound matron. 
Recognition. Horror. Yana raised the hairpin. The woman 
broke, scrambling on all fours into the shadows. Coward. The 
fading scuff of retreat echoed.

CHAPTER TWENTY FOUR 
DUNYA  
 
Dunya’s eyelids flickered open to the rhythm of ambulance 
lights, painting her vision in splashes of primary colors. She 
felt the cold press of a pill against her lips. 
“Drink this, ” a voice commanded, like an echo from 
somewhere far away.

clink of the pill hitting the gurney loud in her ears. Enough. 
Every cell in her body recoiled at the thought of someone else 
making choices for her. Her chest tightened. 
“It’s for the pain,” the paramedic insisted, a fringe of worry 
in his tone.

stomach and thighs with their cold elegance . The paramedic 
reached for her again, but she turned her head, looking for

glinting—an image distorted through the haze of pain and 
consciousness that threatened to pull Dunya under once 
more.

Lucky to be alive? What a joke. What was left for her? 
Parents dead, husband dead. Maria had betrayed her. Then 
that damned contract had walked her straight into a chapel 
under the Akhmatova Railways. She’d read the words, cut off 
her hair, and laid it on the page like a fucking signature. White 
light. A hooded shape wait ing behind her when it cleared. 
Whatever the ritual had done, she’d authenticated it herself. 
Maybe she’d opened something. Maybe she’d only given it 
permission. Ghosts in the machine hounded her, the city was 
engulfed in flames, witches wove through its achi ng streets. 
And her own lower body, from her midriff to her thighs, was 
charred and still demanding braces to mimic some semblance 
of normal movement. 
What the fuck is the point to all this? The question pounded 
through her, a relentless echo that matched the throb of her 
burnt torso and the wail of sirens. 
Her father and mother were dead. Dugal was dead. Vesna 
disappeared whenever Dunya got close enough to need an 
answer. Maria had taken the one trust Dunya still had and 
broken it open. Even Serafim’s sermons kept returning, all 
that talk about descending into darkness to find some deeper 
vision. Dunya had descended. She had found a book, a 
hooded woman, and another trap she had helped spring on 
herself.

those.” 
Dunya felt a cool numbness begin  to seep into her limbs . 
She shrugged nonchalantly and asked, “What’s in these, 
anyway?” 
“A modified exovegeta composition,” the paramedic replied, 
voice edged with a mixture of annoyance and frustration. “It’s 
the perfect painkiller.” 
“And d on’t worry, ” he continued, trying to regain 
professional composure. “They have self-terminating sensors 
in them, designed to prevent an overdose.” 
“Figures,” Dunya muttered with a scoff. Even this decision 
had been stripped of its finality. She cursed under her breath, 
resenting the invisible safety nets that seemed to unfurl with 
every attempt to regain some semblance of control in her life. 
As the ambulance jostled over the city ’s uneven roads, 
Dunya’s gaze locked onto the smaller of the two gunblades 
sheathed on the Black Wolf’s utility belt. Her mind, hazed by 
the painkillers, nonetheless worked with a grim clarity as she 
calculated her next move. 
Maybe the gunblade was the one decision nobody could 
reverse, reroute, or administer for her. She was tired of waking 
inside choices other people had already made. This one would 
belong to her. 
“We’re almost at the burn unit,” the paramedic announced.

The burn unit was too close. Dunya fixed on the gunblade, 
studying the grip, estimating its weight, calculating how 
quickly she could clear the sheath. The idea stopped being a 
possibility and became a route. 
She feigned a gasp, clutched where her skin blistered, and 
doubled over. Reacting to her distress, the paramedic moved 
quickly towards Dunya, his alarm evident.  Just then, the 
ambulance rocked sharply on a turn. The sudden movement, 
compounded by the distraction of the paramedic ’s reaction, 
caused the Black Wolf to shift her weight unexpectedly. The 
formidable woman stumbled, her massive frame toppling over 
with a crashing thud. In the ensuing chaos, Dunya ’s hand 
shot out to the gunblade’s hilt. 
Vesna. Maria. Mom, Dad, Dugal. Dead, gone, or somewhere 
Dunya could no longer reach. She was done with contracts, 
riddles, and waking up in a body someone else had decided to 
preserve. The gunblade offered one clean command, and for 
once she held the permissions.  
She gripped the weapon, its weight a sudden anchor in her 
shaking hand. A switch flicked, a hiss sounded, and the blade 
sprang forth, ready and exact. Turning the blade towards her 
legs, scarred and raw, she began to slice. I want it all to end. 
Her body strained under the rapid exertion until, inevitably, 
her vision narrowed—darkness crept in from the edges  until 
the gunblade’s grip grew slick in her weakening grasp. She felt 
the hard texture slip from her fingers, the clink of metal-on-
metal ringing sharply as it hit the floor. Her body, now limp 
and spent, followed the weapon ’s descent . H er sense of 
upended disorientation only grew as she came to rest against 
the shifting, vibrating surface that should have been the floor 
of the ambulance. 
No static this time. Just black.

CHAPTER TWENTY FIVE 
VESNA  
 
The moment Vesna heard the news, she left the front line—
Goga Borisova, newly risen from technician to aspirant of the 
Black Wolves, now stood at the helm. A flicker of doubt 
brushed Vesna ’s mind, of whether Goga ’s greenness could 
withstand the turmoil of command. But the urgent call 
overshadowed all, pulling her to the crash scene  without 
hesitation. 
The landscape flew by in a disorienting rush as Vesna 
neared the sirens’ wail. The ambulance lay on its side like a 
toppled behemoth, its underbelly exposed to the night. The 
back doors, its skeletal wings, were flung wide—an open maw 
of desperation beckoning.  
With urgency heavy in her chest, Vesna wrenched the 
ambulance doors wider, her pulse racing in tandem with the 
chaos that greeted her. Between the disarray of shattered 
glass and scattered medical tools, Dunya lay motionless. How 
could you? Vesna’s gaze traced the line of each injury, her eyes 
pausing on the severe third -degree burns and scars that 
marred Dunya’s legs, the worst of them stark white against 
her skin. But the distinctive marks of a gunblade signaled only 
one harrowing reality: a self-inflicted wound.  
A bitter knot formed in her gut as she realized, with grave 
familiarity, that she’d seen many Wolves do the same in their 
darkest moments.  Beside Dunya, the formidable Kovalenko—
unmistakable for her massive stature, a known ogre within 
the walls of Fort Ivan—worked deftly with the paramedic. The 
pair acted as a single entity, their efforts syncing to carefully 
secure Dunya onto a backboard with gentle, yet urgent 
precision.

another set of doors, her body now a battlefield for the 
surgeons to conquer.

walked through, settled like lead in Vesna ’s heart. She had 
seen Dunya walk through fire before, steady and fearless, but 
this was different. Vesna’s eyes stung, a volatile mix of anger 
and sorrow surging beneath the surface, threatening to spill 
over.

“Did you really think that you could ascend to the heights 
of the Syndicate from where you stand now? ” the woman 
added. 
That probing question clawed at her, a spectral doubt that 
had lurked unspoken in every shadowed corner of her mind , 
on every mission, during every fight . Vesna understood the 
harsh truth in the woman ’s words: The Wolves were mighty, 
but their strength, much like the towering pines of a vast 
forest, could be felled in a single stroke by one wielding the 
power of the storm. It was a stark reflection of a truth Vesna 
had never allowed herself to fully consider —the reality that 
even the most indomitable warrior stood vulnerable before the 
intricate, merciless game of politics. 
The woman continued, “It’s a rare sight to see a Black Wolf 
transition to the Board. And Zakharovna...she always knew 
that wasn’t your true role. Chaos, Vesna, that’s what you were 
there to create. You were used to shake the foundations, not 
to be the one that rebuilds them. If you must know, the boss 
is onto something big. If she succeeds, we won’t need firefights 
and muscle  anymore. But your role hasn ’t changed —it’s 
crucial, and we need you safe for now. So, move.”  
Vesna felt the ground splinter beneath her. Dunya’s safety, 
the future of the Wolves, her own place at the helm —all 
teetered on the precipice of her next choice. 
She clenched her fists tighter, her mind a whirlwind of 
conflict. Abandoning Dunya, especially now, churned in her 
stomach like acid. How could she justify running to save 
herself when she hadn ’t been there for her, over and over,  
when Dunya needed her most? The ID in her hand was a 
siren’s call to survival, but every fiber of her being resisted. 
“Stay with her ,” Vesna whispered.  “Don’t let her wake up 
alone.”

CHAPTER TWENTY SIX 
MARIA  
 
Maria’s reflection flickered on the display ’s surface as she 
willed it to life. The projection lit up, unveiling the newsreel 
footage: a veil of smoke obscured the city’s skyline, and flames 
roared with primal hunger as they consumed the dogwood 
trees that had long stood sentinel along downtown 
boulevards. 
“The Coven,” Mayor Rylova declared, her voice cutting 
through the crackle of the dying ember, “is behind these 
atrocities. They ’re terrorists. And they will answer for their 
crimes.” 
Maria studied the mayor, whose practiced smile betrayed 
nothing. 
“These trees,” the mayor continued, “represented our city’s 
prosperity, our resurgence from a troubled history. For thirty 
years, they flourished. And now, in mere hours, they ’re 
reduced to ash.” 
The camera panned to another cluster of scorched trees. 
Nearby, a squad of Hive infantry, clad in identical gray military 
gear with black visors and weapons glinting under the harsh 
sunlight, stood vigil outside City Hall. 
“We will not stand for this,” Rylova vowed, her voice 
unwavering. “We will identify the guilty, and we will deliver 
justice.” 
Maria cut the feed. “The old beekeeper ’s got it all wrong,” 
she spat. “The Coven ’s not some organized group. It ’s just a 
rabble—a bunch of disgruntled misfits looking for meaning in 
chaos.”

The door creaked open, and Maria heard the familiar 
rhythm of footsteps . Serafim’s, unmistakable. She came up 
close behind Maria, her voice low. “The attacks are getting 
worse. There’s a pattern.” 
Maria scoffed. “They’re torching trees. Why trees? We’ve got 
a whole forest of them on the city outskirts. If they wanted to 
halt progress, why not burn a church? A monument?” 
“It’s symbolic. A message of defiance.” 
Shadows cast by the newsreel danced across the walls.  
Maria stood. “I’ve got enough evidence,” she said. “I ’ll expose 
her.” 
“We need a body,” Serafim said. “We need to know who ’s 
funding them.” 
“The Hive ’s control of the mayorship is the only barrier 
against Syndicate dominance. It ’ll be altogether eight years 
before they officially hold the Board again,” Maria said. 
“The Hive?” Serafim ’s voice dripped with sarcasm. “What 
have they got to do with this?” 
A moment of clarity struck Maria. They’d disrupted capital 
markets for years, hindering the city ’s expansion beyond the 
peninsula. Now, as the Syndicate teetered on civil conflict, the 
Hive posed as saviors. 
“They’re in on it,” Maria said. “They always have been.”

They all bore responsibility for the crisis now unfolding —
and they would all face the reckoning.

launched an offensive against the police following a damning

harvesting its own citizens to nourish Babushka, the

been happening for over a decade.

Given their history of scanning students and staff with 
unnerving frequency, the revelation wasn’t entirely shocking. 
But why now? What deeper play was unfolding beneath the 
surface?

constructing something... more elaborate. Maria’s mind raced 
with the thought of an intricate database, a digital

CHAPTER TWENTY SEVEN 
KLARA  
 
The air shuddered inside the small chapel carved into the 
wall of the Akhmatova Railways. Jagged stone framed a 
weathered pine altar, and three sconces burned above it, their 
flames wavering whenever the rails groaned deeper in the 
earth. The room was packed with outlaws and cravens, eager 
fires rousing inside them, straining to break free from mortal 
bonds. 
“Sisters and brothers,” Klara declared, “today marks a 
critical juncture in our conflict. The Syndicate, that vile cartel 
of politicians, soldiers, and scoundrels, has ruled with an iron 
fist for far too long. We have suffered under their despotism, 
and now, our moment for vengeance has come!” 
The congregation’s voices surged, swelling in fervor around 
her. Klara’s smile sharpened. With a commanding sweep of 
her arms, the voices fell silent. “Tonight”,” she declared, “we 
invoke the spirit of vengeance to aid us. We will harness our 
magic and bring this civil war to its crushing end!” 
Klara’s gaze swept over the crowd as the cheers rose again, 
swelling into a storm. The air before her shimmered, and a 
sudden burst of light formed an image. Her breath caught at 
the sight of the hovering figure —an ancient crone, draped in 
tattered black r obes, hunched and frail. Yet from it, an 
unmistakable energy pulsed. The projection’s eyes locked with 
Klara’s, and its lips curled into a smile.  
“I am here to aid you,” the spirit rasped. “Tell me what you 
desire, and I shall grant you the might to seize it.” 
Klara's arms shot out in a triumphant sweep. “I want the 
Syndicate!”

“Far above us, the fires converge,” Klara roared. “The

“Far above us, the fires converge,” Klara roared. “The 
Syndicate crumbles as we speak. This is only the beginning.” 
Pra Matron Vatraliyna rose, a satisfied smile playing on her 
cracked white lips, the only part of her face visible beneath 
the hood. She lifted her hands, and the tumult quickly abated. 
“Victory is within our grasp,” she proclaimed. “Sisters and 
brothers, let us force the Syndicate to their knees. Now is the 
time to reclaim what is rightfully ours.” 
The congregation erupted again, their voices rising into a 
frenzied storm. Klara’s pulse quickened as Vatraliyna 
approached, draping her arms over Klara’s shoulders. “You 
are the future of our Coven,” she said. “No one can stand in 
your way.” 
Vatraliyna stepped forward, her robe as dark as the 
shadows clinging to the chapel’s walls. The fabric whispered 
against the stone floor as she moved, her presence a quiet 
force. Beneath her hood, eyes glowed green and red, locking 
the assembly in an almost tangible hold.  
“Klara shall lead the final assault,” Vatraliyna’s voice rang 
out. “The chosen will accompany her. Together, we will 
dismantle the Syndicate’s dominion!” 
Cheers erupted, a thunderous affirmation of Vatraliyna’s  
words. Among the surging bodies, the revelers parted as she 
moved through them with swift purpose. Klara’s gaze followed, 
watching the sable robe slip through the archway like a 
shadow vanishing into the night. Vatraliyna disappeared just 
as the revelry began to swell.

With a subtle gesture from Klara, the room exploded into 
celebration. Shadows flickered and danced as the assembly 
gave in to wild abandon. The air throbbed with war cries, 
shifting into a primal chorus of ecstasy. Hands reached out, 
not merely touching bu t claiming, as claws and grasping 
fingers met in a feverish communion. A ritualistic fervor swept 
through the crowd, binding them in a shared, ravenous 
hunger for the battle ahead. 
Klara stood at the epicenter,  arms lifted toward the dark 
ceiling. Power surged through her, fueling each incantation. 
In one hand, a silver knife gleamed; in the other, a mortar of 
blood-red communion stones pulsed with an eerie glow. 
As the ritual’s energy reached its peak, Klara allowed a 
moment of reflection. The outlaws surrounding her, once 
defiant lords of volition, had been reshaped by the exovegeta. 
She had foreseen how it would peel back the years, freeing 
them from time’s weig ht, but it had also made them pliable. 
The compound dissolved their fierce independence, unlocking 
a malleability she had carefully harnessed. Watching their 
fervent devotion, Klara understood the drug’s dual nature: it 
bestowed the illusion of youth while binding them to her 
vision, forging warriors from wanderers at the cost of the 
autonomy they could no longer reclaim.  She had once dosed 
pain to keep bodies alive; now she dosed belief and called it 
salvation. 
The frenzied crowd of outlaws and cravens surged toward 
her, and Klara basked in the heat and frenzy as she 
brandished her blade. She reveled in the chaos. With a sudden 
motion, she thrust her arms upward, a conduit for the dark 
power coursing through her. Energy surged from the depths, 
channeled through her raised limbs, coiling into black 
lightning that wrapped around the bloodstones.

As the air crackled with the storm she had summoned, 
Klara lowered her arms and stepped forward, ready to lead her 
chosen into the heart of their wild sacrament. 
Her dagger, now blazing with annihilation’s fire, cut 
through the chaotic crowd. Her acolytes mirrored her every 
move—extensions of her deadly will, entwined in the ritual’s 
deadly rhythm. Blades flashed, blood spilled, anointing the 
ground in dark reverence. Klara’s cry pierced the air, marking 
the ritual’s climax as men and women fell in perfect unison. 
One by one, the bodies were dragged into place, forming a grim 
circle of the fallen. As blood pooled in the pattern they created, 
the frenzy dissolved into a haunting stillness. Encircled by her 
loyal followers, Klara surveyed the crimson ring—a testament 
to their unity and sacrifice. 
Lifting her gaze from the carnage, Klara felt the weight of 
her actions settle over her like a shadow. She stared at the 
blood coating her skin, a flicker of dissonance stirring within. 
Beneath the triumph, a whisper of remorse crept into her 
thoughts. 
What have I become?  The question no longer stopped her, 
but it still knew where to cut. 
She recalled the days when her hands brought healing 
instead of death. Her past as a nurse, tending to the weak and 
mending the broken, felt like a distant life, a world away from 
the carnage she now commanded. 
The Hive ’s principles are my commandments now; the 
Coven, my sanctuary.  
She inhaled deeply, forcing herself to stand firm against the 
flood of memories. Sorrow for the lost, for those used as mere 
pawns in a war greater and darker than any one soul, clashed 
with the satisfaction of power and purpose. This is the path I 
must walk, she reminded herself, stifling the creeping regret. 
The sacrifices today pave the road to reclamation.

The Coven’s cheers rose, their voices merging into a single, 
powerful chorus. Klara could feel their collective strength 
surging through her, each sister’s power feeding into the 
whole. 
“Natasha will lead our assault,” Klara continued . “Follow 
her command, and victory is certain.” 
Natasha stepped forward, her eyes bright with eager 
anticipation—a hunger Klara knew had been simmering 
beneath the surface for far too long. 
“Come, sisters,” Natasha called, her voice sharp and 
commanding. “Destiny awaits!” She turned, knife in hand, 
and led the Coven forward. They followed her as one, a 
shadowy procession slipping into the tunnels, their footsteps 
a soft, rhythmic echo against the concrete concourse. 
Klara returned her gaze to the woman in green, a strange 
calm settling over her as their eyes locked. The initial blaze of 
tension had shifted, giving way to something deeper, more 
unsettling. In the slender woman’s  sharp blue stare, Klara 
glimpsed fleeting whispers of another world, another time. 
The metro station beneath them shuddered violently, an 
explosion echoing from afar.  The woman’s lips twisted into a 
savage snarl. “You can call me Marzanna,” she said. 
Klara barely had time to register the name before Marzanna 
grabbed her arm and yanked her into the cover of the 
shadows.

pictured the millions of eyes fixed on the projections 
throughout the city, waiting for what would come next.  
“We have made a chilling discovery. There is a coup, right 
within the ranks of our very police force. Senior officers...our 
own people...have betrayed us, have conspired against their 
government.”

on our citizens. The details of these experiments...they ’re 
harrowing, beyond what any of us could have imagined.” 
“As many of you are aware, the Black Wolves, under the 
command of former Syndicate operative Vesna Volkova, have 
failed in their attempt to impose martial law, and in their 
retreat are now terrorizing those who sought to bring the truth 
to light. We call upon you, the people of Gred, to resist any 
orders they  may issue. With our strength and your 
unwavering support, we can thwart this coup before it inflicts 
further devastation.” 
 “The Syndicate...the government you’ve placed your trust

timed mockery. The moment felt too heavy for such levity, as 
if Nikitin couldn’t grasp the weight of what was at stake. “It all 
falls into place... The vile whispers... Nina’s circle, the scoffing 
at galas over rumors too ghastly to speak aloud... and Ivan 
Sorokin’s suicide—a tragic act born from a harrowing truth 
unraveled—that his ‘daughter’, in fact,  was sired by none 
other than the king who never came to be. We must locate this 
living testament to their indiscretion and turn it to our 
advantage. This is our moment to lift the Battalion to its 
rightful zenith. It’s our time ascend, Nikitin.”

Tatyana turned in her chair, her gaze shifting to the window 
and lingering on the troops marching below.  The soldiers, 
adorned in green military uniforms, were distinguished by 
gold runes that glinted in the sunlight, a touch of regal 
elegance to their martial appearance. Their rifles were poised 
with disciplined precision. Tatyana hadn’t seen her army this 
prepared for battle in years, and a part of her, a part honed 
by old skirmishes and older victories, rued the absence of a 
good war. 
Nikitin leaned forward slightly, the soft light from the 
room’s lone lamp casting shifting shadows across her face. 
“You’re suggesting we risk everything,” she said. 
“We have been pawns for too long, bent to the whims of 
shadow rulers. It’s time we take control of the board,” Tatyana 
said. 
“And abandon the Charter,” Nikitin added. 
“As if they all haven’t already,” Tatyana said. “Now we play 
catch-up; we ’ve been too honorable in our dealings with 
scum.” 
“And the people—how will they react to our coup? ” Nikitin 
asked. 
“Coup? Have you been listening at all?  This, this is a 
revolution.” 
There was a slight, almost imperceptible shift in Nikitin ’s 
stance—enough for Tatyana, who had spent decades learning 
this general’s silent tells—to discern agreement. 
“Then what comes next...” Nikitin had stopped questioning. 
Now, she was listening. 
Tatyana felt her smile return. “...is order.”

The Grand Mariner’s Cathedral swelled with a congregation 
of seasoned souls. Enforcers with scars that told tales of 
battles long fought, elder women etched by wisdom, and 
military veterans with a glint of discipline in their eyes filled 
every pew and chai r. Tatyana navigated this throng of aged 
strength, nodding to familiar faces as she passed. At the front, 
the Battalion stood in formation, their green and gold 
uniforms a sharp contrast against the pristine white marble. 
Tatyana saluted crisply, and the response was instant: the 
soldiers roared, their faces ignited with fervor, rallied to the 
call of duty. They quickly formed a line that stretched from the 
entrance to where Matron General Nikitin stood, a silent 
sentinel a t her dais, her back rigid, her expression 
unreadable. 
As the soldiers’ roars faded into a charged silence, Tatyana 
moved closer to Nikitin. She leaned in, receiving the whispered 
update directly into her ear: “The Hive’s force concentration 
has slowed, but make no mistake—those damned witches are 
assembling.” 
With a curt nod, Tatyana acknowledged the update and 
turned her gaze toward the west doors. Commander Goga 
Borisova entered, flanked by her elite Black Wolves. 
As Tatyana advanced toward the chancel, the crowd parted 
like a sea obeying an invisible tide. Two figures rose from the 
midst, commanding the space: Grand Mariner Veronika 
Lagunov, her mane of silver glowing under the cathedral’s 
light, her gaze sharp and  unyielding; and at her side, 
Commodore Alexandra Baranov, a steady shadow to the 
towering leader. 
Tatyana locked eyes with the Grand Mariner. “I have a 
proposition for you, Lagunov.” 
“Haven’t you done enough?” the Grand Mariner snapped.

shifting sands of your politics.”

fight the current of change already set in motion , Tatyana

A faint sense of triumph stirred in Tatyana as their eyes met—

orchestrated within the Mariner’s ranks.

forces and confidants drifting toward the gravity of Tatyana’s

CHAPTER TWENTY NINE 
DUNYA  
 
Freezing stillness swallowed her. Limbs drifted, weightless, 
and one thought kept pulsing like static: 
Why am I still here? I wanted it all to end. 
Vesna had gone silent. Maria had cut the line. Dugal was 
dead. Different failure modes, same result: Dunya was alone 
while everyone else still had a hand on the systems keeping 
her alive. 
Disposable, she thought. Useful until damaged, then routed 
somewhere quiet. 
Serafim’s voice surfaced in the dark, followed by the 
memory of the gunblade. Cold steel. Pain. Warmth running 
where it should not. Then black. 
The Skelet returned next, metal wrapped around legs that 
no longer answered without permission. Even the suicide 
attempt had failed closed. Sensors, medics, and dosage limits. 
She could not stand, could not die, could not make one clean 
decision without another system overruling it. 
Was I not even strong enough to finish that? 
Why didn’t it work? 
A stubborn thump echoed somewhere within, faint but 
insistent, like a coal refusing to die. A feather -light warmth 
drifted across her, as if someone had tugged the blanket 
higher over a body she could no longer feel, and the void’s chill 
began—almost imperceptibly—to loosen its grip.

Thread by thread, the numbness unraveled. Cool rain 
pricked skin that wasn’t quite hers, the sterile tang thinning 
into the earthy breath of damp soil and tender green. 
Somewhere at the frayed edge of awareness, a monotone 
buzz—machines keeping vigil —thinned to a hairline hum . 
Through the crack, a single birdsong threaded the dark. Each 
note tugged at her, urging her to shrug off the velvet hush and 
rise. 
Could it be? The thought formed slowly, breaking through 
the darkness. 
Is this...another chance? 
Do I deserve one? 
Do I even want one? 
The shift was ephemeral, like the swift silence of a blink. It 
blurred at the edges, and when it sharpened again, it was not 
grass brushing the soles of her feet as she had half-expected, 
but the feel of earth compacting beneath paws. 
The echo of her own heartbeat was now a rhythm set to the 
cadence of a run. Dunya glanced down. Limbs, cloaked in 
deep-red fur banded with black stripes, struck against the 
earth, affirming her new wild form. She was a tiger. 
With each bound forward, the world streaked past her in a 
vibrant smear of lush greens and burnished umber.  Fern 
fronds brushed her flanks and cool loam burst beneath her 
pads; the forest exhaled with every bound, its rhythm 
matching her own. 
This isn’t real. But may be, just maybe, I can control it this 
time.

Blood drummed in her ears. Every coil of muscle struck 
sparks against the ache, forcing it back. The forest’s mossy 
breath mingled with a ghost of antiseptic that scratched her 
throat, and with it came the faint beep…beep…beep—its 
rhythm tilting, stretching—until it feathered into the two-note 
trill of an unseen bird overhead. White ceiling panels flickered 
behind her eyes, then shattered into shards of sunlight. Cold 
steel had once slashed across her thighs; now cool soil sifted 
beneath her claws. She gulped the green air and ran on, 
willing the land itself to teach her how to breathe. 
Her pace slowed from a run to a lope. Sirens and hospital 
lights receded until the forest was the only active process left. 
Her body answered immediately and completely, without 
wheels, braces, or hands lifting her without permission. 
She knew it was not real. She also knew she did not care 
yet.  
Reality intruded with the patter of hooves.  A deer —a 
creature from her half -remembered hikes in the virgin old -
growth boreal forests of Bystrinsky—bounded across the 
misty alpine meadow  with a desperate grace. As it leapt 
behind a looming pine, its ensuing sprint towards the ravine 
hinted at an urgency Dunya recognized all too well. A slip on 
mossy ground, a tumbling figure, and the deer was a fraction 
away from the abyss. 
She bounded once, twice, then exploded forward, muscles 
firing before thought could catch up. 
Warm flesh yielded  beneath her jaws and the deer’s last 
tremor rattled up her teeth, falling in step with her own 
pounding heartbeat. Iron washed her tongue, and with it came 
staccato flashes: restraints biting skin, fluorescent glare, 
corridors that smelled of bleach. She shook them off, gulped 
air that tasted of leaf mold and rain, but a thin blade of cold 
slid along her flank, sharp er than any wind. The forest

these flames moved with purpose. They drew her in with their 
allure, yet the prickling heat on her skin held her at bay. 
From the heart of the conflagration, silhouettes took form, 
their hair a molten cascade of silver and ember. 
Dunya’s eyes were drawn to one figure, swathed in a robe 
of obsidian. The garment flowed, almost liquid in its 
movement, with intricate patterns stitched in silver thread 
glistening against the fire’s backdrop. 
She absorbed the sight, and the cloaked figure detached 
from the group, her posture resolute against the tide of 
searing flames. “We stand as the Coven’s chosen,” she 
declared, her voice rising above the inferno. 
The surrounding chorus raised their voices, weaving a 
haunting harmony that momentarily subdued the fire’s 
insatiable hunger. 
Then, in a stark and sudden blaze, the figures burst into 
pillars of flame that consumed the space they occupied.

Dunya recoiled, arm thrust over her face to fend off the 
onslaught of light. 
Time seemed to stretch, each second an eternity as the fiery 
intensity gradually waned. When the figures finally dissipated, 
the inferno’s brilliance dimmed and reshaped, revealing a 
majestic edifice beneath its embers. Looming spires and 
intricate carvings stood defiantly amid the flames. 
Dunya’s breath hitched, memories rushing in like a torrent. 
She could hear the dawn bells of the Grand Mariner’s 
Cathedral, their chimes a distant lullaby from her youth. The 
vibrancy of the stained-glass windows seemed to dance before 
her eyes, recounting tales of heroic sailors and age -old 
legends. 
And the chill of the stone floor —she felt it again, as if she 
were a young girl sitting through Sunday sermons. 
Beside her, the imagined grip of her babushka’s hand 
anchored her, the whispered prayers a bridge to a time when 
the old religions were honored and revered. 
“Don’t fear the dark currents, my child, ” her grandmother 
had said, her voice a weave of comfort and mystery. “They too 
lead to the same great sea.” 
But the embrace of those days was now but a touch. Dunya 
could still feel her grandmother’s fingers tangled in hers, the 
soft murmur of ancient prayers in the dim light of the 
cathedral. Baba Medvedova, lost to the tides of time, had left 
her with a treasured trove of memories. 
And as the amber flames danced wild, that once peaceful 
past was brutally interrupted by the chilling roar of battle that 
surged across the horizon. 
From the protective shadows of white birch, soldiers 
charged forward, their armor catching and reflecting the 
tempestuous glow around them.

Among them, a formidable woman in a rugged leather 
jacket stood out, her posture alone declaring her dominance 
over the battlefield. Her companion, clothed in a dull green 
overcoat, moved with the grace of a hunting feline. Short silver 
hair framed her fac e while her deep blue eyes, sharp and 
focused, scanned the scene, ever calculating. 
Behind them, two more women emerged, their age evident 
but deceptive, for they were anything but frail. Their seasoned 
faces were a map of countless battles, eyes holding the weight 
of innumerable wars. Clad in mercenary gear tailored from 
reinforced leath er and steel, they drew their weapons: a 
gunblade and a sniper rifle, ancient craft complementing 
modern tech. 
And as the four women plunged into the fray, a symphony 
of clashing metal and arcane whispers erupted. 
The battle collapsed into a mirrored chamber. Dunya was 
bound again, and the man who had broken her body stood 
close enough to reach. 
She drove the blade into him before whatever had built the 
room could choose for her. 
His blood warmed the steel. The deer flashed through her 
mind, its throat crushed between tiger jaws. Something was 
forcing an equivalence between them: prey, target, body, 
consequence. Cheap moral theater. 
The comparison was wrong. The deer had tried to live. He 
had chosen what he did to her. 
The room broke back into forest. As a tiger, she could smell 
blood and fear without confusing either one with justice. The 
man was gone. Her scars were not. Killing him had not 
rewritten a single line. 
Still, her legs worked. Her body belonged to her. For now, 
that was enough.

She pressed on through the forest in pursuit of new prey. 
This was her domain,  and it was bountiful; she intended to  
traverse it all. 
A shape peeled away from the timberline, huge and silent, 
paws padding into the clearing where the deer lay.  The 
newcomer halted at the blood -damp grass, settling into a 
predator’s stillness that sent a prickling warning up Dunya’s 
spine. 
She roared, and her challenge rumbled through the forest, 
a primal sound full of ferocity as she bared her fangs at the 
formidable wolf before her, its blue eyes meeting hers with an 
unflinching gaze. 
They circled each other in a calculated dance, each step a 
silent measure of the other ’s strength. The wolf loomed , 
shoulders like stone,  yet Dunya felt her own power course 
from within—a deep, unbreakable bond with the forest itself . 
She was not afraid. 
In a burst of speed, Dunya lunged for the wolf’s throat. The 
wolf twisted clear and its teeth clamped down on her flank, 
sending fire skittering across her ribs. She lurched sideways, 
claws ripping furrows through the leaf litter, breath ragged 
with pain. 
Several paces now separated them, her blood dripping onto 
churned earth while the wolf’s muzzle gleamed dark and wet. 
Their eyes locked. In the next heartbeat, tiger and wolf 
collided, fur, dust, and crimson churning together. The great 
wolf reared onto it s hind legs and let loose a howl that split 
the moonlit canopy. Dunya answered, raw and resonant, and 
drove herself forward.

if painted, Zakharovna surveyed the horizon. Amid the ruins,
a network of fractured arches and splintered spires, stood the
remains of a massive cathedral, its dome collapsed. Encircling
it were the old birch trees, now charred in a forest turned to
coal.

life.

tang that nipped at the back of her throat. “Every foundation 
needs its ashes.” 
Yelena bridged the distance between them. “This was our 
home... And you—” 
“It’s evolution, Yelena. The world evolves. We have evolved,” 
Zakharovna interrupted, turning to meet her  bright green  
eyes.

“And she showed her true colors. Weakness. Fear, ” 
Zakharovna retorted. 
She watched as Yelena floated to the balcony ’s edge, the 
crumbling structure offering a stark view of their shattered 
world. In the dimming twilight, Yelena ’s silhouette stood tall 
and imposing.
