She made her departure from the high-rise. It was a pillar 
of modern design, untouched by the disaster that had 
ravaged its neighbors—a tribute not only to the advanced 
materials it was built with but to Zakharovna’s foresight in 
demanding such protections. In a city perpetually gripped by 
cold, fire-proof buildings had once seemed frivolous to the 
Board. 
When she reached ground level, the limousine was already 
there. She slid into its shadowed interior. Zakharovna settled 
back, the tinted windows offering her solitude as she 
surveyed the fractured bones of her domain. Her city. Her 
responsibility. Her canvas for rebirth. 
Reaching the outskirts of Gred, where the disarray of 
urban destruction dissolved into the pristine expanse of 
Kamchatka, she arrived at an inconspicuous garage cradled 
by the distant, sweeping rise of mountains. For miles, the 
snow stretched out before her, a vast canvas of white framed 
by dark forests. 
Inside the garage her snowmobile was primed for 
departure. Zakharovna mounted the vehicle and, with a 
sharp twist of the throttle, shot forward into the snow. As 
she gained speed, her eyes swept over the terrain she left 
behind. The towering form of Koryaksky volcano, a colossal 
specter, watched over the land with timeless vigilance. She 
edged the snowmobile faster, and as she accelerated into the 
open wilderness, the biting chill of the air whipped against 
her face. 
 
∆∆∆ 
 
Sokoch was a picturesque town of a hundred thousand 
souls, its towering walls a fortress against the outside world

Zakharovna shook her head, sensing a heaviness in 
Orkon’s demeanor that she hadn’t noticed before.

his features—fear for her prolonged absence, and perhaps, a 
deeper trepidation about the demands she might now place 
upon him. 
“The Hive’s agents have seeped into every crevice,” he said, 
the words heavy with unspoken truths. 
She nodded slowly, acknowledging the pervasive reach of 
their adversaries. Zakharovna’s return wasn’t just a matter of 
physical distance; it was a re -entry into a web of intrigue 
Orkon had been left to navigate, one that now clung to him 
with invisible threads. 
In the resistance  against Yelena’s incursions , he had 
become an emblem of guidance, his counsel sought after, his 
strategies employed. But she could see the toll it had taken—
a constant, unnerving dance with danger that left him taut, 
like a bowstring ready to snap. 
“You’re needed by my side, Orkon. There are forces stirring 
that we must confront together,” she said. 
Zakharovna’s mind sifted through memories—echoes of the 
countless times she and Orkon had navigated caverns of 
mystery, side by side, hearts pounding. The silent pact 
between them, their unspoken ritual for seeking elusive 
answers, felt more relevant than ever. The truth awaited them 
once again, if they dared to search.

CHAPTER THIRTY ONE 
DUNYA 
 
The forest rang with their clash, claws raking, jaws 
snapping, bodies crashing through soil and leaf litter. Growls 
tore the silence until they broke into ragged gasps, each 
movement slower than the last. 
At dawn’s first light the frenzy faltered, giving way to a taut 
stillness. Both stood battered, breaths dragging in the cold 
morning air. Then Dunya lunged, closing the gap in a blur. 
Her teeth locked at the wolf’s neck. A savage shake ended it. 
Silence fell heavier than the fight itself. 
The wolf lay still. No triumph came, only the hollow 
aftertaste of victory. Her claws blurred, reshaping into wheels 
that caught and turned beneath her, the faint rattle of rubber 
on stone echoing the rhythm of her heartbeat. The sound 
pulled her back from  the feral edge and anchored her in the 
world she knew. 
A cabin loaded around her in pieces: walls, shelves, maps, 
a blank journal. Someone wanted her to write. Of course. Even 
here, an interface was asking for input. 
She touched the page. Images surfaced without timestamps 
or source tags. Memory, dream, injected prompt. No way to 
verify any of it. 
Then she stood. 
Intent became movement without a Skelet or brace 
mediating between them. Dunya crossed to the window and 
pushed it open before the dream could take the ability back. 
The Three Brothers rose through the fog.

through the surf anyway, because absence was easier to 
manipulate than memory. 
Back then, Dunya had believed the rocks could hold 
forever. Now she knew endurance was only failure on a longer 
clock.  
“I can’t swim!”  Young Dunya’s voice cracked, the depths 
below mocking her as her tin foil boat capsized. Her fists 
clenched in futile pursuit. 
“No need,” her father’s voice carried over the water. “In the 
city, your wits will be your lifeline.” 
“When can I learn to swim?” she had once asked him. 
“When your wits fail you,” he’d said, pulling her close in a 
bear hug. 
Her mother had taken her small hand, pointing toward the 
Three Brothers. “How long, do you think, before even they are 
claimed by the sea?” Her mother’s voice wavered, as if afraid 
of her own words. 
“Never. They’ll stand their ground,” young Dunya had said, 
pulling her hand free. 
Years rolled on, and the cliffs that once inspired awe now 
only sharpened the tears clouding her vision. Gone was the 
youthful illusion that they could hold back any disaster, least 
of all Zakharovna’s rise. 
Turning her gaze beyond the Three Brothers, Dunya settled 
on the distant trio of mountains: Vilyuchik, Mutnovsky, and 
Gorely. The volcanoes formed a sweeping arc on the horizon, 
their snow-kissed peaks piercing the sky.

For a fleeting moment the interplay of shadow and fading 
light on the cliffs cast illusions, whispering of ancient 
watchers. Wolves seemed to stir in the crags, their shapes 
trailing down the ravines. She searched the heavens, half -
expecting to see them si lhouetted there, predators waiting in 
quiet judgment. None came. Only the mountains stood 
witness, and Dunya was left with her thoughts once more. 
Two routes opened through the terrain. One looped back 
into familiar woods. The other ran west into blank map. 
The choice felt staged. Standing still would still count as an 
answer. 
Dunya took the unknown path. 
During a year of salvage survey work for the road offices, 
Dunya roamed west, eyes searching for any flicker of life. 
What she found instead were endless expanses of gray. 
Back then, Zakharovna was only a myth to her, a legendary 
wolf said to have prowled these lands for as long as memory 
could reach. Yet when the Reconstruction swept through, 
laying the groundwork for a new age, her grandfather had 
cautioned, “Zakharovna will succumb to this upheaval, mark 
my words. She’ll be her own downfall, and ours.”  
Those were the words of Grigori Bocharov, the family’s oak, 
stern and unbending. He had spoken them to Dunya’s father 
with grave certainty: “She spells doom for our entire clan.” 
Her father had only laughed, spitting into the sand and 
making an obscene gesture. Dunya’s mother, watching the 
mockery, slapped him. “What’s gotten into you?” she 
whispered harshly, though the blow had not hurt him. He only 
laughed louder and turned away on another of his adventures, 
never saying where or why.

Years later, she found him alone, lost in the depths of a 
portrait of her mother, Marina. His fingers traced the frame, 
and the redness in his eyes betrayed the weight of his loss.  
“You got old,” Dunya said quietly. 
He gave a soft chuckle, brushing his face as if to scatter the 
years. “Time didn’t wait for me, not even on the battlefield.”  
“And Mother,” she answered, “she didn’t have the chance to 
wait either.” 
He nodded solemnly. “Every day, I feel the gaping void she 
left behind.” 
Dunya hesitated, then asked softly, “Zakharovna’s 
prototype, the one she claimed could cheat death. Did you 
ever consider it?” 
A shadow crossed his face as he looked away. “It was a false 
hope, Dunyasha. A desperate gambit that came too late. Even 
if it had worked, such things carry their own price. Your 
mother’s spirit was meant for the stars, not bound here by 
unnatural means.” He had kept that promise. Later, he tasked 
Dugal with building a small rocket, and together they released 
her ashes into the sky, the family whispering their farewells 
as she rose to the heavens. 
Dunya watched his gaze drift, fixed on memories. “I rejoined 
my old regiment,” he murmured, “the one I served in before 
your time.”  
Her heart tightened. To return to war when he was already 
past the age of most soldiers. Why? Whatever the reason, it 
led him to kill an old man. 
Zakharov had once inspired him, had once made him 
believe with grand tales of revolution and rebirth. Named for 
the Marshal himself, he had led the Black Wolves against the 
Strangers’ Revolt and painted himself as a figure of change.

from fire and contradiction. Her father had once believed 
Zakharov’s promises, but in the eleventh hour of rebellion he 
had cast his lot with the Strangers. They silenced the tyrant, 
yet his vision outlived him. The bitter cold claimed the rebels, 
the last wolves vanished into the expanse, but Zakharov’s

His sister carried them forward. Under Zakharovna, the city 
rose from the ruins, her reign shaping an empire that grew 
and flourished. To Dunya it felt like a mockery, as if the 
defiance her father had clung to had been erased, and the 
future had followed a course that had been waiting all along. 
Dunya audited her father’s story the way she audited 
damaged code. He had been brave, ruthless, late, and 
sometimes wrong. Gred had survived him and betrayed him 
at the same time. 
“I’m no warrior,” he had once told her. “Just an old soul 
who knew when to pull the trigger.”

Later, when she spoke of confronting Zakharovna, he had 
warned her plainly. “You don’t just walk into the fucking wolf’s 
den, Dunya. It’s a death wish.” 
“She took Dugal from me.” 
“Dugal was gone long before Zakharovna’s involvement. 
You know it, Dunyasha.” 
That part still hurt because it was true. 
Then Dugal appeared beside her, golden hair, brown eyes, 
carbon dust clinging to his overalls. The likeness was too clean 
to trust, and it gave him words he had never spoken on a 
balcony he had never seen. 
“One day you’ll take it back from Zakharovna’s grip,” the 
copy said. 
Dunya almost laughed. Dugal had hated speeches. He 
would have asked whether she had an exit route, enough 
charge in the railgun, and something to eat afterward. 
Her father appeared again, urging restraint after choosing 
the dangerous path himself. Protection, command, self -
destruction. The Bocharov family kept shipping the same bug 
under different names. 
Neither man could authorize what came next. 
This was still partly vengeance. Calling it justice would not 
make the code cleaner. But Zakharovna had taken bodies, 
minds, and choices from too many people to leave running. 
Dunya would act because the system had to be stopped, not 
because the dead demanded it.  
She turned and stepped back into the cabin. On the moss-
covered bed she let herself sink down, the last warmth of the 
day clinging faintly to her skin while outside the moons 
climbed into the twilight sky. From the shelter of the woods, 
distant howls rose and converged.

The cabin fell away. Dunya stood on a boundless plain, its 
surface shimmering like skin stretched tight over something 
deeper. Each step sent ripples through it, light and shadow 
folding like water. The crescents above shifted, not moons at 
all but eyes, unblinking, waiting. 
A tremor ran through her chest. She reached for breath, 
but the air came thin, threaded with static. Voices whispered 
at the edge of hearing, not words but tones, as if a thousand 
signals bled together. 
She steadied herself. Her fingers flexed, expecting the 
phantom feel of a trigger, the weight of her wheels, the pull of 
gravity. None of it came. Only that boundless plain, thinning 
further with every beat of her heart. 
Beneath it, the beeps finally resolved into the rhythm of a 
monitor, the first real thing she had found. 
Dunya followed the rhythm back without accepting any role 
the dream had assigned her. She returned as herself, angry, 
unfinished, and still online. 
Beep. Beep. Beep.

MARIA

alive. Shapes rippled through the haze, gathering form until a 
face emerged from the red, one she knew too well. Babushka.

a shawl that seemed to swallow the light around it.

wanted her to remember.

name louder might shatter the illusion. 
The figure stepped forward. The light revealed her face, a 
familiar face that Maria had not seen in what felt like a 
lifetime. It was indeed her mentor.

warmth.

matter-of-fact. “Your intel spurred me there, too late to change 
my fate. But in truth, I knew it was coming, and I knew what 
I had to do next.”

CHAPTER THIRTY THREE 
DUNYA  
 
Beep. Beep. Beep. 
A sharp inhale tore through her, like breaking the surface 
after too long underwater. Antiseptic filled her nose. Linen 
scraped her skin. Beeps and whispers tangled with the last 
howl of the forest before the white room forced itself into place. 
Her eyes opened into hard white light. Prime Infirmary. The 
monitor slowed as her breathing did. 
The ceiling was cracked in the same places she 
remembered. Real, then, or at least consistent enough to pass 
a first check. The room pulled up the older failure 
automatically: botched spinal procedure, leaking 
cerebrospinal fluid, pressure so severe that m oving her head 
had felt like trying to lift the planet. 
She could still hear a nurse repeating acetabulum and 
sacrum until the words became labels for two more parts of 
her body everyone else seemed to own. 
I’m alive. I think. 
A young woman stepped into the glare. Dunya recognized 
the inky curls and the voice, but neither belonged in this 
room. 
“Can you tell me how you feel?” The woman’s voice was soft 
as a bell chime, steadying in the silence.  Dunya’s head spun 
as she tried to rise, a heaviness in her limbs arguing against 
the movement. Her eyes dropped to her legs: smooth skin 
where scars should have been. “What...happened to me?” 
“What’s the last thing you remember? ” Her question 
trembled, carrying fears she didn’t name.

“Where are my clothes... My things?” 
The woman clasped her hand, uncertain but firm. “Try to 
stay calm. You’ve been through an ordeal.” 
Dunya’s gaze drifted over the crisscrossing scars that 
remained across her abdomen and arms. The frantic drive to 
the hospital came back in fragments. 
She’d fought, trapped between life and death, grappling 
with a Black Wolf for the gunblade. Through spirals of pain 
and fire-laced delirium, she’d moved with desperate purpose, 
turning the weapon on herself just as the world tipped into 
darkness.  
“I... I did this.” 
“Yes. You were in a bad place, real bad, but you clawed your 
way out. Vesna found you in the fire and stayed with you 
through the ambulance transfer. The graft beds repaired the 
worst of the burns while you were under. You’re stable, but 
the Skelet has to carry the load for now. Before she went back 
to the fighting, she left this with me and told me not to let you 
wake up alone.” 
Vesna. The name brought back her hands on Dunya’s 
shoulders, the argument neither of them had finished, the 
pressure of her fingers around Dunya’s hand as the 
ambulance doors closed. She had come back only long enough 
to leave again. 
The woman offered her a slender, velvet -lined case. Its 
polished mahogany exterior was fastened with delicate brass 
clasps. She opened it. 
Inside lay the collar necklace, its abalone centerpiece 
catching the dim light in a splintered spectrum. Dunya lifted 
it, the cold metallic braids and vibrant shell stark against her 
palm. Our day at the beach... The only day of sunshine Gred 
had seen in a decade... That smile when I handed it to her...

Serafim offered a rueful smile. “No, you’re awake. The

siphons data from minds like yours.” 
Dunya’s eyes widened. “You... But why?” 
Serafim laid a hand on Dunya’s shoulder. “I got out,” she 
said. “Then I realized Zakharovna was still using the link to 
reach you. I came back to cut it.” 
Dunya absorbed this, the pieces of her fragmented 
memories slowly forming a coherent picture. “And now?”  
“I broke enough of the link that the dreams should stop,” 
Serafim said. “Zakharovna shouldn’t be able to pull you 
through the same way again.”  She hesitated, then pointed 
toward the side desk. “You need to eat. Soup and bread. It’s 
not much, but it’s real food.” 
Only then did the smell reach Dunya, rich and earthy, 
drifting into her awareness as if the memory of hunger had 
suddenly found her again. 
“I thought the Syndicate nabbed you after I...” 
“I’m not the only one who dodged a charge of treason,” 
Serafim said, settling beside her and sliding the food across.

Dunya felt Serafim’s hands move quickly, securing the 
exoskeleton around her with a series of clicks and hisses. She 
stayed seated, half -hidden behind frosted glass that should 
have blurred her into a vague shadow, while the uncertain 
presence lingered on the other side. 
The door’s protest under another round of pounding sent a 
jolt through Dunya, her heart hitching at the sound. Then, 
with a creak that cut through the silence, a figure edged in. 
An elderly woman stood there, her eyes swirling with worry. 
The nurse who had  been a shadow of comfort in her haze of 
pain now framed the doorway, her voice sharp in the air. “You 
mustn’t move so much yet, you need to recover,” she chided, 
her gaze fixed on the last few marks that marred Dunya’s 
newly grown skin. 
A flash of suspicion flickered in Serafim’s eyes, narrowing 
as she studied the nurse’s demeanor. Before Dunya could 
process the shift, Serafim sprang into action, a blur of motion 
that sent the woman crashing to the floor. She planted her 
foot firmly on the woman’s chest, and the door swung wide to 
reveal startled faces in the hallway. Her sidearm snapped up, 
leveled at the intruders.

words hung heavy, dense with threat, over the group now 
frozen with unease. 
Another nurse approached with hesitant steps, her hand 
unsteady as she extended a small device. When it touched the 
implant at the base of Dunya’s neck, a sudden tingle shot 
through her, a sharp and surprising sting that caught her 
breath short. Wordlessly, the hand that had wavered only a 
moment ago now moved decisively, passing the device into the 
firm hold of Serafim.  
“Thank you,” Serafim said, lowering the pistol. “We’ll be 
leaving now.” 
Her eyes flicked to the door, then back to Dunya. “We need 
to move.” 
Dunya folded the necklace back into its velvet lining and 
kept the mahogany case in her lap. The Skelet hugged her legs 
with its familiar weight, each segment locked along the 
outside of her limbs, the faint pinprick at her spine where the 
rig had jacked i nto her nerves. Serafim gripped the chair 
handles and pushed her forward with urgency. The sick bay 
slipped behind them, and the sterile corridors stretched past 
in a blur. 
In a shadowed alcove Serafim slowed, leaning down, her 
breath steady despite the rush. “How long until you can 
walk?” 
“I’ve got it from here.” Dunya took the case from her lap and 
pushed herself upright.  The act of standing, strange after 
what felt like weeks in limbo, sent her balance tilting for a 
moment, but the Skelet’s frame caught her, its support 
pouring strength back into her body. She met Serafim’s gaze. 
“I can stand. Don’t mistake that for trust. I understand what 
you told yourself. I haven’t decided what that changes.”

trust me. I knew Vesna had been at Yelagin and helped hunt

isn’t, and that makes it worse.” She clicked the brass clasp

them.”

order. “Then follow me.”

The snow-blanketed streets, windswept and desolate, bore 
the weight of injured soldiers with missing limbs and hollow 
stares, the remnants of battle. Dunya and Serafim moved 
cautiously, stepping around a motionless woman whose 
severed leg lay in a dried po ol of blood. The sight tugged at 
Dunya, but war’s brutal reality left no room to dwell on the 
fallen. 
As they neared Serafim’s trike, Dunya’s eyes caught the 
cobalt blue of its frame, vivid against the white snow. 
Serafim patted the cobalt frame. “Rostislava. She’s been 
getting me out of trouble since I was sixteen.” 
“Fourteen years,” Dunya said. 
“Apparently.” 
Dunya glanced at her. “That word’s doing a lot of work.” 
“I’m thirty. Started taking exo at twenty-two.” 
“Forty-one,” Dunya said. “Also, apparently.” 
Every morning she swallowed an exovegeta tablet before the 
HUD could begin counting down. It felt less like medicine now 
than a humiliation ritual, another reminder that the 
babachain kept her tethered. Skip a dose and her vitals would 
collapse within hours. The system would flood her vision with 
alerts and summon help before neglect could finish the job. 
Serafim swung onto the seat. “Get on.”

had slowed to a murmur as residents sought refuge or tended 
to the wounded. The further they went, the streets coiled like 
abandoned concrete snakes, shadowy figures darting between 
distant buildings.  
“We’re heading to see an old friend: Doctor Fedorova,” 
Serafim shouted over the roar of the engine. “She was deep in 
Zakharovna’s projects, knew her strategies inside out. I grew 
up around those games.” 
Clutching her seat as they sped through the snow -
blanketed park, Dunya called out, “What was Fedorova’s 
specialty?” 
“Memory,” Serafim replied, eyes fixed ahead. 
As the mansion loomed into view, a figure darted across the 
drive. Small, quick. Dunya stiffened, her hand tightening on 
the seat, but Serafim adjusted course without hesitation. 
“Was that—?” Dunya’s voice caught. 
When they dismounted at the gates, she saw them again: 
two young girls slipping through a side passage just inside the 
doors, their giggles trailing before vanishing into the dark.

the shifting light. Charred scraps of cloth hung from their 
shoulders like old battle standards, brittle and heavy with age. 
Their empty eyeholes seemed to follow her, colder than any 
steel. 
Her gaze climbed higher, drawn from the watching masks 
to the brilliance above. Crystal chandeliers cascaded from the 
ceiling like frozen waterfalls, refracting a kaleidoscope of light 
across the timeworn marble floor. Ahead, a massive oak 
staircase dominated the foyer, its dark steps worn smooth by 
decades of footfalls. 
Serafim led her beside the stairs to a small door. The knob 
groaned under her grip, and with a grating creak it opened 
onto a vast chamber. Dunya stepped in, the musty scent of 
old paper drifting over her. She could hardly remember the 
last time she’d smel led it. Her eyes followed the towering 
shelves that climbed toward the lofty ceiling, rows of tomes 
packed tight, their spines cracked and faded. 
They passed through and crossed a small canteen, polished 
cabinets flashing their reflections back at them. Further down 
the hall, muffled voices leaked from behind a closed door 
where a large gray lock dangled open. Serafim turned the 
handle and eased it wide.

walls, consoles blinking with rhythmic light. The air smelled 
of solder and burnt circuitry, sharp and acrid, tugging at 
Dunya’s memory of fried headsets and overworked boards. At 
the center sat a w oman, her hair ashen, wrapped in a blue 
cotton robe beneath a flame -retardant yellow jacket. Wires 
trailed from her arm into the machinery, pulsing blue and red.  
Her skin was threaded with silver ports, machine fused to 
flesh. One eye was pale and natural, the other faintly aglow. 
When she moved, her gaze cut with precision, landing on 
Dunya first. For a moment they held each other’s solitude in 
silence. 
Then, with slow deliberation, her eyes slid to Serafim, as if 
drawn by invisible wires. 
“You brought her,” the woman said, her pale eye fixed on 
Dunya. “After nearly losing the key twice.” 
“She’s here,” Serafim said. “We still can’t open the archive.” 
“My ciphers?” 
“Your ciphers.” 
Dunya edged closer, drawn to the web of wires at the 
woman’s feet. Holographic glyphs shimmered in the air, 
spinning symbols and shifting fragments. “What are these 
for?” she asked. 
“They’re extensions of my memory,” the woman whispered. 
“I can hold every detail, sift through every fragment. The 
system filters out the noise, distills my thoughts to their 
essence.” 
“You offload working memory into the array,” Dunya said. 
“It holds the fragments while you decide what matters.” 
“It returns them in ranked order,” the woman said. “Useful, 
until the ranking starts pretending to be judgment.

Zakharovna Central loomed ahead, its bulk blotting out the 
skyline. For the first time, Dunya saw it as a monument to its 
namesake’s ego. Rostislava’s quiet hum was the only sound in 
the dead streets, the trike’s pulse fading as Serafim cut the 
engine. 
They dismounted and crossed to a side door half-hidden in 
ivy. Serafim found the latch without hesitation, the kind of 
entrance only someone with clearance or secrets would know. 
The hinges groaned low, then swallowed them into the dark. 
Inside, the air was damp. Weak bulbs threw small islands 
of light, leaving long stretches of corridor in shadow. Paint 
curled from the walls, and the sour smell of mold clung to 
everything. Dunya kept her knife ready, the Skelet’s weight 
steadying her legs. 
The Wolves patrolled somewhere ahead. Their presence 
pressed at the edge of her vision, not yet visible but impossible 
to ignore. Each step had to be measured, each breath held 
tight, as if the station itself might give them away. 
The first encounter came quickly. Two guards rounded the 
bend, carbon armor catching what little light there was. 
Dunya’s hand closed on her butterfly knife, the chill of the 
steel grounding her. 
Before she could move, Serafim slipped a coin -sized disc 
from her pocket. She pressed the button once. 
The Wolves faltered mid-step. Their helmets jerked as if the 
ground had tilted under them, then both crumpled, armor 
clattering against the tiles. 
Dunya shot Serafim a glance but kept moving. No time to 
dwell.

Dunya’s surroundings shifted, and she stood again in the 
phantasmal landscape that had become too familiar. Towering 
above, the colossal tree loomed, its trunks entwined like a 
grotesque monument reaching for the cobalt sky.  The 
branches, laden with glowing fruit, swayed gently, their leaves 
whispering a haunting melody that made her shudder. 
At the tree’s base, a machine bound a throng of souls whose 
wails clawed at her. However often she saw it, the horror never 
dulled. Blood seeped down the gnarled bark, pooling thick 
around the roots. Vines hung overhead, waiting to drag down 
anyone who faltered in the crimson tide.  A body plummeted 
from the treetop, the dreadful sound of its impact a grim 
punctuation she’d come to anticipate, but it still made her 
flinch. 
From the twisted limbs, a bird swooped, violet eyes burning. 
It landed on the fallen body and tilted its head at Dunya, as if 
in recognition. With an unexpected strength, it grasped the 
fabric of the woman’s clothes in its beak and began to drag 
the body towards the river of blood, its wings flapping with the 
effort. As the corpse touched the crimson flow, the bird 
released its burden and with a sharp cry, ascended rapidly 
into the gloom above.

At that very moment, as the ripples of blood widened from 
the body ’s entry, a woman materialized from the hushed 
shadows. She seemed to step through the same unseen veil 
that the bird had vanished beyond, her appearance as sudden 
and silent as its departure. Clad in the slate jacket and red -
tinted goggles she was well known for, she moved with urgent 
purpose, pushing past the spot where Dunya stood, her focus 
fixed on the grim task ahead. 
Doctor Anastasia Zakharovna paused, head turning slightly 
toward Dunya. She sniffed the air, eyes narrowing, a predator 
testing the wind. But then, as if dismissing an errant thought, 
she returned to her duties. With a brusque motion, 
Zakharovna resumed her work, severing the bonds that held 
a man to the inhumane device. Her knife plunged again and 
again until the man’s body stilled, sinking into shadow. 
Adrift in the river of blood, Dunya’s gaze caught the bound 
faces. One was eerily like Vesna’s, purplish strands lost in the 
crimson tide. Another had black hair plastered, hazel eyes 
frozen in plea. A third was framed in sandy locks, blue eyes 
fixed in po rcelain stillness. Beyond them, rows of others 
receded into shadow, the machine feeding on them all. 
In eerie unison, their heads turned toward Dunya. 
Recognition passed down the line, and the nightmare 
tightened around her intrusion. 
Farther down the line, a dark-haired woman fixed her gaze 
on Dunya. She lifted one finger and moved it left. 
A barrier snapped into place around Dunya. 
Across the distance, Zakharovna tensed, head snapping up, 
eyes narrowing as if she had sensed something wrong. Her 
lips began to move, shaping a command, summoning an 
unseen force to crush the disruption. 
Dunya reeled, the weight of all those searching stares too 
much to bear.

Guided by instinct more than sight, she stripped the device 
from her head and let it clatter onto the table. 
As it fell, the nightmarish echoes—the screams of the tree-
bound souls—began to fade.  She drew in a deep breath, the 
cool, stale air of the room washing away the stifling terror of 
that waking dream. The cramped space, its jumble of 
technology and dim corners, grounded her in the tangible 
chaos of the real. 
“Dunya.” Serafim waited until she looked up. “Tell me what 
you saw before it starts changing.” 
“It wasn’t just a vision. It had latency, resistance, feedback. 
Whatever those people felt, the system carried it clean enough 
to reach me.” 
“Then the signal held both ways,” Serafim said. “They may 
have felt you too.” 
Her hand settled on Dunya’s shoulder, then withdrew. “We 
stop here. We copy the logs, take them to Xenia, and no one 
goes back in until you ask.” 
As Dunya prepared to stand, a fragmented image from the 
simulation flashed, the last face in the sequence. Her breath 
caught. 
“Maria...” The name slipped out, heavy with realization. She 
was in there, tangled in that macabre dimension.

stores are running on fumes. Until Yelena gets manufacturing

Battalion’s lockdown has seen to that—they’ve choked us dry

Marzanna nodded, her initial apprehension seeming to 
morph into focus. Klara crept low towards the line, staying out 
of sight of the patrolling figures on deck, their forms 
intermittently silhouetted by the outbreaks of gunfire. 
Klara eyed the sloping dock, calculating the natural path 
the oil would take towards the ship nestled below.  
Then, she cut the line, stepping back as the thick, dark oil 
gushed forth. In just moments, it surged across the wharf, 
following the gentle incline that directed it straight towards 
the vessel. 
Klara tracked the expanding slick for a moment, ensuring 
it reached the desired course. Satisfied, she slipped back to 
where Marzanna stood, concealed by the maze of containers. 
Klara whispered to her, “Now, Marz. Fire it up.” 
“Here goes nothing.” From deep within the pocket of her 
green trench coat, she retrieved a small blue pouch. Klara 
observed as the white powder stood out vividly against 
Marzanna’s palm. 
The docks’ brine-laden breeze toyed with Marzanna’s short, 
silver-white hair as she brought the powder to her mouth. “Be 
ready for anything,” she warned before coating her tongue 
with it.

annihilated ship. What remained was but a sable slick, dotted 
with the ghostly remnants of melted steel beams and charred 
flotsam, marking where the stronghold had been.

silver hair plummeted towards her. She darted forward, her 
arms outstretched. As Marzanna’s form collided with her 
shoulder, Klara sank into a crouch, her strength guiding the 
descent. Gently, she placed Marzanna down on the cool

“The kid’s catching her breath,” Klara mentioned, gesturing 
towards the secured transport. “Torched herself out. But she’ll 
be back on her feet soon enough.” 
Shmelova, her attention momentarily diverted from the 
glowing tactical tablet, offered a half-smile that tugged at the 
edge of her lips. “She proved quite the blaze,” the captain said. 
“Delivered the firestorm you promised.” 
“She did.” Klara nodded with pride, observing the 
industrious movement of their forces through the harbor. 
“And once she’s back up, I’ll talk to Yelena about harnessing 
that hellfire for the rest of the army.” The thought came too 
easily, and that was what unsettled her. 
Kolya Zhukova, the grizzled former Battalion colonel who 
had recently sided with the Hive insurgency, emerged from 
behind the shattered husk of an armored transport. She 
walked towards Klara. 
“Controlling such a force won’t be easy,” Zhukova observed, 
pushing a loose strand of red -white hair back into the 
disciplined bun atop her head. “But if it’s feasible, it would 
irrevocably tip the scales of power in our favor.” 
“Challenge accepted, Colonel,” Klara said. She suppressed 
a knowing smirk, aware that any sign of their unspoken 
camaraderie had no place in front of the captain. 
Shmelova shifted her focus to the horizon where the 
shadows gave way to the fading light. “We’ll need every 
advantage we can get. The Battalion won’t relent in their 
counterattacks, and neither will the Grand Mariner’s loyalists. 
This harbor,” she said, gesturing to the sprawling docks that 
buzzed with the aftermath of their victory, “is just the 
beginning.”

Captain Shmelova gave one last scan of the battlefield 
updates on her tablet before tucking it securely into her 
uniform’s side compartment. A sense of urgency washed over 
her features. “I need to return to command—Yelena is already 
preparing her victory l ap, and she’ll require a substantial 
security detail when she stakes her claim publicly. It’ll be a 
show of force, and it must go smoothly.” 
Klara nodded, catching Zhukova’s eye briefly as Shmelova  
spoke. “Maintain the perimeter while I’m gone. We need to 
ensure no one can disrupt her moment. The eyes of those still 
sitting on the fence will be watching, judging if we’re capable 
of holding power.” 
Klara nodded. “You can count on us, Captain.” 
With that, Shmelova briskly turned on her heel and walked 
away. 
Examining Zhukova’s stoic face, Klara let out a playful jab. 
“Hard to believe you could take living under those tight-wads 
as long as you did. Taking their orders without question.” 
Zhukova’s eyes twinkled with a mix of mischief and 
defiance. “What’s a wait these days when nobody dies, and we 
haven’t seen war in a decade? I was getting bored. Almost 
thought Yelena didn’t have it in her.” Shaking her head lightly, 
she continued, “Anyway, with Grigoreva out of the picture, it 
wasn’t hard securing intel from her successor. Orlov didn’t see 
what was coming; got too comfortable in her new power too 
quickly.” 
Klara laughed, her head tilting back just slightly. “Comfort 
and power—a toxic mix. Always makes for surprise openings.” 
That much, at least, the Syndicate had taught her well. 
Zhukova agreed with a grunt, “Indeed.” 
Klara caught Zhukova’s eye, a flicker of profound accord 
passing between them. “For the Coven,” Klara said solemnly.

CHAPTER THIRTY FIVE 
DUNYA  
 
“Well, if it ain’t a motherfucker,” they hissed.  
Serafim’s reaction was subtle but revealing. A slight flinch, 
a tightening around the eyes. 
Dimitra’s posture hit a nerve, scraping at old scars. That 
readiness to crush, that cold edge, she knew it too well. Once, 
people like that would have cornered her. Now she caught the 
strain in Dimitra’s jaw, the forced detachment in Serafim’s 
stance. They tried to hide the turmoil, but she saw through it. 
She saw the shit beneath their skin. 
“You owe me her freedom, Dimitra,” Serafim said. “Yana’s 
debt was settled the moment I paid the price.”  
“Oh, living in the past, are we?” Dimitra scoffed. 
“You forfeited that claim when you started double-dealing,” 
Serafim said. “She walks free. Now.” 
Dimitra advanced with a menacing snarl, hand twitching 
near their hip in a clear threat. “No one takes wha t’s mine. 
You really think you can  swipe my money-maker and live to 
see another day? Not a chance.” 
The bouncers flanking Dimitra tensed. Both were bald, 
their skin slick with sweat, muscles ballooned from too many 
exo-stims. Thick cords ran along their necks like overstrained 
cables. Dunya could smell the ozone off their dermal rigs. One 
twitch, and they’d be on her. 
The servos in her legs stirred, a low vibration she could feel 
more than hear. Power coiled through her thighs. Her hand 
drifted toward the railgun at her hip. “Let her go,” she said, 
voice steady.

the chaos around them. 
The harbor district crept into view, darker than the rest of 
Gred. The air hung dense, a low mist clinging to the ground. 
Firelight flickered on the horizon, rising from what looked like 
the husks of old warships. For a moment she thought she saw 
movement in the glow, but the illusion vanished with the next 
breath. 
Yana’s sudden intake of breath snapped Dunya out of her 
trance as Serafim pulled Rostislava to a hard stop at the 
roadside. The engine’s hum faded, leaving only the soft tick of 
cooling metal. They dismounted together, the air thick with 
unspoken urgency. Serafim glanced toward the dark stretch 
ahead, hand brushing the control device in her pocket. “I’ll 
keep Rostislava ready,” she said quietly. “If things go south, 
one ping and she’ll be in war mode.” 
Yana nodded once and started forward, leading them into a 
narrow alley lit by the weak pulse of a single streetlamp. The 
light faltered as they passed, and Dunya had the uneasy sense 
that the shadows were following.

followed edged with a practiced welcome that didn’t quite 
match their look. “Right on time. Come in.” 
The slot slid shut and Dunya heard the heavy click of the 
door unlock. The sound echoed like the start of a countdown. 
The warehouse looked busy enough to hide a small army. 
Workers in black moved between packing benches and sealed 
crates. At the center, a short brown -haired woman waited 
beside a hawk on a carved perch. 
The bird tracked Dunya before the woman did, its eyes 
moving from her Skelet to Serafim and back, recording 
whatever human watchers missed. 
“Rada Ivanov,” the woman said, offering her hand. “And this 
is Seryozha. He keeps an eye on the docks for me. You’d be 
surprised how much he sees from above.” 
Dunya shook her hand without looking away from the 
hawk. Serafim could spoof cameras. A bird required different 
lies. 
Rada led them to a workbench and opened a metal box. 
Blue vials with gold labels sat beside surgical tools.

Dependency packaged as opportunity.

hypocrites—gave me a right good laugh . Unlike them, you 
don’t shy away from getting your hands dirty. That ’s exactly 
what we need right now.”

could have been mistaken for praise.

Dunya let out a soft laugh. “Let’s not count our zats before 
they hatch.”

CHAPTER THIRTY SIX 
ZAKHAROVNA  
 
The tranquil expanse of Lake Nachikinskoye lay before her, 
its glassy surface reflecting the distant mountains, dense 
forests, and hazy blue sky above. At the water ’s edge, 
Zakharovna submerged her hand in the shallows, inhaling 
deeply. Each ripple that spread from her touch reminded her 
of Maria, of that fragmented part of her soul that she sought 
to mend . She watched as those ripples  danced across the 
surface, each one a silent echo of  thoughts swirling in her 
mind. 
In this secluded forest spot on her family’s ancestral lands, 
only she and Orkon  knew of its existence. Our last  refuge. 
Orkon sat nearby, eyes closed, hands resting on his knees. 
Clad in a black robe with rolled -up sleeves and a woven belt, 
his head was shaven except for a few strands of curly black 
hair above his ears. His gray beard formed a rough square on 
his chin, while raven feathers adorned his cloak, and a wolf’s 
jawbone hung from his neck on a leather thong. 
“Do you know what I see when I look at myself in the water, 
Orkon?” 
“You see the past that you remember.” 
Zakharovna nodded. “But that isn’t what’s truly there, is it? 
It’s merely an illusion.” 
“A message from the gods.” 
“Yes, but you know I’ve never been one for paganism, ” she 
conceded. 
“The gods are speaking to you, Anastasia. It is crucial that 
you listen.”

us,” she said, her gaze lingering on the clear water of the lake.

these years. ” Her fingers traced invisible patterns on the 
surface, sending ripples distorting her reflection.  Zakhar, the 
name itself, was an echo that stretched longer than any quest 
for immortality she dared to pursue.  And yet, it is by 
Zakharovna that I am known to the world. 
Orkon nodded. “You were too young to understand, too 
innocent to bear such a wound. It was not a burden meant for 
you, Anastasia.” 
“I never understood how much my mother suffered . Her 
heart bore the scars of his departure until the day she died. 
After...after she was gone, I felt lost.” 
“And I did all I could to guide you, as I would my own sister, 
you know that.”

CHAPTER THIRTY SEVEN 
VESNA  
 
“Where the hell have you been? ” Fury and worry clashed 
within Vesna as she glared at Zakharovna  through the 
projection. 
“Evidently not where you expected me to be.” 
“You drop off grid, leave chaos in your wake, and now you 
stroll in like nothing’s happened?” 
“A necessary disappearance. Chaos is, after all, part of the 
greater pattern,” Zakharovna retorted, her tone measured and 
cool.  
“Design? There are Wolves who won ’t follow me because 
they think I’m your puppet. And then there’s Dunya...” 
Zakharovna’s gaze snapped to Vesna with penetrating 
sharpness. “What of her?” she asked, the casual tilt of her 
head belying an undercurrent of surprise that Vesna 
instinctively recognized. 
“She was hurt. Badly.” 
“The cost of war. We each pay it in turn.” 
“And what have you paid, exactly?” Vesna leaned in. “While 
we’re bleeding out here, you’re playing the shadows.” 
“With stakes so high, sometimes the shadows are where we 
see clearest, ” Zakharovna replied. “You think so linearly, 
Vesna. The battlefield isn’t just blood and ground.” 
Vesna’s jaw tightened. “And yet, it’s the blood and ground 
that’s remembered, not the whispers in the dark.” 
Zakharovna smiled thinly. “History is written by the victors, 
dear Vesna—remembered as they wish it to be.”

CHAPTER THIRTY EIGHT 
MARIA  
 
Cold seeped through the thin sheet and settled in her 
bones. The mattress wasn’t hers. Its weight and give felt off, a 
slick dampness clinging to the fabric and turning her 
stomach. The smell rose next, sour and heavy, like something 
left to steep in its own humidity. 
She drew a breath, expecting the familiar quiet hum of 
orientation to meet her. Nothing answered. Only the rasp of 
air through lungs that felt borrowed, and a body she wasn’t 
sure would hold her if she tried to sit up. 
She tried again, louder. “Help!” 
The word fell flat in the stale air, swallowed by a room that 
didn’t bother to answer. 
Maria teetered to her feet, her senses absorbing the room’s 
grandeur. Velvet armchairs stood their guard, fortress -like, 
before a fireplace boasting only anemic, smudged flames. 
Opulence dripped from each corner, an ostentatious mélange 
of gold -rimmed fram es and vibrant, garish portraits. Faces 
stared back at her, each a haunting echo of past lives, their 
iterations spanning what felt like eons in this timeless realm. 
She approached the windows. They should have been  her 
escape, her connection to the world beyond this gilded prison. 
But the glass refused to budge under her frantic efforts. Panic 
threaded its way through her mind as the truth set in . The 
windows were not really there.

image unsettled her. An aged, weary face with short white hair 
stared back, framing sharp blue eyes and a square jaw. The

to disorient and manipulate her? Nobody escaped 
Zakharovna’s wrath. Tatyana  Romanova was dead, and the 
thought sent a chilling shiver down her spine.

Once, Zakharovna had been the pivot of Maria’s loyalty, the 
central point of her unwavering devotion. Yet, Zakharovna 
had offered only disdain, casting her into an endless cycle of 
resurrection. To be a slave, condemned to rebirth in manifold 
vessels for each new task. And the objective? The eternal 
perpetuation of  her. But what worth could there  be in an 
endless soul, divorced from the tangible form that others 
knew?

replaced with mechanical indifference. In that bleak 
understanding, the frayed edges of her psyche began to 
unravel. 
“Help!” Her voice echoed through the chamber  once more. 
“Someone, please!” 
Fury and sorrow warred within her, tears carving their way 
down her cheeks. It wasn’t death that tormented her, but the 
relentless cycle of living, dying, and being forced to return 
again and again that weighed her down. Each reincarnation 
stripped away a part of her she couldn’t quite recall, and with 
each new life, she felt further trapped in a never-ending maze 
where the exit seemed forever out of reach. 
She released a weary breath. In the embrace of darkness, 
Maria lingered at the precipice , a quantum existence, both 
alive and dead, awaiting the resolution of her paradox. 
Her thoughts inevitably drifted to Dunya. Her confidant, her 
ally, now absent in her hour of need. Maria recalled the 
countless days they had spent together, immersed in virtual, 
especially at the Night Café. That digital haven, with its 
ambient glow and the soft murmur of coded conversations and 
crypto-croissants, had been their sanctuary, a place where 
plans were hatched and secrets shared. The memories of 
those moments, vivid and bittersweet, tugged at her heart. 
I betrayed you, Dunya. I used you, manipulated you for my 
own ends, to reach her. Forgive me. I’m sorry. 
The specter of other transgressions materialized before her. 
Memories of Anna and the hapless junkies Maria had 
ensnared flooded her mind, their thoughts ravaged in pursuit 
of a just cause that had devolved into something twisted. 
Innocents, casualties of a war gone awry. Yet, she couldn’t 
shoulder the blame entirely. Zakharovna had been harvesting 
souls long before Maria’s inception.

the hem and cuffs, hugged her form softly, enhancing an 
authoritative yet graceful silhouette.

ago, she ’d been calling out, her voice echoing with 
desperation. Now, as Vesna stood before her, uncertainty 
swirled within her. “Did you come to take me to Zakharovna? 
What’s left for me out there, other than an endless cycle of 
suffering?” 
“Endless is not a luxury you can afford  right now,” Vesna 
said, her tone firm. 
“Endless is all I know.” 
“Listen, Maria. I’m here to help.” 
“Help with what?”  
“You were fighting on the wrong side.” 
“The wrong side?”  Maria shot back. “If you wanted me on 
your side, you wouldn ’t have  locked me up.  Why are you 
here?” 
“The city burns, but not by Zakharovna ’s hand, ” Vesna 
said. “She fights to stem the tide, to contain the  real inferno. 
Yelena controls the Syndicate  now. You must see the larger 
game. The boss  has her designs, and they ’re not without 
reason.”

throbbed with life. Colors vibrated with an alien intensity, the 
wind whispered secrets to the leaves, and a single ray of 
sunlight broke through the cloud cover, blessing the ground 
below with its warm touch. 
For a moment, Maria was caught in a strange calm, a 
welcome reprieve from her recent confinement and the chaos 
of the world outside. 
“Welcome to our sanctuary,” Zakharovna said, her lips 
curling into a smile as she gestured towards the lush 
greenery. “In this place, the rose is king. Its petals hold the 
essence of life.” 
Maria found herself enveloped in a tangle of awe and unease 
as she observed Zakharovna. The old crone’s bearing had not 
changed. Even now, draped in a flowing silk gown, she held 
the room in the palm of her hand. A sulfur rose nestled in her 
hair caught Maria’s eye, adding a regal touch that seemed to 
elevate Zakharovna ’s already stately demeanor.  There she 
stood, an embodiment of a queen, poised, ruling over her 
domain with an iron will cloaked in the soft allure of velvet. 
In that instant, Maria was overwhelmed by a tide of 
unanswered questions. How had Zakharovna created this 
place? Why was she brought here? What was her own destiny 
in all of this? 
Zakharovna’s laughter echoed, blending with the gentle 
rustling of leaves. “Even in the face of desolation, life finds a 
way.”

thousand innocent lives. And for what? Your magnum opus?”

can’t accept this...  Your rationalizing, your justifications. I 
can’t bear it anymore .” In a choked whisper, she said, “No 
more lies. No more half-truths.” 
Maria turned and hastily retreated through the garden ’s 
maze. Each step was a bid for distance, for a moment away 
from the weight of Zakharovna ’s promises and the all-
consuming reality they unveiled.

CHAPTER THIRTY NINE 
VESNA  
 
The infantry  advanced in formation, each synchronized 
step reflecting their discipline. A tide of gray uniforms and 
faceless black visors  surged forward, cleaving the crowd 
gathered outside the rally. As the people ’s exuberant cries 
overpowered the speaker ’s voice, every soldier maintained 
their stature, embodying the Syndicate’s new military and its 
claim to power. 
Soldiers or drones? Vesna wondered. 
From her vantage point at the edge of the crowd, she 
studied the precise, mechanical flow of their ranks, a sharp 
contrast to the restless energy of the gathered spectators. At 
her flank, Marfa and Gala stood ready. Even behind their 
scarves, their eyes remained vivid and focused. 
The chill winds that usually swept through the plaza were, 
for a moment, less biting than the fear moving through the 
crowd. A different kind of warmth held them together, not 
from sun or shelter, but from the rumors that drew the 
huddled masses close. They leaned into one another for 
comfort, bracing again st the cold and against the growing 
dread of the Coven’s shadow over their lives. 
Casually, Vesna’s hand lingered near the concealed 
titanium alloy pistol under her coat. In her other hand, a half-
smoked cigarette dangled, a potential distraction in her 
arsenal. By her feet, an unremarkable briefcase sat, its 
contents crucial to her mission. Inside, the  disassembled 
parts of a sniper rifle lay hidden, poised to be swiftly put 
together and deployed in the imminent operation that awaited 
her.

architect of a future where every voice, every action, 
contributes to our shared progress. No, progress isn’t some 
far-flung dream! It’s our collective duty, our shared destiny.

Vesna stopped and turned around, feeling a wave of shock 
as Yelena triumphantly raised her fist. The crowd hushed, a 
quiet that enveloped the space and hinted at their focused 
attention. Cold dread clenched Vesna ’s heart as a flurry of 
thoughts raced through her mind: Why would Yelena risk so 
much? Is she really going to seize total power now? Disband 
the other parties? Vesna didn’t blink at Tatyana’s death; it was 
the predictable end for someone who misplaced her trust. Yet, 
misjudging Yelena’s ambition had always been dangerous. It 
doesn’t matter. She’ll be dead soon. 
Vesna’s eyes locked with Yelena’s across the sea of people, 
a momentary connection that sent a jolt through her. She felt 
a sudden, almost irresistible urge to pull the trigger right 
there. But she relented to her discipline. 
Tightening her jacket ’s hood, she blended among the 
encircling soldiers, who were focused on the crowd, guns 
drawn, primed to defend their matron. Vesna moved between 
them, her presence just another shadow among the vigilant 
guardians. Gala followed closely behind. They crossed the 
street bordering the  main plaza and entered the dilapidated 
ruins of the old Hotel Kamchatsky.

Vesna followed, climbing the decaying stairwell, her steps 
quick and determined. The political machinations wrought by 
Yelena and her Hive weighed heavily on her mind: many of her 
benefactors at the  University now lay in shambles, the 
Battalion forced into a humiliating retreat, and her once -
devoted Black Wolves torn between divided loyalties.  Lucky, 
she mused to herself, most of them are now bolstering Hive 
union buildings across the city , far from their new 
headquarters. And despite gaining strength, Zakharovna still 
lurked in the shadows. Vesna’s only defense against Yelena’s 
wrath consisted of those few Black Wolf units who remained 
steadfast in their loyalty, and the handful of nearby University 
marine brigades , strategically positioned yet sparse in 
number. 
With each flight of stairs she ascended, Vesna ’s thoughts 
lingered on Yelena ’s penchant to sway the masses with 
nothing but her words and vision. The idea of ending Yelena’s 
manipulative charisma, of silencing her for good, fueled her 
skyward. Vesna wondered what Yelena’s brains would look 
like dashed across the stage. 
Reaching the eleventh floor, Vesna found it completely 
deserted. Her confidence surged as she stepped through the 
door, quickly moving to the window that offered a strategic 
view of the stage below. Swiftly, she positioned a chair to gain 
an optimal vantage point. There, at the edge of  the vacant 
room, Vesna’s set up her sniping position, ready to execute.

the stage. Yelena was crouched over Valentina’s corpse,

practiced arc. She squeezed off a shot. The bullet found its

woman’s body.

fell.

weaving through the crush of bodies between them. The shot 
had done more than wound; it had cracked open a moment 
the whole city had been bracing for. She needed to reach the 
director, now only a heartbeat away, before anyone else seized 
the advantage.

her to a brutal crawl. Yelena’s bodyguards forced their way 
toward Yelena, forming a wall of armor between Vesna and 
her target. A pair of them spotted her breaking through the 
crowd and moved to intercept.

firing tight, controlled shots at the gaps in their formation. 
One guard dropped, another staggered as a round bit into her 
vest. The rest didn’t fall back; they surged toward her, trying

fire in the chaos. 
Vesna shoved past grasping hands, slipped under a half -
tackle, and pressed forward through the opening her shots 
had carved.

older woman’s gaze, once steely with command, shimmered 
with unmasked fear. The space between predator and prey 
shrank with every one of Vesna’s steps.

visor from Yelena’s forehead. A fired shot followed, and a cloud

eyes—a common shade of hazel rather than Yelena ’s distinct

chaos, but she was still pinned, her body pressed into the cold

do was  watch as the fire spread . She wasn’t in control 
anymore. If she ever had been. Fury rose in her chest, but it 
was quickly smothered by the cold, unfamiliar acceptance of 
her failure.

Through the haze and smoke, Yelena’s infantry emerged, 
their figures barely visible at first, then sharpening as they 
advanced. But they were stopped in their tracks by the Black 
Wolves, who formed a perimeter around her ; they gestured 
with a stern authority that seemed to suggest that they owned 
the situation, her fate included. 
Vesna’s end was now hurtling towards her, inevitable as the 
setting sun, and in its shadow, all else paled to insignificance. 
“For the Syndicate .” Lawlessness and chaos reigned  now, 
devoid of any guiding principles. A realm where the strong 
wielded power and the weak were crushed. She could have 
flourished there, but on the precipice of death, that future was 
lost. A bitter laugh threatened to escape, but anger and defeat 
smothered it, turning it into a stifled sob beneath the weight 
of the Wolves’ restraint. 
The world would keep spinning without her. She wondered 
if Zakharovna would forgive her capture. Her thoughts drifted 
to her pack, questioning their whereabouts and whether 
they’d thrive without her. They always had. Death no longer 
frightened Vesna . S ince leaving behind all her past for so 
many months, she ’d long ago accepted her transient 
existence. 
Instinctively, Vesna ’s mind clutched at the thought of 
Dunya. Regret threaded through her as she realized that only 
at the brink of her own demise or at that of Dunya’s own did 
she fully embrace the tenderness of those shared times. She 
remembered Dunya’s laughter, the cadence of her voice, how 
they forged pockets of peace in the turmoil of their exhausting 
lives. It was Dunya’s light that seemed to cast the longest 
shadow, one that offered Vesna a respite, if only in fleeting 
memory.

CHAPTER FOURTY 
YELENA 
 
Bathed in the sterile chamber ’s pallid glow, Valentina’s 
mutilated body lay tethered by fragile strands of viscera. Her 
fingers, stiff, grasped at a life forever beyond her reach. 
Yelena, rooted at the observation window, watched as each 
breath she exhaled misted the glass. The moment of 
Valentina’s death replayed in her mind like a record with a 
skip, refusing to move forward. “They took her from me,” she 
whispered to the quiet room. 
Lev Rozhkov’s muffled response emanated through the 
plastic mask concealing his face. “We will find her.” As Chief 
Neurosurgeon, Dr. Rozhkov was one of the few immortal men 
left in Gred with political standing. Often overlooked, he was 
a gaunt figure with a countenance marked by time and 
wisdom. He had served the Board with unwavering loyalty for 
decades and  had saved  innumerable souls from oblivion. 
Yelena prayed that Valentina wouldn’t be his last. 
Valentina had been a child of two worlds. Petrova blood 
pulled her close, close enough that Yelena could look at her 
and see Katerina in the angle of her face, in the stubborn lift 
of her chin. But the Hive had claimed her too, dressing blood 
in duty until aunt and niece met more often in offices and 
Board chambers than around a family table. Yelena had kept 
her close and built every prote ction she could around her. 
Valentina had still been exposed. It had never been enough. 
Their family had already been cut open twice: first when 
their father was poisoned, then when Katerina’s husband died 
in that blizzard, killed over a gold vein like the world had not 
taken enough from them already.

Taking Valentina in had never felt like duty. It had felt like 
the only thing left to do for Katerina. Every day, Yelena saw 
her sister in the girl. Not the Black Wolf the Syndicate had 
made, but the woman before it all, quick to laugh, stubborn, 
still clean of what Gred would later demand from everyone. 
Valentina had kept that part alive. Her softness should have 
been beaten out of her, but it never was. She still believed 
workers deserved to be heard. Still walked into labor disputes 
as if hope were a tool and not a wound waiting to open. 
Katerina’s brightness, her husband’s reckless optimism, all of 
it had survived in Valentina. 
And now it was gone. 
“And if we don’t?” Yelena’s voice cracked. She shifted in her 
chair, crossing her arms to hide their quivering. She had 
already lost so much, so many dear to her, and now she faced 
the possibility of losing even the remaining fragments of 
Valentina’s essence. Dr. Rozhkov’s efforts to preserve 
Valentina’s neural net were her last hope, the final thread 
connecting her to the young woman who had been like a 
daughter to her. It was a delicate process skirting the edge of 
legality, reserved exclusively for those with access to the city's 
most powerful and secretive circles. 
“We will. Your niece is resourceful like you. She’ll make the 
connection.” 
Yelena’s stomach roiled. Valentina had been a good 
woman—compassionate, nurturing, and kind —qualities 
Yelena lacked. Yelena regretted burdening her with the 
Board’s weight, even if it was for their mutual benefit and the 
prosperity of their party and city. Now, there was no one left 
to ignite her blood as Valentina had, no one to share the 
intricacies of their ambitious schemes, knowledge hard -
earned through peril and shared only in whispers between 
confidants.

straightening her disheveled silk shirt. “Who fixes this damn 
city when I can’t protect my own blood?” 
Dr. Rozhkov replied, his composure and conviction  
something Yelena wished she could summon. “In the 
wreckage, there’s always a chance for rebirth.”  
“Rebirth? You talk of rebirth when we’re standing in an ash 
heap? Save your platitudes, Doctor. What we need is a 
miracle, not a rebirth. ” She paused, her gaze dropping for a 
moment before locking back onto Rozhkov. “You can’t fix this. 
No one can.”

facade with its intricate marble honeycombs. The Hive’s 
namesake etched in stone—a testament to their strength and 
unity—now hung in the balance, vulnerable to the onslaught 
of outside forces.

offer encouragement. She didn ’t pray for their safety or 
apologize for their injuries.

machinery. Yelena’s eyes moved from the epicenter, across the 
debris-strewn landscape, to the ambulances lined at the 
plaza’s edge. Each vehicle, bristling with advanced medical 
equipment, stood ready to play its part in the delicate 
operation. 
Beyond the gathering medical teams , the Prime Infirmary 
loomed, its walls housing Dr. Rozhkov’s team of specialists 
and tech-healers. It was there that they would undertake the 
painstaking process of extracting Valentina from her neural 
tomb. Yelena imagined them, huddled over their consoles, 
weaving through data streams to salvage and nurture the 
essence of her niece back to a semblance of life, to be housed 
in a digital vessel. 
And a s she envisioned this, Yelena couldn ’t shake the 
feeling of dissonance. This process, no matter how advanced, 
couldn’t replicate the Valentina she knew. Life in virtual was 
a far cry from the physical, breathing presence of her niece.

Ascension, despite every advantage that should have kept 
them close. The serum had lurched forward in strange bursts 
while its ugliest failures somehow missed the women nearest 
the doctor. Then there was Vesna, suddenly younger, 
stronger, moving through Gred as if the years had been peeled 
off her. 
Aisyt. Yelena had heard the name before, buried in 
University gossip and half-finished accusations. She had filed 
it away with everything else Zakharovna kept behind locked 
doors. 
Now the pieces pressed together hard enough to make her 
temples ache. If Marzanna was telling the truth, Zakharovna 
had been sitting on something far stranger than another 
serum. If she was lying, she knew exactly which old suspicions 
to disturb. 
This woman is playing me for a fool. 
Marzanna said nothing more. 
That irritated Yelena more than another explanation would 
have. The woman had named Aisyt, tied it to Vesna, and 
reduced the impossible to a few words about patterns. If there 
was a trick here, Yelena wanted to find the seam and tear it 
open.

heart.

at her. They had sworn to defend the city, to uphold the 
Charter, yet they had forsaken her leadership for 
Zakharovna’s deceptive promises.

to end , how Zakharovna had so easily swayed the Wolves, 
disrupting the fragile balance she had fought so hard to 
maintain.

Narrowing her eyes, Yelena caught the glint of scopes, each 
one trained on the scrambling soldiers below. 
Her attention shifted  again as a group of enemy Black 
Wolves burst onto the scene. Their gunblades caught the light, 
flashing menacingly as they moved into combat  formation.

stood, the way they moved, cast long shadows across the 
battlefield, shadows that twisted and turned, almost dragon -
like, in a dance of blue and red hues.

robust statures and large, muscular arms belying their old 
bodies and white hair. Each strike was swift and brutal, their

watched, a mix of horror and fascination, as they snapped 
necks and crushed heads with their swords and bare fists ,

As Yelena watched, a sharp pain throbbed in her head, each 
heartbeat amplifying the sensation. She gritted her teeth, 
fighting the disorientation that threatened to overtake her in 
the heat of battle. Through the fray, she caught glimpses of 
their commander, a fleeting purple shadow darting between 
encounters, moving deftly behind the formidable wall of black 
steel formed by her forces. Vesna orchestrated the army like a 
cruel chess player. 
The young commander ’s voice, sharp and venomous, 
pierced the air. “You’ll regret ever challenging us, witch!” she 
bellowed, her eyes locking with Yelena’s in a defiant glare. 
Yelena wiped the dust from her face with a grim smile. 
“Your time is over, girl!” Raising her gunblade high, she turned 
to her troops. “For our future—attack!” 
The moment the Black Wolves breached her van, Yelena’s 
pulse quickened with a surge of adrenaline. Her side forces, 
previously marching parallel in nearby alleys, sprang into 
action. The air was filled with their unified battle cry, “Bor’ba! 
Bor’ba!” echoing their readiness. As they surged across  the 
throughfare, Yelena felt the ground thrumming beneath the 
collective might of her soldiers. The vibration ascended 
through her boots. 
The charge transformed seamlessly into an orchestrated 
push under Yelena’s command. She observed as a multitude 
of gray uniforms, each wearing a black visor, raised their rifles 
in unison. The air, already electric with battle cries, now 
crackled. A downpour of relentless, piercing bullets followed. 
The disciplined volleys from Yelena ’s forces took the Black 
Wolves off balance, the unexpected rifle fire slicing through 
their ranks. But just as quickly as the ambush had unfolded, 
the fierce warriors adapted. With mechanical precision, their 
gunblades transformed, unfolding into large shi elds. Each 
segment clicked into place as if it were a satellite array

Yelena became a force of nature, her every movement driven 
by a singular purpose. She lunged towards the Black Wolves’ 
shield wall. With a powerful thrust, she struck at the wall, her 
blade meeting the first shield with a resounding crash. The 
impact sent shockwaves through the line, creating a small 
fissure in the otherwise impenetrable barrier. Seizing the 
moment, she twisted her weapon, prying the shield away and 
opening a path through the stunned ranks. 
As she engaged another, the clash of their blades sent 
sparks flying. In the heat of the moment, a brief yet potent 
thought coursed through Yelena ’s mind. They won ’t dare 
swarm me. Not me. They ’re too proud. She shifted her weight 
and, with a surge of force, knocked aside the soldier’s weapon. 
Her gunblade sliced down in a swift, decisive motion.  The 
soldier, clad in black, fell to the ground, a clear gap now 
formed in the wall of bodies. 
Yelena pushed forward through the opening, her heart 
pounding. She understood the enormous risk , yet her focus 
was singular. Vesna, visible now through the breach she had 
created. 
Beside and behind her, she could hear Klara meet the 
enemy at full force, her own gunblade slashing down 
ruthlessly through the defense of another. The defender barely 
had a chance to parry before Klara  sliced through her 
attempts in a clean, undeniable arc. With an agile sidestep, 
she deftly dodged a counterattack, pivoting to land a 
punishing strike even as she swept past. 
Marzanna, too, joined the action, her movements sharp and 
precise. She delivered sudden, forceful thrusts, each one more 
impactful than the last.

two at a time . And Yelena, having once held the esteemed 
position of the city ’s first Pra Matron Chair, understood this 
better than anyone . It was a rule she knew well, a rule that 
many of these warriors, once under her command, would not 
dare break. 
From within the tight ring of Black Wolves, a figure 
detached itself with a deliberate, almost theatrical slowness. 
It was Vesna , finally . The immediate area around them 
seemed to freeze, the jostling of heavy forms fading into a 
tense hush. Yelena’s eyes locked onto Vesna’s. They were cold, 
calculating; the younger woman’s gaze was filled with a blend 
of contempt and challenge. 
“You’ll never be Queen, ” Vesna said casually, her voice 
slicing through the suspended silence.  
“I have my sights set much higher,” Yelena countered. In a 
fluid motion, she detached the blade from her gunblade, 
discarding the heavy firearm component. The blade alone in 
her hands felt swift, light, and perfectly balanced. Ideal for the 
imminent close-quarters combat. 
“Mechanor, Vesna,” Yelena said. “This city wasn ’t built on 
bullets and lead alone . It was  honed on the snowy plains of 
our forefathers. Or have you forgotten the old ways?” 
Vesna’s expression twisted, a visible clash of anger and 
embarrassment playing across her face . Yelena saw a swift 
movement and heard a distinctive click as Vesna disengaged 
her own gunblade, the stock clattering to the ground . “You 
cling to old traditions.”

existence.

heat, peeling away like wax dripping from a candle.

motionless before her. What was once a symbol of strength

CHAPTER FOURTY ONE 
DUNYA  
 
Word of Maria’s sentencing spread across the babachain 
with the speed of rumor. 
Dunya’s avatar appeared at the edge of The Town Square, 
the Arkyv’s virtual heart, recast as a digital echo of Uritsky 
Square. She wondered, as with everything in the Arkyv, if it’d 
ever looked like this at all. The Summer Palace facade and the 
Alexandra Column rose like ghostly monuments, framing a 
space where avatars from every stream gathered to witness 
Gred’s triumphs, and more often, its staged displays of power. 
The Square throbbed with an unsettling energy. Simulated 
odors filled Dunya’s senses, exhaust from tanks mixing with 
the acrid sting of ceremonial gunfire, as pungent here as in 
real life. 
The crowd pressed forward toward the grotesque 
centerpiece of the event: an execution machine, the latest 
invention of Vedmak, the Mad Tinkerer. In Gred, where death 
no longer held finality and age had lost its claim on the body, 
ordinary punishment carried little weight. Only executions in 
the virtual realm could enforce order, a deterrent meant to be 
as enduring as the endless lives it governed. 
Dunya stood at the edge of the throng, her attention caught 
like the rest by the emergence of a single figure. 
The voices fell away. Yelena Petrova, once the Hive’s guiding 
hand and now calling herself Director of Gred, advanced to 
the stage. Dunya’s heart quickened as the matriarch settled 
beside the execution device. The air seemed to shift under 
Yelena’s gaze, e ach second of waiting winding tighter in

justice demands more. Today we reveal the true Pra Matron of

The zk-ID had vanished from the active set. Dunya widened 
the query, checked the prior state, then searched for 
termination proofs. The identity was inactive, but its 
termination had produced no clean null proof. The ledger 
showed absence where a death should have left damage. 
“The chain says she’s gone,” Dunya said. “It can’t prove she 
died.” 
“Hold on...” Yana leaned closer to the rollup. “That last state 
hash doesn’t add up either.”  
Serafim hunched forward  as she  murmured, “She hasn’t 
been active for weeks...” Then, sharper: “Whoever that was on 
stage, it wasn’t Maria. Rollups don’t just rewrite themselves. 
Something’s pulling strings.” 
Dunya studied her in silence. The edge in Serafim’s voice 
wasn’t shock. It was recognition. She had probably known 
Maria had been missing from the active chain for weeks and 
hadn’t cared to say it aloud. Still, Dunya was almost grateful 
she’d seen the lie firsthand. The lengths the Hive would go to 
turn an absence into a public death were worth remembering.  
“Only one way to find out,” Yana said. 
Dunya watched  as Yana reached out toward the 
unassuming black cube that rested on the coffee table. A tap, 
a gentle swish, and Yana ’s headset came to life, cradling her 
face in a halo of hardlight.  Streams of hashed light cascaded 
across her visor, decrypting in silent bursts. 
“I’ve got something, ” Yana said . “Maria’s zk-ID wasn ’t 
terminated. It was tumbled through privacy relays, scrambled 
but still verifiable. Clever.” 
Serafim’s voice was uneasy, but her eyes betrayed a 
glimmer of hope. “Looks like they zk-fragged her. She’s out 
there, scattered across sub-rollups, proofs without a parent.”

trod a path of careful detachment, always cognizant of the 
capricious sway of the masses.

There she was, a solitary point of consciousness, reaching 
for a lifeline into her brother’s mind. The mindgraft’s tendrils 
probed her memories, searching for the synaptic echo that 
would lead her to Alexei. 
One particular moment  crystallized and drifted closer, a 
clandestine evening from their youth, shared in the cloistered 
corner of their father’s den. They were huddled over the 
forbidden pages of The Brothers Karamazov.  The delicate 
paper cracked under their touch. That book, a tome of moral 
complexity, had captivated them both, first in their youth and 
then more deeply as they grew older, its themes of faith, 
doubt, and brotherhood weaving into the fabric of their lives , 
right up until the day Alexei died. 
A stirring of warmth ebbed through Zakharovna ’s being at 
the recollection, the emotional response to the trigger 
sharpening her focus. It was a sense of kinship, intense and 
sincere, that acted as the needed catalyst. Grief and pride, 
shared at the downfalls and triumphs that Dostoevsky had so 
eloquently penned, had bound them closer, their young minds 
ignited by the raw humanity leaping from the pages. Alexei, 
impassioned, had always been drawn to Dmitri’s fervor, while 
she saw reflections of herself in the rational Ivan. 
With their joint reverence for the novel as her compass, she 
could feel the static begin to dissipate, replaced by the 
burgeoning outline of her brother’s thoughts and emotions. 
She could almost hear Alexei’s voice  now, a disembodied 
murmur threading through the reverberating signal of the 
mindgraft. With tentative acceptance, she let the neurostream 
guide her along the conduit of their shared past, his essence 
growing clearer as she journeyed through layers of digital and 
genetic memory. The anchor was set, the connection made, 
and the darkness gave way to the unfolding panorama of his 
mind.

The immersive reality of the mindgraft settled, reshaping 
the blackness into the familiar yet distant outlines of 
Petropavlovsk’s war-riven outskirts. Now an observer in her 
own memories, she watched her past self approach the 
command tent where Alexei oversaw the defenses. The siege 
was relentless, the silhouettes of armored vehicles looming 
beyond the Strangers’ fortifications under a bruised sky. 
Zakharovna’s younger self entered the canvas tent flapping 
in the biting wind. Alexei turned, his face etched with the 
exasperations of leadership, but his eyes softened upon seeing 
his sister. “They’re shelling the east ridge again, ” he said 
without preamble, gesturing towards the crude map sprawled 
across the table. 
Zakharovna watched her past iteration leaning over the 
map, her fingers tracing the contours of the landscape that 
would soon become part of their new city. “If we can hold the 
ridge,” her past self proposed, “it will give us the high ground. 
Once the Strangers retreat, the city could use the opportunity 
to rebuild...assert more control.” 
The very mention of ‘control’ had Alexei raising an eyebrow. 
“It’s not just about control, sister. It ’s the people. They ’re 
restless, uncertain not just of their survival, but of what Gred 
will demand of them after.” 
“Have a little faith in me, brother,” she stated confidently. 
“We will hold our ground against this tempest and stay true 
to who we’ve always been. And the people of Gred will know it 
too. They are not pawns to be swayed by the Strangers’ silver 
tongues.” 
Alexei’s expression softened; she knew he caught the weight 
in the new name, not bound by the old word —grad—but 
reaching beyond it, a promise in a world where no cities 
remained. “Then let’s ensure our city lives up to its promise.

finding Anastasia’s sides in a series of calculated tickles. She 
erupted into involuntary peals of laughter. 
As Anastasia tried to escape the relentless tickling, Orkon 
leaned in, a roguish twinkle playing in his deep -set eyes. “If 
my bridge falls to pieces, it ’d be an honor for it to be at the 
hands—or should I say, laughter —of Kamchatka ’s most 
formidable mind, ” he flirted, his chuckle low and inviting. 
“Though, perhaps a personal collapse wouldn’t be so perilous, 
provided you’re there to catch me.” 
Alexei chimed in, a jesting tone lacing his words, “Careful, 
‘brother-in-law’, your mechanic’s hands might just find more 
work than they bargained for with this one. And don’t get too 
comfortable, Putin still has a war to lose!” 
“Oh, come on, Alexei. Orkon is like a brother to both of us. 
Enough with your teasing,” Anastasia protested, shaking her 
head but unable to suppress a smile. 
She looked between the two young men, and then her  
expression grew more serious. “And damned if either of you 
are conscripted in this blasted war.”

glow of the candlelight. Here, in the flickering shadows, they 
were a family, a united front in the face of a world teetering on 
the precipice of monumental transformation. 
As the dacha scene dissolved and grapevine-like memories 
reached through the receding glow, Zakharovna was thrust 
into the stark, angular light of a different day: a day seared 
permanently into her own life’s design. 
She found herself standing in a barren corridor of the 
makeshift headquarters, the air thick with a tension that 
coated her lungs like ash. It was quieter than it should have 
been, the usual clangor of orders and boots on metal floors 
suspiciously absent. Trailing the memoryscape, she rounded 
the corner and stopped short. 
Before her, the austere lines of Alexei’s prone form stood in 
stark contrast against the dull gray of the concrete. The once-
strong pulse of hope lay still, his shirt crimson with blood, a 
wound torn through their cause and through her spirit. This 
was the  fulcrum, the moment when her understanding of 
revolution, of humanity, and of brotherhood began to twist 
into something unrecognizable.
