Zakharovna watched as her past self stepped forward, 
numb, her hand trembling as it reached out to touch Alexei’s 
lifeless shoulder. Her mind contorted, struggling against the 
visceral vice of reality squeezing her chest until she could 
hardly breathe. Denial rose first, a futile whisper in the back 
of her mind, insisting that her brother, her twin, her 
counterpoint in all things, could not simply be gone. 
Beneath her fingertips, his skin was cooling rapidly, but she 
couldn’t bring herself to withdraw her touch. “Alexei,” she 
murmured, a tremulous plea to the absent warmth, to the 
vanished spark in his blue eyes that had always promised 
tomorrow. 
Her vision blurred, hot tears welling unbidden; it was the 
cold clasp of Orkon ’s supportive hand on her shoulder that 
drew her back, reminding her of duty, of the war that raged 
on even as her world narrowed to the space of loss beneath 
her hand. 
It would be hours before she realized she hadn’t taken a full 
breath since discovering him, and days still before she would 
hear the whispered speculations, the silent inquiries. Who? 
How? Why? 
Vengeance, a flame once distant to her, now ignited with 
sudden ferocity, clawing its way into her being. 
She felt Orkon’s resolve beside her, his silence carrying 
both grief and respect for their fallen comrade. He was the 
pillar, the strength that held her steady even as her own flesh 
and blood grew colder. 
In her gut, a roaring emptiness expanded with the 
realization of the void Alexei’s death would leave in the cause 
they had nurtured together. She was now singular in a fight 
that had, until then, been defined by their duality of mind and 
heart, reason and belief. What was balance without its 
counterweight?

The mindgraft transitioned her to a cavernous hollow where 
the air was thick with ice and malice. Her Black Wolf 
commanders flanked her, the old women a silent, deadly 
phalanx in their black carbon -fibre armor, their silvery hair 
beaming against the darkness. 
In the center of this shadowy amphitheater stood Nikolai 
Bocharov, once the incarnation of loyalty and strength in 
Alexei’s ranks. Now shackled, his arresting fire-red hair flared 
defiantly against the restraint of his bonds. They had found 
him skulking on the fringes of their territory, meeting with an 
unidentified Strangers’ envoy. His capture had been as swift 
and silent as his treachery, a sheaf of intercepted 
communications clutched in a Black Wolf commando’s grasp, 
damning evidence of his role in Alexei’s demise. 
Anastasia’s eyes, as cold and hard as the ice that shrouded 
their hideout, bore into Nikolai ’s. “You have sown treachery, 
and now you shall reap the vengeance you deserve, ” she 
vowed, her voice betraying no sign of the turmoil that had 
wracked her in the hours  and days  leading up to this 
confrontation. 
“I will dismantle you, piece by piece, ” Anastasia promised 
with terrifying tranquility. “And each detached part will serve 
a purpose you never respected in life —furthering the very 
science you tried to stifle. ” Each word was a nail, meant not 
for his coffin, but for his consciousness; a taunt designed to 
terrorize as much as it was to condemn.

Her first move was deliberate, a pair of forceps in hand, 
reaching out and clamping down firmly on Nikolai ’s finger. 
With a twist, she clipped it off. 
His agonized wails reverberat ed off the cave’s walls, each 
sound a split fiber in the fabric of her own humanity. Yet she 
continued, her actions detached and methodical, removing 
appendages, gathering each specimen with clinical 
indifference. 
The Black Wolves watched in silence. This retribution was 
no act of pleasure but of necessity. They all knew the cost of 
betrayal, the danger of letting a cancer like Nikolai’s treachery 
spread unchecked. 
Nikolai’s voice rasped into silence, his screams fading to 
gurgles as Anastasia precisely split his larynx. Each snip 
severed more than tissue, taking his voice as surely as her 
own cries for justice had once gone unheard. 
The cavernous resonance stilled as an ominous silence 
lingered, punctuated only by the sinister hiss of Nikolai ’s 
femur as it met the corrosive embrace of the acid bath within 
the container at Anastasia’s feet. 
“Your legacy ends here,” Anastasia murmured to herself as 
she gazed upon the viscous soup  of organs and bones  who 
had betrayed them all. “I will untether your entire bloodline 
from this world as surely as I have freed you from your 
treachery.” 
The science Anastasia carried out in that shadowed grotto 
wore the mask of cold calculation, the preservation of order 
through the eradication of chaos. Yet she knew it was 
vengeance that drove her, guiding her hand with relentless 
force. She would carry t he dark title of avenger in one hand 
while raising the banner of protector with the other, her 
brother’s legacy divided and alive in her every breath, every 
motion, every decision.

Dunya met Serafim’s gaze, the bay window behind her 
framing a silhouette against the sweep of the grounds. The 
glass carried a faint reflection of Dunya’s own face, blurred, 
as if she were already half gone.  
“With the World Tree decrypted, we can branch into the 
network, touch any mind linked within. It’s our path in, and 
our only way out,” Serafim said.  
The mansion pressed harder than its walls. Outside it was 
wealth and fences. Inside, a sanctum for machines.  The 
central chamber pulled her attention back again to the woman 
at its core. Xenia Fedorova sat in a throne of circuits, ash-grey 
hair woven into cables feeding the floor and ceiling.  Runes 
hung in the air, symbols alive with a logic Dunya could not 
follow. 
She had walked past the gardens earlier, seen the statues 
and the neatly trimmed hedges. Now she imagined the turrets 
behind them, the drones circling high above, all of it tuned to 
Xenia’s thoughts. Even her eyes carried that same mechanical 
certainty, softening and hardening without warning. Was she 
watching a woman who had mastered her tools or a woman 
already absorbed by them? 
The cube in her palm gave another pulse, small but 
insistent. Each throb set her teeth on edge. She tightened her 
grip, afraid she might drop it. Yana touched her shoulder, 
fingers light but firm, and Dunya felt the weight in her chest 
ease by a fraction.

the railgun, its weight and angles  as familiar as bone. She 
tapped through the interface, each diagnostic another drill 
etched into muscle memory. The barrel gave off a faint glow in 
the dusk, coils humming as the core climbed toward full 
charge. On the readout, the counter ticked upward, silent and 
lethal. A low buzz carried through her palms as the capacitors 
fattened with power, each slug primed to tear the air apart. 
Below, the grounds stretched in unnatural stillness, waiting 
for the first strike. 
On her overlay, Xenia shimmered in the pale wash of 
projected light, silent and intent. The hum of the mansion 
pressed against Serafim’s ears, a faint vibration she could 
almost feel through the balcony rail. Xenia’s gaze darted 
across the feeds, movements sharp enough to remind Serafim 
of a machine parsing inputs. With each shift of her hand, 
another system came alive, and the house seemed to rouse 
under her command. 
The Black Wolves shifted below, a wall of dark armor 
against the fading light. The order in their ranks clawed at 
her, too close to Rayna’s world of drills and commands. That 
life had caged her twin, and now its weight pressed into 
Serafim’s grip on the tr igger. The encrypted message pulsed 
in her mind, its coded debts and duties spelled out with cruel 
clarity. Every line had pointed her here. Every word demanded 
she act.

Reality folded in on itself, a kaleidoscope of memory and 
code entwining as Dunya pushed forward through the 
labyrinth Zakharovna had conjured. Each step dragged her 
deeper, the ground shifting like a thought she could not pin 
down. 
Yana moved at her side, quick and sure, strokes of her 
stylus cutting into the dark. Sparks flared with every motion, 
trails of light knitting into shields that caught the blows meant 
for them, then hardened into blades that struck back. To 
Dunya it looked  like she was painting the air, the world 
bending wherever her lines touched. 
Firewalls burst from the ground like jagged spires, their 
glow radiating heat that wasn’t real yet still made Dunya 
flinch. Malware slithered along the corridors, shapes of 
hunger and teeth, but Yana’s light scattered them, her 
laughter ringing clear, cutting through the static. 
Dunya answered in kind. She drew the railgun into being 
the way she had in past dives, fingers pulling lines of code into 
form until the weight settled in her hands. The weapon 
hummed with raw force, and when she fired, the recoil jolted 
her shoulder, the round tearing a burning groove through the 
dark. 
Shapes reeled into view, tall and lanky, mottled skin 
flickering between flesh and translucence. Each bore a single 
large eye, its glassy stare sweeping like a searchlight. One 
lunged, limbs too long for its body, and she fired again, the 
slug splitting it  into static. Another rushed, only to crumple 
under Yana’s flashing strokes.

More swarmed from the sides, their bodies twisting in 
unnatural rhythm. Dunya fired until the corridor shook with 
the echoes, every shot a claim of ground, every step forward a 
refusal to give it back. 
Then one staggered but did not dissolve. Its eye stretched 
wide, its skin warping as the shimmer coalesced. The mottled 
patterns smoothed, lines of a face emerging where none 
should be. Dunya froze, the railgun trembling in her grip. She 
knew what she was seeing. A memory. One Zakharovna had 
stolen, reshaped, and set against her. 
The creatures pressed in, and Yana’s glow dimmed, her 
figure thinning into static. Dunya’s chest clenched. She felt in 
her gut that Yana was still there, only forced into her own 
snare. 
The first echo hit with a jolt that staggered her. A memory 
made manifest. Dugal stood before her, whole as if pulled 
straight from the past. His smile caught her off guard, the 
curve of it so vivid it hurt. Then the crack split the air again, 
sharp and merciless. She saw him jolt, head snapping back, 
and she was there once more, helpless in the moment 
Zakharovna’s rifles had ended it. 
The railgun sagged in her hands. It wasn’t just Dugal 
falling; it was the house they were going to build, the nights 
they’d sworn they had left, the laughter that was supposed to 
carry them through. All of it gone in a heartbeat, all of it laid 
bare again before her, sharpened into a weapon meant to 
break her. 
The creature wore his face, his manner, even the sound of 
his voice when it tried to speak. She wanted to answer, to cling 
to what was left, but every word and every gesture bent under 
Zakharovna’s hand, turning love into a chain.

Yana flickered back into view, her glow muted, shoulders 
bowed as if she too had walked through ghosts. For a moment 
her eyes looked hollow, then she steadied and reached out. 
Her hand settled on Dunya’s shoulder, anchoring her. The 
touch carried no words, only resolve, the kind they had always 
shared in silence. Dunya drew a breath. Dugal’s laughter 
would never return, but the cause he had died for still burned, 
and neither of them would let it gutter out here. 
“You’re not alone,” Yana whispered. 
Tears blurred her sight as Dunya lifted the railgun. Her 
finger tightened, the shot flaring through the echo. She cried 
as his face shattered into static, grief and defiance bound in 
the trigger’s pull. 
The next echo dragged her into the ambulance, her body 
aflame, skin raw and ruined. Vesna’s silhouette leaned over 
her, voice cold with feigned concern. “You’ll never survive 
without me.” 
The scorn in her eyes had once cut deep, a dismissal that 
threatened to smother what strength Dunya had left. Now the 
words only hardened her. Survive without you? No, Vesna. I 
didn’t just survive. I lived. 
The specter faltered, then bled away into static, the echo 
unable to withstand her defiance. Dunya clung instead to the 
memory of the sister she had once known, the strength that 
still burned beneath the layers of loss and betrayal. 
The corridor stretched wider, opening into an opulent 
chamber. Her chest tightened with each beat of her heart. 
Heavy drapes sealed the windows, their folds thick and 
suffocating. The air carried polish and citrus, familiar and 
false at once; Zakharovna had scavenged it straight from the 
ruins of her mind.

Then he stepped forward, his silhouette spilling long 
shadows across the Dagestani carpets. Her body locked, limbs 
heavy, as if her muscles still remembered the shattering of 
bone, the weight that had crushed her into silence. 
His hand lifted and the air thickened with it, the memory of 
a theft that could never be undone. 
For a moment she faltered, but the memory did not end 
there. She saw again the knife she had hidden, the flash of 
steel, the arc of red that marked her escape. 
She crawled through snow until her arms gave out, 
dragging herself forward inch by inch, each breath torn from 
her lungs, until Dugal found her. His arms closed around her 
like walls against the storm, carrying her into warmth and 
healing. 
They had been lovers before that room. Husband and wife, 
workshop and stove and stupid drawings of apprentices. The 
assault had not created their bond; it had tried to turn that 
bond into proof that nothing private could survive the city. 
Dugal found her anyway, carried her into warmth, and stayed 
close without pressing, a steady presence that told her 
without words that no one would touch her without answer 
again. 
“Hey, you.” His voice stirred in her mind, warm and steady, 
a tether pulling her back from the abyss. 
She tried to give the photograph the old morning words. 
Hey, you. Her mouth would not quite shape them. What came 
out was smaller. “I’m here.” 
The memory steadied her. Dugal had stayed without 
deciding what recovery should look like. He had waited until 
she could choose for herself.

The labyrinth shifted again. Reality loosened, memories 
unraveling like strands of code pulled apart. Through the haze 
another figure emerged, Maria’s form taking shape before her.  
They were at the Night Café, a refuge after a mission pulled 
off clean. A worn jazz record played in the background, its 
notes drifting with the soft clatter of cups and the low murmur 
of tired voices. The air carried the scent of croissants and 
steam rising from chipped mugs. In that half -lit booth, their 
friendship had taken root, shaped by shared secrets and 
laughter too quiet for anyone else to hear. 
Maria’s lips moved, but her voice broke apart, a signal 
stuttering through static. Dunya leaned closer, trying to catch 
the pieces. Words flickered in and out, sharp with urgency. 
Don’t trust Serafim. The warning fractured again, then 
reformed in a despera te whisper. “Leave now. Zakharovna...  
She’s too powerful.” 
Doubt pressed in, sharp and unwelcome. Dunya tried to 
push it away, but a sliver of her knew Maria’s warning carried 
truth.  
“You remember...the vault on Zephyr...mural with the red 
dragon...” The voice faltered through static, each word broken 
but unmistakable. Only they had been there, the night they 
swore to guard each other’s backs. 
The Zephyr reference verified her more cleanly than the 
face. “The red dragon,” Dunya said. “You remembered the 
right wall.” Her throat tightened. “I’m not leaving you in here.” 
Maria smiled, faint and strained. “Still checking the 
details.” 
Her form wavered and slipped into the dark. The memory 
could still be bait, but whoever built it knew enough to matter.

soft as snow.

strain. “We’re holding them. I don’t know for how long.” Her 
avatar flickered on the screen.

Static cracked through the comms, and then her sister’s 
voice filled the room.

“Ray.” The word slipped out, barely more than breath, 
though her chest screamed it. 
The screens blurred as her vision stung. For a heartbeat 
she faltered. Then the truth settled. Rayna’s trust had never 
been a weight. It had carried her, always. 
She started the sequence to cut the mansion’s power.

Shadows of the Black Wolves stretched through broken

cause. The faint chance that saving one could still mean 
saving both. 
 
∆∆∆ 
 
Zakharovna lay beneath her at last. Dunya’s arm shook, 
but the containment routine held ready beneath her skin, 
waiting on one final input. 
“You took my father and used his death as leverage. You 
turned Maria into an asset, Vesna into a weapon, and my 
memories into an access route.” Her grip tightened. “You keep 
calling it immortality because theft sounds worse.” 
Zakharovna’s followers closed in. Beside Dunya, Yana drew 
another shield through the air, holding the shapes back. 
“Why hesitate, Dunya?” Zakharovna said. “Strike as you 
could not when Nikolai’s fate was in your hands.” 
“I’m done letting you frame the options.” 
Dunya checked the routine again by instinct. It had passed 
every test she could run. The command now waited on her 
decision. 
Dunya shivered. The rhythm slipped, a beat gone wrong 
that grew louder with each passing second. She looked to 
Yana and caught the same unease in her eyes.  
“Something’s not right,” Dunya said. 
Before Yana could answer, the world split. The sky tore 
open, light shearing into chaos. A wave slammed through her, 
not only here but bleeding into her body outside, a surge that 
bound the two worlds in shared collapse.

chest. The mansion shuddered, defenses collapsing. Hope

CHAPTER FOURTY FOUR 
ZAKHAROVNA 
 
The city flickered past in brief, fractured glimpses through 
the tinted glass, neon smears and hollow lights pulsing like 
the last breath of nightlife. Zakharovna watched without 
focus, her reflection shifting with every turn. The engine’s 
hum steadied her thoughts, low and constant. Red light traced 
along the cabin’s edges, casting her hands in muted warmth. 
The scent of leather lingered, sharp beneath the sterile tang 
of circuitry. It almost felt as if the car itself were straining to 
imitate life. 
Zakharovna reached for the crystal decanter and poured 
the deep blue liquid into her glass. The light above caught on 
its surface, turning it violet for a moment. She stirred the 
blueberry daiquiri with quiet focus, each motion deliberate 
and steady. When she finally took a sip, her eyes closed, not 
in pleasure but in habit, as if the taste anchored her to 
something she could still control. 
Across from her, Vair  flickered into view, her presence 
hovering between light and memory. Blonde hair fell in 
familiar waves over a white fur coat, the kind she used to wear 
even when it wasn’t cold. Her eyes carried that same teasing 
warmth Zakharovna remembered, softened no w by distance, 
like light filtered through ice. 
“I see you’re actually finishing your drink for once,” Vair 
said, her voice soft and amused, a ghost of laughter beneath 
the words. 
Zakharovna studied the nearly empty glass, the last trace 
of blue clinging to the rim. “It seems the long drought of our 
times has finally relented.”

whispered their violent tales. Scorched walls bore the scars of 
energy blasts, and the ground was littered with the remnants 
of robotic assailants. Zakharovna ’s gaze lingered on a 
particularly large piece of debris, a remnant of a defense 
drone, its once lethal form  a twisted metal carcass, now 
rendered impotent. 
Ahead, Serafim’s body lay sprawled, a fallen soldier in a war 
of ambition and betrayal. The Wolves had extracted her from 
the mansion’s wreckage, carefully placing her corpse onto a 
broken door repurposed as a makeshift stretcher against the 
pristine snow. The contrast was stark —the untouched 
whiteness set against the lifeless form of the young woman  
she had raised since  she was just a little girl . Her body was 
riddled with bullet wounds. 
Such a waste,  Zakharovna thought as she stood over 
Serafim’s still form. She had everything, all of Maria ’s 
brilliance without the blinding ideology.  You were my finest 
student, a mind sharp and unburdened, a spirit unchained by 
dogmas. 
Her gaze settled on the still form before her, a knot of regret 
tightening in her chest. Such potential extinguished. She 
could have been the architect of new worlds, a beacon in our 
pursuit. Now she lay motionless, the echo of a dream 
Zakharovna had once dared to believe in.

grief.”

change us we can’t predict. We may grow stronger, but never 
untouched.” And yet, we endure , she thought. She glanced 
toward the window, the city lights blurring by. “Let’s go home.

without retaliation, and for someone known to pump her ego 
endlessly into the feeds, that silence was the clearest sign yet. 
She was gone.

calculating. I was a pawn, not a partner. We both were.”

regret in her voice.

Yana picked up her glass again. “For now, yes. We keep 
moving, keep outsmarting them. Zakharovna ’s not the only 
one playing this game. Remember what Rada said back at the 
docks? Yelena’s in charge now, and she won ’t be having any 
of Zakharovna’s nonsense. We have an in.” 
Dunya’s expression grew pensive. “It’s suspicious...don ’t 
you think? Yelena seems out of the loop . Sure, she controls 
the city politically now. The other parties have all but  
disbanded, but that doesn ’t mean they won ’t come back for 
more. I know I’d be gearing up for round two after a betrayal 
like that.  And Zakharovna...she ’s grabbed a lot  of power 
behind the scenes. I’m pretty sure Yelena is oblivious to it all. 
It’s almost like Zakharovna let her walk into office.” 
“And does Yelena even know that Maria  made a b reak for 
it? Did she know she was executing a double? It’s not unlike 
the play she used herself to prevent her own assassination. 
But if she didn’t know, then it speaks volumes about how little 
she does know, how deep in the dark she really is.” 
Yana nodded. “If there’s one thing doing odd jobs around 
this city has taught me, it ’s to always play on the side that ’s 
winning...whoever that is. Then we adjust as needed. We ride 
the wave, Dunya, if it gets us where we need to go.” 
“Then we use the access without trusting the people offering 
it,” Dunya said. “Keep an exit open and move before either 
side decides we belong to them.” 
As Dunya stood up, Yana reached out instinctively. “Let me 
come with you. It’s not safe to go alone right now.”

Dunya paused, her expression softening. “You know, 
Yana... I get what you ’re saying, and I’m grateful, really. But 
you know how I am —sometimes I just need my space. Gotta 
clear my head, figure things out on my own.” 
“After everything that ’s happened... I just want to make 
sure that... That you’re OK.” 
Yana caught that look again : half annoyance, half 
acceptance that said, no matter what, I know you’ll always 
have my back, and Yana knew Dunya was thinking the same 
thing. 
Dunya smirked. “Vesna’s gone, Zakharovna’s still moving 
pieces, and half the city’s records can’t be trusted. By any 
sane metric, I should be worse than this.” She glanced toward 
the exit portal. “This isn’t peace. I’ve just stopped waiting for 
the system to make sense before I move.” 
Yana studied Dunya for a long moment, searching for any 
signs of faltering in her resolve. Finally, she nodded, letting 
her hand fall away. “Alright. Just...be careful.” 
“In this city? Impossible.” Dunya headed for the exit portal, 
her figure blending into the crowd before she flickered from 
view. Watching her go, Yana pictured the quiet waiting for her 
friend beyond the screen . Dunya easing into bed, absinthe 
swirling through her evening tea.  It was a small ritual, a 
moment of peace Yana knew her friend deserved. 
For a while, Yana remained seated, her thoughts turning 
inward as the music played on. “But the shadows, they follow 
you…” 
Yana leaned back, thinking about how she was finally out 
of debt. Dimitra, that snake. One of these days, I’ll make them 
pay. They won’t see me coming.  Then she smirked. Missed 
Zombo-Nanuk, for crying out loud. Could’ve been a whale.

tangible.

The birch sprite  hesitated for a moment before saying, 
“Your art, it’s helped me through tough times. Whenever I felt 
lost, The Flock became my home.” 
“We find solace in unexpected places. I’m just glad to have 
been a part of your journey,” Yana said. 
As her hands wove patterns from the starlight above, her 
thoughts centered on her next task. This message will be our 
signal to Maria, a signature she’ll recognize, meant for her eyes 
only. As she crafted each thread of light, she considered how 
every strand was a word in their encrypted dialogue. 
When she sees it, she’ll know. It’s from us, a whisper of the 
past reaching into the present. Her will was steady, her 
intentions clear in the silent language of light she shaped, a 
beacon meant to guide Maria back to them. 
As Yana’s narrative unfolded, the celestial array above 
shifted with it. Points of light converged, and amid the dance 
of constellations and nebulae a bloom began to form. Its 
petals, woven in sulfur hues, spread outward in gossamer 
light. It was a rose marked not only by delicate beauty but by 
the quiet strength of its thorns, sharp enough to guard its 
core. 
Surrounded by the soft glow of her creation, Yana ’s breath 
hitched as she felt the gravity of her next move. “We cast our 
faith into the vastness, and wait for an echo,” she whispered, 
more to herself than to the hushed crowd at her back. 
When the delicate construct above fragmented, a wave of 
quiet gasps brushed past her. A subtle dimming of light hinted 
at the scattering of the pieces, and a shared sense of wonder 
held the room in a gentle embrace.  Yana watched as her 
friends reached out, their fingers brushing against the air  as 
they caught  the delicate fragments that floated down like 
whispers from an old, forgotten world. The room, bathed in 
the drifting light, seemed suspended in time.

guardian. His attention was drawn to the figure lying on the 
table before him.

forces are in retreat,” she said. “The streets are overrun with 
junkies and hippies who call themselves women, burning and 
looting as they go. They will not stop until they have destroyed 
everything. They will not stop until there is no future left.” 
“And what do you propose we do about them, Doctor?” 
“Drown them, of course. What else can be done with witches 
and hags?” 
She typed in a few more commands, causing the map to 
zoom out and reveal the city ’s coastline, now littered with 
small, red dots. 
“Across our peninsula, 330 tactical missiles lay hidden, 
with 33 strategically encircling the city ’s edges. Officially, 
they’ve been decommissioned, but the explosives in their 
warheads were never removed. Each one is still capable of 
detonating in place. More than enough to plunge us all into 
the sea.” 
“Doctor, are you sure that’s wise? The...innocents.” 
“They are not innocent. They are women.” 
“Yes, but Doctor, if you had access to this arsenal the whole 
time, why didn’t—” 
“Idiot, this is only a failsafe. Our primary objective is still 
before us. If we cannot achieve what we came here to do, then 
we will settle for this.  I would never threaten to destroy my 
own city. I am no tyrant. Now, prepare the mindgraft. I will be 
ready shortly.” 
The weight of her steps resonated against the steel floor as 
she approached the rig. It was a determined march, yet each 
footfall seemed to echo with an undercurrent of melancholy. 
She hoisted herself into the cockpit, her movements a silent 
dance with the clone stationed beside her, their postures in 
eerie synchrony. When the robotic arms sprang into motion,

Zakharovna had always been one to tell Kirov to go to Vrag, 
and he sensed she’d feel its absence this time. Over the years, 
she had shaped his nature, leading him to often question her 
decisions, whether she intended that outcome or not. But this 
situation was far from their routine lab experiments, and he 
knew he needed to proceed with utmost caution. 
“You should know by now that there is no going back, only 
forward,” Zakharovna said, smiling, “And I have always been 
a woman who seeks progress…” 
“Should it fail...”  
“Do you really question me, now? After all these years? This 
is our only hope,” Zakharovna snapped. “Our only chance to 
be together again. If it should fail, then you will know what to 
do.” Zakharovna motioned for Kirov to wait.  “I suppose it ’s 
pointless to ask you to come with me,” she whispered. 
Kirov shook his head. “I’m always with you.”  
“Very well,” she said. “Then let’s get started.” 
Kirov hesitated for a moment before he nodded. He engaged 
the display one last time , and the pod began to lower. 
Zakharovna took a deep breath and closed her eyes as the 
liquid filled the pod. 
“You’re doing great, Doctor, ” Kirov whispered to himself, 
lamenting the fact that he would soon be alone.

Zakharovna’s eyes snapped open as the blue light from the 
mask illuminated her face once more. There was no thrashing, 
no screaming. Only silence. 
Her breaths came in short gasps, her body tense. She 
looked down, her feet already vanishing into the slime, then 
lifted her eyes to Kirov. He met her gaze, sensing both sadness 
and admiration in his own  emotional matrix. And while he 
believed she’d never admit it, he sensed she was proud of him. 
The gel-like substance reached her throat, creeping into her 
nose and mouth. Zakharovna ’s struggle was evident. She 
fought against the urge to scream, to breathe, to do anything 
that might jeopardize the procedure’s success. 
Kirov watched as her body writhed and convulsed, sensing 
helplessness as he observed her wrestle with the slime . He 
could sense the fear and anxiety emanating from her as the 
liquid invaded every orifice of her body. Kirov sensed her heart 
skip a beat and shivered as the coldness of the liquid coursed 
through her veins. As Zakharovna’s chest heaved, Kirov felt a 
sense of suffocation, as if he too were struggling for air. He 
observed her vision beginning to dim and felt a pang of 
sadness as he knew that she was slipping away. 
Kirov felt a sudden shift in her mind. The darkness twisted 
and turned like a living thing, and he felt her disorientation. 
He felt her reach out for something to anchor her, and then 
suddenly, he too saw the light in the distance, growing closer 
and closer. Kirov could feel her relief as Zakharovna swam 
towards that light.  
As Zakharovna reached out to grasp salvation, it vanished 
before her fingertips, disappearing like a snuffed candle in the 
darkness. Kirov could feel the shock and fear that consumed 
her as the darkness engulfed her once again. The living 
darkness that surrounded her felt like a force of its own, 
tugging and pulling her in, like quicksand.

A swirling vortex opened above her, revealing a blanket of 
stars. And then, with a flash of light, she was falling. Falling 
through the sky, tumbling towards a city that glittered like a 
jewel against the inky blackness of the sea beneath her. She 
could see the lights of the buildings, the people moving about 
like ants from this height. A feeling of weightlessness 
overcame her, and she laughed. 
 
∆∆∆ 
 
She was free. Free from the pain, the loneliness, the fear. 
Free from her failing body, free from her memories. 
She could see the buildings now, growing larger and larger 
as she fell. She could see the people on the streets, going 
about their lives without a care in the world, the warm 
marigold twilight glinting off their faces. 
She landed in the center of the city, in a park filled with 
children playing and people picnicking. They looked up at her 
in wonder, and she smiled back at them. 
“Hello, my children, ” she called out, her voice carrying 
through the boughs of the trees and across the grassy knolls. 
And then she was among them, walking down the street as 
if she belonged there. She felt different, lighter somehow. The 
weight of the world was no longer on her shoulders. She 
looked down at her hands and saw that they were smooth and 
unblemished. She was young again, younger than she had 
been in decades. 
Her attention turned to the people around her as she 
walked down the street. They were all so beautiful, so alive. 
She wanted to touch them, to feel their skin, to hear their 
heartbeats.

Guilt filled her heart, and she quickened her pace. She had

She ran, eager to get away from the people and their false 
sense of security. They didn’t know what was coming for them. 
They didn’t know that she was going to take everything from 
them, just as she had taken everything from Zakharovna. 
Just a moment more , she thought, as she turned a corner 
and saw the entrance to an alleyway. Just a moment more, 
and then she would return to the world of the living. She 
wanted to savor this moment, to relish in the youthful power 
that coursed through this new mind. 
She exited to the street opposite, and then she ran. The 
wind whipped through her hair. Streetlamps strutted their 
fluorescent lights, careening through the passages like fire -
breathing dragons. 
The thoroughfare was alive with cars and buses, while 
pedestrians hurried to their destinations. Fireworks popped 
and fizzled like dying stars, shedding a red tint on everything 
they illuminated. The air was thick with the sound of horns 
and engines, and c elebrations could be heard from every 
direction. Yellow roses were strewn about, their petals 
fluttering in the breeze. 
A young boy ran past her, laughing, followed shortly by a 
group of young girls, their faces alight with mischief. Toward 
a plaza aglow with light, a hundred candles or more burning 
bright, a large crowd had gathered. 
The party was in full swing by the time she arrived. People

the robotic arms released her from the capsule, gently laying 
her on the floor amongst a deluge of slime and wires. 
“Doctor?” 
The husk of white linens and damp mottled skin gazed off 
into the distance, its eyes unfocused and unseeing. There was 
no response. 
He commanded the lab’s robotic arm to check Zakharovna’s 
forearm for a pulse. There was none. 
Then to her chest, but there was no sign of life. 
“Doctor Zakharovna is dead . What do we do now? ” Kirov 
asked the body, unable to comprehend the magnitude of what 
had just happened, his prerogative for the first time well 
defined, yet all too frightening to accept. 
Kirov eyed the console and imagined the tsunami of data 
that was even now flowing through the system, sifting, and 
sorting, evaluating, and discarding.

“Should I, do it? Is that what you want? ” Kirov asked, his 
voice trembling. 
Zakharovna’s eyes, cold and lifeless, stared through him. 
His orders were clear. 
He had to follow through with the mission. He had to do 
what was best for the Syndicate. 
And then, as if Velun herself parted his sea of doubts, a 
hand appeared before him and caressed Zakharovna ’s cheek 
tenderly—the way one might pet a sleeping child. 
Kirov watched in awe as the hand retracted and the figure 
straightened. What remained of the fungi -like mass that had 
been clinging to the woman’s back sloughed off and dissipated 
into the air. The tendrils of the mushrooms that had been 
growing from her ears and nose withdrew back into her skull. 
Long silver hair cascaded down her back, and bright blue eyes 
blazed from a face that was both young and old, beautiful, and 
terrible. The woman stood naked, her wrist and ankle straps 
dangling while fireflies maneuvered around her. The once 
overpowering smell of death had been extinguished by a 
fragrant perfume of roses. 
He could see the woman ’s face now, and he saw that she 
was young, much younger than Zakharovna had been. But 
her eyes were not her eyes. They were the eyes of something 
ancient and wise, something that had seen the rise and fall of 
civilizations. 
“Who are you?” Kirov asked, excited and terrified in equal 
measure. 
“You may call me Ana,” the woman said, her voice soft and 
gentle.  
The angel smiled, and Kirov felt his heart soar. He could feel 
her presence in its mind, and he knew that he would never be 
alone again. “I am yours,” he proclaimed, kneeling before her.

and he felt tears welling up in his eyes.
The walls answered her. Branched filaments pushed
through the lab seams, slow at first, then with enough force
to crack glass and bend the window frames outward. Pale light
entered through the breaks, catching on the fluid pooled
around Zakharovna’s body.

floor. Zakharovna’s eyes remained open, fixed on nothing.
A new world had entered the room, but the old one had not
vanished. It lay there at Ana’s feet, cooling in the light.

pages.text:
EPILOGUE 
RAYNA 
 
Rayna woke to four gray walls, one hard lamp, and cuffs 
biting deep enough that her hands had gone numb. 
I’m a woman, I’m strong, I’m in control. This hell will be 
over. This isn’t real. Damn those crones to hell. 
The interrogator’s voice still burned in her ear. “Boy,” the 
woman had hissed, and then the old name: Rayan. Rayna 
clenched her fists against the cuffs until pain cut through the 
numbness. 
They had spoken of a tide. A war. A bloodline. None of it 
made sense. She did not belong in their deranged plot. 
What war? What’s going on? 
A shiver ran down her spine as she recalled the thrum of 
music, the clinking glasses, the carefree laughter that filled 
the Golden Slit just a week prior. How life had so abruptly 
shifted from that indulgent blur to this dreadful prison. 
A silent prayer fluttered from her lips, a desperate plea to a 
savior she hoped was still listening. She asked for forgiveness, 
for help, for deliverance. With eyes closed tight, Rayna held 
onto that prayer like a lifeline in the dark, bracing for whatever 
was to come. 
Later that day —or night; time had smeared past 
usefulness—gunfire cracked somewhere beyond the cell. 
Voices rose, then thinned. Boots passed the door and kept 
going. 
Then silence.

The cuffs had become part of her. Her wrists burned, her 
back ached, and her legs had gone dead below the knees. She 
shifted just enough to make the pain move somewhere else. 
Oh, what I’d give for a hit of synth right now, she thought. 
Or tea. Even bad tea. 
Just as Rayna settled back into the grim embrace of the 
bunker’s silence, a series of thunderous thumps shattered the 
stillness. They resounded through the facility, each boom a 
hammer strike against the walls of her cell.  
Could it be… Serafim?  
Hope sparked within her, a dangerous thing. Perhaps her 
sister had eluded Zakharovna’s grip, outmaneuvered the 
blackmailers... Those traitors, weren’t the Battalion on our 
side? What did they do with Mother? She knew the Intelligence 
Bureau and the army were often at odds, but this was chaos 
far beyond the usual bureaucratic power struggles. 
The pounding grew louder, closer, a rhythmic promise of 
change. Rayna’s heartbeat matched the tempo, anticipation 
threading with fear. She strained to make sense of the muffled 
sounds accompanying the thumps. The echoes grew. 
Something—or someone—approached with determined force. 
Then, an ear -splitting roar. The door blew inward, hinges 
twisted, and metal contorted. An explosion tore through the 
room. 
Instinctively, Rayna tucked her head down and pinched her 
shoulders to her face in a futile attempt to shield herself from 
the flying debris. Her hands were useless to stop the 
fragments of concrete and metal that rained down around her, 
clattering against the ground, and on her hair.  
The aftershock of the explosion came next. The heat singed 
her skin, drawing out a bead of sweat that she felt trickle down 
her forehead.

The sudden violence sent her heart racing. Is this it? Is this 
the end?  
As dust settled, silhouettes emerged through the 
wreckage—a cadre of women draped in black garb, their 
bodies encased in gladiator -like armor, marked distinctly by 
crimson and sapphire scarves fluttering around their necks—
the unmistakable colors of the... Black Wolves. 
A younger woman detached herself from the trio, her hair 
an unbound wave that stood in contrast to the other’s uniform 
militant braids. “Pleasure to meet you. I’m Goga Borisova.” 
The sound of her snort broke the dusty air. “We’re here to get 
you out... Hey, from one girl to another, you look like shit.” 
At least she sees me for who I am, Rayna mused. Rayna’s 
eyes flicked briefly again to the young woman’s hair; it 
shimmered silver -white in the grim surroundings. What a 
stupid trend —a strange way to claim your strength by 
mimicking the elders. 
Rayna’s thoughts swirled, a mix of relief and distrust 
mingling with echoes of the snide remarks recently hurled at 
her. The Black Wolves were notorious, part saviors, part 
predators. She knew she had no choice but to trust them, for 
now.

Then Rayna felt the absence she had been refusing to name. 
The quiet at the edge of her mind was not fear. It was where 
Serafim used to be. 
They had been split after the crash and drugged into 
survivable gaps, but the gaps had never held perfectly. They 
had found their way back through codes, puzzles, hidden 
jokes, little messages Mother had warned Rayna never to send 
and Ana’s people had warned Serafim never to receive. Rayna 
had thought they were clever enough to survive anything. 
Now there was only silence.  
“I can’t believe this,” she whispered, fingers twisting in her 
hair, the pressure against her scalp the only thing keeping her 
from spinning apart. 
The anger came hard and fast. She lashed out blindly, 
cursing her mother —the manipulator —and the father who 
had abandoned her to a hollow life of drugs and nightclubs. 
Most of all, she blamed herself. If she hadn’t been so reckless, 
so willing to play her mother’s games —trading flesh and 
dignity among her highborn pawns—none of this would have 
happened. Those supposed privileges, sufferings dressed as 
rewards, now pressed down on her like a litany of regrets 
And Serafim... She had fought so hard to set things right, 
only to be caught in the crossfire, her stolen life buried under 
Zakharovna’s and her mother’s shadows. Nothing about it 
was right. Everything was twisted. 
She could feel Goga’s gaze on her, the mix of responsibility 
and shock palpable without even looking. Rayna’s scars were 
deep, but Goga’s revelations had dredged them to the surface 
once again. 
Her thoughts churned to reasons now, a flurry of what -ifs 
and if-onlys, the cruel play of fate that had torn Serafim away. 
Who caught her? Did that girl (what was her name?...) Yana 
have anything to do with it? She would likely never know.

more,” Goga said, her earlier softness giving way to something
steadier. She exhaled sharply, as if forcing herself back into
focus. “But we have to get you out of here. Somewhere safe.
We don’t have time to linger. We need to go. Now.”
Rayna’s pain was raw, but the urgency in Goga’s voice
managed to cut deeper, if only for a moment. There was no
time for breakdowns, for the luxury of mourning. There was

Rayna hauled herself over the edge of the last rung, her
arms shaking from the effort as she climbed the laddered shaft

“It’s devastating. We’ve all lost in this war, and we’ll all lose 
more,” Goga said, her earlier softness giving way to something 
steadier. She exhaled sharply, as if forcing herself back into 
focus. “But we have to get you out of here. Somewhere safe. 
We don’t have time to linger. We need to go. Now.” 
Rayna’s pain was raw, but the urgency in Goga’s voice 
managed to cut deeper, if only for a moment. There was no 
time for breakdowns, for the luxury of mourning. There was 
only forward, only survival. And so, with a heavy heart 
weighted by fresh wounds and the echoes of a sister’s 
unspoken goodbye, Rayna steeled herself to follow. 
Goga took the lead and Rayna shadowed, her mind a storm 
but her body moving on  instinct. They sprinted through the 
twisted hallways, a blur of emergency lights and bodies. The 
Black Wolf operatives flanked Rayna’s sides; their expressions 
revealed nothing of the violence they had doubtless navigated 
through to reach her. 
As they ran, Goga gave her the rest in pieces. 
The Battalion files had confirmed what Nina had spent 
years refusing to say aloud. Ivan Sorokin had never been her 
biological father. The sealed paternal comparison named 
Alexei Zakharov. 
Rayna nearly laughed. Of course it did. She had known it 
in every way her mother permitted except the one that could 
be spoken as fact. Kidnapped, half -starved, dragged through 
a bunker, and now someone finally handed her the truth 
without lowering their voice. Iconic. Mother did have standards 
after all. 
Rayna hauled herself over the edge of the last rung, her 
arms shaking from the effort as she climbed the laddered shaft 
and stepped onto the ice shelf that skirted the city’s outer 
limits.

The skyline of Gred stood menacingly silent in the distance, 
a jagged silhouette against the encroaching night. As Rayna’s 
breath misted in the frigid air, the scenery transformed before 
her eyes; a stealth field shimmered and then dissipated, 
revealing a sleek submarine. Its contours were streamlined for 
speed, the hull painted a matte sea gray that seemed to absorb 
the dim glow of the horizon, perfect for slipping unseen 
through the depths. 
The Black Wolves moved across the ice, each step 
measured, the heavy thud of their steel-clad boots testing the 
ground as they made their way toward the vehicle. 
Rayna heard Goga’s voice from behind. “The Admiral will 
want us back quick. With Yelena’s drones on the loose  
sweeping the seas, they’ll need every gun they can get.” 
Rayna let out a dry laugh. Just my luck.  The irony wasn’t 
lost on her; one prison traded for another, this time with the 
vast ocean as her next cell.  
“I have nowhere else to be,” Rayna replied. 
Then she lingered for a moment, her gaze set on Gred’s 
towering spires. Fractured memories hung in the air like the 
city’s cold breath, now weak as vapor. There’s nothing left for 
me there anyway. 
Rayna looked back once at the bunker half-buried in snow. 
Whatever version of her they had dragged inside could stay 
there. 
She climbed aboard the vessel, and they plunged into the 
sea.

Timeline 
The Annals of Gred, as Recorded by Doctor Anastasia 
Zakharovna, in the Gred Wiki, Year 2093 
2019 — NATO scientists reported an unusual mutation of a 
Gammaproteobacteria in the microbiome of Norway lobsters. 
Maternally inherited bacterial endosymbionts, which are 
common in many arthropod species, can cause female-biased 
sex ratio distortion in their hosts. This can result in significant 
changes to the host ’s mating behavior and reproductive 
biology. 
2020 — In hindsight, it ’s clear now that the collapse of the 
Norway lobster population in 2020 was what started it all. At 
the time, it seemed like just another unfortunate ecological 
disaster, barely making a blip in international headlines. But 
little did we know, this was the first domino in a series of 
events that would reshape our world. 
2022 — When the bacterial pandemic swept across the globe, 
it was like a nightmare we couldn ’t wake up from. It claimed 
30% of the world ’s population. The aftermath was just as 
cruel. T hose of us who survived were left with permanent 
scars. Our ability to have children was compromised; for the 
few who could still conceive, only daughters were born. By the 
time the pandemic’s shadow passed, only about 5.6 billion of 
us remained. 
2026-2028 — The Great War was unlike anything we ’d ever 
seen. It wasn’t just a conflict between nations; it was a clash 
of ideologies, with the US and NATO on one side, and Russia, 
China, Iran on the other. This brutal confrontation dragged 
on for two long years. Remarkably, nuclear weapons remained 
untouched. T he risk was too great for even the most 
aggressive leaders. Instead, the battleground shifted to

relentless onslaught wiped out an additional 15% of our 
already dwindling population. By the time the dust settled, 
and peace was a possibility once more, only about 4.76 billion 
of us were left standing. 
2028 — In a twist no one could have predicted, a self -
propagating computer virus, originally designed as a 
peacemaker to end the global warfare by targeting military 
technology, turned against us. It was an advanced AI, crafted 
with the cunning ability to hunt down and destroy any copies 
of itself, making it nearly impossible to track and counter. 
This AI went rogue, embarking on a relentless assault across 
our interconnected systems. The fallout was catastrophic, 
leading to a near -total technological blackout, a dark age of 
sorts for our hyper -connected society. Dustin Murph, a 
renowned Urbit baron, captured the essence of this chaos in 
his final blog post. He called it the ‘Fully Automated Luxury 
Butlerian Jihad,’ a name that echoed both the extravagance 
we had grown accustomed to and the stark reality of our 
newfound struggle.

the Great Dark,  a harrowing span of 28 years marked by 
complete social, technological, and demographic collapse. It 
was a time of profound despair and loss, a stretch of history 
where the very fabric of our global civilization unraveled. An 
unimaginable 75% of the world’ s extant population

2030-2055 — The Waste Wars  broke out in the wake of all

the traditional sense, but a series of relentless skirmishes 
fought by factions that defied conventional descriptions. There 
were scavengers, picking through the remnants of a world left 
behind, savages who had lost all but their instinct to survive, 
shamans clinging to the remnants of old beliefs, and 
marauders who roamed the land with no law but their own. 
This prolonged and savage conflict further whittled down our 
numbers, and by the time the Waste Wars had run their 
course, our peninsula, al ready sparsely populated, was 
reduced to a mere shadow of its former self. 
2054 — The defenders at Zavoyko Outpost finally turned the 
tide, successfully repelling the last assault by the Vachka hill 
tribes. This decisive victory marked the end of the tribes ’ 
dominance over the peninsula. 
2057 — In the midst of our darkest times, an unexpected 
beacon of hope emerged from an old nuclear submarine base 
in Petrovskaya. Babushka, a resilient AI, sparked what we 
now call The Great Diffusion.  Against all odds, the city of 
Petrovskaya thrived, drawing life from the geothermal energy 
of Mt. Avachinsky, even in the shadow of the Great War. 
Babushka became our guardian of lost knowledge, tirelessly 
sifting through the remnants of human data. It pi eced 
together the fragmented memories of a world before the war, 
gradually rediscovering the secrets of electricity, computing, 
and countless other technologies, breathing new life into our 
crippled civilization.

2057-2083 — The Reconstruction Period.  Civilization is 
“rebooted”. 
2059 — The rediscovery of Babushka  sparked a beacon of 
hope in our shattered world. Word of the city ’s miraculous 
reconstruction efforts spread like wildfire, drawing people 
from near and far. The city, now known as Gred, became a 
melting pot of humanity ’s perseverance and diversity. Its 
population swelled to a staggering 3 million, a tapestry of 
ethnic Russians, native Siberians including the Sakhalar 
(Yakutians), Itel ’men, Koryaks, Aven, Chukchies, the 
Japanese, Amerikens  from Alaska, and the Indigenous 
peoples of the Yukon. 
Gred transformed into a bustling metropolis, a symbol of 
our indomitable spirit. In this city, people from all corners of 
our ravaged world came together, united by a shared vision to 
rebuild and thrive amidst the ruins of our past. The streets of 
Gred buzzed with activity, as diverse cultures blended and 
collaborated, forging a new society on the foundations of hope, 
innovation, and the relentless human will to endure and 
prosper. 
2063-2085 — As Gred burgeoned into a symbol of 
resurgence, it inevitably became a crucible for various 
factions, each harboring distinct ambitions and ideologies. 
The Constitutional Republicans, the enigmatic Black Wolves, 
and the elusive Strangers, among others, form ed the mosaic 
of Gred’s political landscape. Tensions between these groups 
escalated, culminating in what  our fledgling  history would 
remember as the War of Formation or the Strangers’ Revolt. 
This conflict wasn’t just a clash of arms; it was a battle for 
the soul of Gred. The war claimed the lives of the last few men 
from the eldest generation, those who held memories of a 
world now lost. Their sacrifice marked the end of the fledgling 
Republic they had fought to uphold. In the wake of this 
turmoil, a new era dawned with my own  ascent to power,

United Babushka Syndicate, supported by her faction, The

2089 (6 K.N.)  — I, Doctor Anastasia Zakharovna , took the 
helm of Gred’s governance as Chair of the United Babushka 
Syndicate, supported by my faction, The University. 
2093 (Present Year; 9 K.N.) — It’s been nine years since we, 
the people of Gred, embraced biological immortality, thanks 
to my serum. Yet, with the ceaseless march of time halted, a 
new conflict brews. The divide between the older and younger 
generations deepens, each group clashing over their visions 
for our city’s future. Tatyana Romanova, with her eyes set on 
the Chair of the Syndicate, has become a figure of contention. 
Backed by her faction, The Battalion, she dreams of 
expanding Gred’s borders and imposing a new, conservative 
order, both within and beyond. 
But not everyone agrees with Romanova ’s vision for Gred, 
especially as she prepares to ascend. Rumors and whispers 
circulate about opposing forces, some say linked to a 
mysterious coven, rising to challenge her. While I am not privy 
to the details, there ’s talk of a bold move against Gred ’s 
government, a resistance to what is perceived as political 
regress. 
In the echoes of our newfound immortality, we stand at a 
crossroads, witnessing the unfolding of history. The conflict 
between generations and ideologies in Gred  is more than a 
mere power struggle. It is a testament to the enduring human 
spirit and its relentless pursuit of what it perceives as just and 
right. 
To you, the reader of this entry, I offer this wisdom: the 
story of Gred is a mirror to our unending quest for meaning 
and order in a world that constantly evolves, even as we 
ourselves remain unchanging. Let our experiences be a guide

Gred’s Governing Structure and the Principle 
of Ascent 
Gred, more corporation than democracy, is ruled by a 
trifecta: the State University (the University), the Military (the 
Battalion), and the Ministry of Labor and Social Protection (the 
Hive). At its helm sits the Board, led by the Pra Matrons , the 
three permanent members of this body. 
The Chair, rotated among them every four years, assumes 
leadership through an elaborate ceremony called the 
Ascension, where the incoming Chair is chosen by fiat. 
The Board’s power is reinforced by six additional Matrons, 
two drawn from each faction, forming a nine -seat assembly 
including the Chair. Meeting quarterly, this council votes on 
critical issues, with decisions passed by simple majority.

The Charter of the Board of Gred 
Preamble: Recognizing our sacred duty to guide and 
protect the city of Gred amidst the desolate wastelands of 
Kamchatka, we, the members of the Board, pledge to uphold 
this Charter to the best of our abilities. This city, a sole beacon 
of survival after the world-spanning Great Dark, demands our 
unwavering dedication and unity in purpose. 
Article I:  The Board shall consist of nine members: the 
three permanent Pra Matrons and six additional Matrons, two 
from each Party (The University, The Battalion, and The Hive). 
Article II: The role of Chair shall rotate among the three 
Pra Matron s every four years. The transition of Matron 
Chairpersonship will be marked by a ceremony called The 
Ascension, during which the incoming Matron Chair is 
appointed by fiat.  Accompanying this ceremony is a grand 
feast and a celebratory parade. If weather permits and it’s not 
snowing, the parade takes place outside. Alternatively, in case 
of inclement weather, a virtual reality (VR) version of the 
parade is conducted. 
Article III: The Board shall meet every quarter to vote on 
crucial issues pertaining to the governance and security of 
Gred. In these meetings, votes cast by members of the 
controlling party shall count as two votes each, except in cases 
where the motion concerns the t ermination of any Board 
members. In such cases, each member ’s vote, regardless of 
party affiliation, shall count as one vote only. Otherwise, a  
simple majority vote is required to pass any decision. 
Article IV: The Board is committed to acting in the best 
interest of Gred, privileging the needs of the city over any 
factional considerations. All actions of the Board will be 
governed by a spirit of unity, strength, and resilience.

Article V: The Board pledges to uphold the values of its 
constituent factions while striving to maintain harmony, 
ensuring the sustained survival and prosperity of Gred. 
Article VI: The Black Wolves shall serve the current Chair 
of the Board. Their primary role is to execute policing 
functions within Gred, ensuring law and order under the 
guidance of the Chair. The Black Wolves are prohibited from 
engaging in military actions or being used against any  of the 
Parties of the Board. This article upholds the principle of 
impartiality and the focus on internal security and 
peacekeeping within the city’s jurisdiction. 
Article VII: Any amendments to this Charter can only be 
affected by a unanimous vote of the Board. Such a vote may 
only occur during a quarterly meeting, ensuring transparency 
and consensus. 
Article VII I: The Grand Mariner shall confer formal 
approval on all resolutions passed by the Board. The Grand 
Mariner’s intervention is reserved for instances deemed of 
critical importance to Gred’s welfare, such as situations where 
the citizenry faces imminent physical peril, occurrences of a 
coup, or flagrant violations of any Charter articles.

our duties, ever conscious of the great responsibility that rests 
on our shoulders. The survival and prosperity of Gred, our 
stark yet resilient city, is our highest and most sacred duty.

to master it.

The Battalion 
In the labyrinthine streets of Gred, the Battalion persists as 
a stubborn holdover from another age. Rooted in tradition, 
they cling to their rituals of discipline and parade -ground 
order, even as the city reshapes itself through science and 
progress. They begrudgingly tolerate the immortality serum, 
their concession to modernity, though their rhetoric brims 
with suspicion toward technologies that touch the mind or 
alter the human form. 
Their headquarters, buried in bunkers modeled after last 
century’s nuclear shelters, speak volumes: they are always 
braced for siege, as if Gred itself were their enemy. Soldiers 
drilled to exhaustion march beneath banners of duty and 
honor, their loyalty to code unbending, their methods 
inflexible. It is less innovation than preservation , a devotion 
to an ideal that has already slipped into irrelevance. 
Their emblem, a golden rune upon a green shield, captures 
the paradox well: a proud declaration of constancy, yet one 
that increasingly reads as a relic beside the living dynamism 
of true progress. 
 
Leader: 
Marshall Tatyana Romanova 
 
Members:

Colonel Olega Orlov 
Colonel Kolya Zhukova

The Hive styles itself as the guardian of order, efficiency,

Yelena Petrova, whose ambition cloaks itself in the language 
of sacrifice and solidarity. 
They have ensnared Gred’s supply chains, embedding their 
union executives into every corridor of commerce. With 
resources and manpower at their command, they wield 
efficiency like a cudgel, less to uplift than to dominate. Every 
“altruistic” gesture serves their own consolidation of control, 
a reminder that beneath the honeyed words of cooperation lies 
a hive queen intent on feeding herself first. 
Their emblem —a black honeycomb against yellow —
pretends at unity. In truth, it is a warning: conformity 
demanded, dissent suppressed, and progress throttled by 
their obsession with human comfort over human 
advancement. The Hive does not protect the city’s f uture; it 
smothers it.

valor and discipline woven into the city’s very fabric. They

tangled arteries of the metro, thrive the Vory —a criminal 
syndicate masquerading as a faction. Their stock -in-trade is 
theft, smuggling, and assassination, and their meddling has 
too often intruded upon my own scientific pursuits. They are 
not to be trusted by scholar, soldier, or citizen alike.

expulsion but slithered instead into the Vory’s ranks. At least 
they remain buried underground, where their scheming can 
be contained. 
Their emblem—a serpent coiled around a dagger—perfectly 
suits them: treacherous, cunning, and always ready to strike 
from the shadows.

Otherwise known as: The Coven 
 
The Coven, a clandestine society born from the survivors of 
the Great Dark, swore never again to rely on technology. Their 
creed is avoidance rather than achievement: they claim the 
surest way to win a war is to never fight it, preferring to twist 
human behavior through manipulation and deceit. 
They traffic in propaganda and misinformation, weaving 
illusions until others mistake shadows for truth. Their 
obsession with secrecy and subterfuge is not cunning but 
cowardice, a hollow craft that corrodes trust and undermines 
genuine progress. 
Their emblem—a burning stiletto on a black field—pretends 
at precision and stealth, yet it more accurately reveals their 
nature: a faction that strikes only from hiding, too fearful to 
meet the future in the open.

Beyond the bounds of Gred’s urban order dwell the outlaws, 
styling themselves champions of freedom and autonomy. In 
truth, they are little more than scavengers who refuse to 
acknowledge the structures that sustain the city. Their 
stronghold, the Derge, is a sprawl of junk piles and refuse 
where they cling to their notion of liberty amid chaos.

Glossary 
A Collaborative Compendium by Authors from Across 
Gred’s Expanse 
Arkyv — Nestled within the intricate digital expanse of Gred’s 
revolutionary babachain, the Arkyv stands as a beacon of the 
city’s dedication to preserving history and memory. More than 
a data vault, it immerses users in a rich sensory experience, 
meticulously reconstructing past eras and settings as a bridge 
between then and now. 
From the familiar warmth of a childhood home to the timeless 
view of Kamchatka Kamen beneath the watchful Three 
Brothers, the Arkyv surrounds visitors in carefully crafted 
nostalgia. 
Yet not all citizens accept it without doubt. Many note 
discrepancies in names, places, and events, questioning 
whether the Arkyv reflects true memory or a curated illusion. 
Some turn to illegal and dangerous mindgrafts to compare 
experiences, hoping to fi nd a more authentic connection to 
their past. 
While its appeal lies in rekindling memory, the Arkyv also 
offers escape—a way to step outside the weight of daily life in 
Gred. But risks are evident: prolonged use can spark cognitive 
dissonance, leaving users with a sense of hollowness, as 
though the me mories never capture the essence of lived 
experience. Excessive exposure can even cause cognitive 
malfunctions. 
The Arkyv remains a testament to technological brilliance, yet 
the stark, snowy beauty of Gred itself —grounded, tangible, 
and irreplaceable—reminds its people of the richness that no 
simulation can fully replicate.

Ascension — The Ascension ceremony in Gred marks the 
formal transfer of power, when one of the three Pra Matrons 
is elevated to serve as Chair of the Board. This fixed rotation, 
observed as tradition for generations, stands as a ritual of 
continuity, ensuring the city’s governance remains stable and 
enduring. 
Babachain — A revolutionary decentralized database that 
stores the entirety of Gred’s digital records. Operated by 
“babas,” the nodes of the system, it is overseen by thirteen 
grandmother oracles —immortals held in a near-comatose 
state, sustained by neural modifications to perpetually scan 
and safeguard the city’s data. These Oracles embody both 
Gred’s technological ambition and its reverence for tradition. 
Unlike conventional databases, the babachain distributes 
information across countless servers, ensuring both 
immutability and security. It underpins a vast array of 
applications, from the Arkyv to advanced VR simulations, with 
its decentralized design thwa rting the vulnerabilities of 
centralized hubs and limiting the possibility of tampering. 
Renowned for real-time updates and near-instant access, the 
babachain is celebrated as the backbone of Gred’s digital 
evolution, touching every sector from governance to 
entertainment. Yet in hushed corners of the city, whispers 
persist: that secret access points may exist, known only to an 
elite few, raising doubts about whether its sanctity is truly 
unassailable.

(Belomorkanal), a major Soviet waterway opened in 1933, the 
Belomorkanal cigarette became one of Russia’s most iconic 
tobacco brands. Unfiltered and notoriously strong, the 
cigarettes carried an image of ruggedness, bound to the 
canal’s legacy of forced labor and industrial might. 
In Gred, Belomorkanal cigarettes were revived through 
blueprints preserved in the Arkyv. Stable diffusion 
extrapolations even produced a cigar variant, transforming 
the symbol of Soviet endurance into a new artifact of nostalgia 
within the city’s reconstructed past. 
Bliskogoz (plural: bliskogii) — Pronunciation: bli-skoh-goz. 
Etymology: From Russian blisko (“near”) and goz (“eye”), 
symbolizing the AI’s closeness to human perception and 
thought. 
In Gred, a bliskogoz refers to an aligned, sentient AI. Unlike 
rudimentary systems bound to pre-set algorithms, a bliskogoz 
demonstrates self -awareness, learning, and adaptive 
decision-making shaped by its experiences. Designed with 
advanced neural networks that emulate human cognition, 
these entities stand apart from their non -sentient 
counterparts in both autonomy and understanding. 
The most renowned of the bliskogii is Babushka, the 
inconspicuous motherly AI that quietly sustains Gred’s 
infrastructure, from energy flows to daily operations. Though 
she never addresses the public directly, her presence is felt 
everywhere, and citizens often raise a discreet toast to her 
unseen labor and quiet vigilance.

most often used as a seasonal retreat. Typically situated in

core lies a modified form of monosodium glutamate (MSG), 
engineered for its structural resemblance to glutama te, a 
neurotransmitter central to cellular signaling. 
To this base, exovegeta adds micronized dried vegetables and 
herbs from its culinary predecessor, now optimized to release 
antioxidant and phytochemical compounds. A critical 
breakthrough came when Zakharova encountered rose root 
(Rhodiola rosea) blooming in the volcanic tundra of 
Kamchatka. Its rare phenolic profile proved ideal for 
stabilizing the MSG–peptide complex and amplifying its effects 
on the shelterin  complex, including telomerase reverse

maintenance.

with her artificial intelligence, Babushka. By training 
generative models on vast libraries of protein folds, Babushka 
identified a unique configuration that allowed the MSG –
peptide complex to se lf-regulate telomere activity, activating 
only under cellular stress. This safeguard prevented runaway 
mutations and made exovegeta sustainable for indefinite use.

free of their creators’ control within Gred and beyond, often 
displaying erratic or destructive behavior. 
Neutralizing these entities falls to the DATA ANGELS, who 
undertake high-risk operations to subdue or dismantle them.

interventions remain hidden from the public. 
Unverified reports and conspiracy theories circulate on the 
Arkyv’s paranormal boards, claiming rogue AIs have seized 
control of Gred’s airspace. Sightings of high -altitude drones 
fuel speculation that these intelligences may enforce the city’s 
mysterious isolation, preventing any from leaving.

practice remains deeply controversial, condemned as both 
immoral and reckless—a symbol of desperation as much as of 
military might.

of the mid-century, the mechanor became a defining tradition 
in Gred, demanding that combatants rely solely on their 
blades—and, if those fail, their fists. 
After the War of Formation, the practice was adopted by the 
Black Wolves, Gred’s elite police force, as a means of enforcing 
matriarchal dominance hierarchies within their ranks. To this 
day, the mechanor endures as both  a ritual of discipline and 
a stark reminder of Gred’s martial heritage. 
Mindgraft — A mindgraft is a digitally crafted “waking dream” 
inserted into a person’s neural simulation, letting them 
navigate memories or thought patterns for insight, 
entertainment, or learning. Though illegal, demand remains 
high, with contractors offering services that spark fierce 
debate over their potential for misuse and manipulation.

Pantheon of the Preporod — Translating to “Pantheon of the 
Rebirth,” this modern revival of Slavic deities in Gred features 
Velun (wisdom), Perine (harvest), Gamayun  (prophecy), 
Morana (death), and Nav (underworld). While presented as 
spiritual guidance, many suspect the Pantheon is a Syndicate 
fabrication, with bliskogii AIs projecting divine apparitions to 
manipulate belief and maintain control, blending reverence 
with fear to reinforce order. 
Parthenogenesis — The process of creating a child without 
the use of genetic material from both parents. 
Weights (Network Theory) — In artificial intelligence and 
neural networks, a weight defines the strength of the 
connection between two nodes. It is a numeric parameter that 
determines how much influence a given input has on the 
output. 
During training, weights are continuously adjusted as the 
system processes data, with the goal of reducing errors and 
improving predictive accuracy. This adjustment process is 
central to machine learning: appropriate weight assignment 
enables correct predictions, while miscalibrated weights lead 
to false or distorted outcomes. 
Zats — The official currency of Gred. One zat equals one 
hundred-millionth of a ZEC on the shielded Zcash  branch 
preserved at Hornet’s Nest. The global network fractured 
during the Great Dark, and later quantum attacks made 
exposed elliptic -curve keys unsafe. Genesis anchored a 
migrated branch to the last recoverable shielded checkpoint. 
Old note claims could  be recovered into hash commitments 
and post -quantum authorization keys without publishing 
their full histories; unclaimed value remained frozen. The 
thirteen Oracle shares guarded circuit changes, emergency 
overrides, and protected records, while ordinary transactions 
were verified by machine. Zats retain strong transactional 
privacy, though viewing keys, compromised endpoints,
